# Percona Operator for MongoDB

> Percona Operator for MongoDB deploys and manages Percona Server for MongoDB replica sets and sharded clusters on Kubernetes, with backups, scaling, upgrades and monitoring.

Each page below is also available as markdown. For the documentation of all Percona products, see https://docs.percona.com/llms.txt.

# Overview

# Percona Operator for MongoDB

The Percona Operator for MongoDB runs and manages Percona Server for MongoDB inside Kubernetes for you. You describe the database you want (for example how many nodes, where to store backups), and the Operator keeps the cluster running that way: it creates the right pods, handles failures, and applies upgrades when you ask for them.

**Why use it?** You get a production-ready MongoDB cluster on Kubernetes without wiring every detail yourself. The Operator handles provisioning, scaling, backups, and high availability so you can focus on building your application or operating the platform.

[Get started](#get-started) [What’s new in version 1.23.1](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/RN/Kubernetes-Operator-for-PSMONGODB-RN1.23.1.html)

What’s coming next

See what the team is working on in the [public roadmap](https://github.com/orgs/percona/projects/10/views/1) , and when to expect it in the [release timeline](https://github.com/orgs/percona/projects/10/views/10) .

# About

# Design and architecture

This section explains how Percona Operator for MongoDB is built: what runs in your Kubernetes cluster, which component is responsible for what, and how the pieces interact. Read it to build a mental model of the system, and come back to it when something fails and you need to know where to look first. If something is failing now, start with [Initial troubleshooting](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/debug.html). The [Glossary](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/glossary.html) explains the Kubernetes and MongoDB terms used in this section.

## What the Operator is

The Operator is a Kubernetes controller that runs as a Deployment named `percona-server-mongodb-operator`. It extends the Kubernetes API with four [Custom Resources](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/glossary.html#custom-resource):

| Custom Resource                   | Short name          | Describes                                                          |
| --------------------------------- | ------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `PerconaServerMongoDB`            | `psmdb`             | The database cluster: a replica set or a sharded cluster           |
| `PerconaServerMongoDBBackup`      | `psmdb-backup`      | One backup                                                         |
| `PerconaServerMongoDBRestore`     | `psmdb-restore`     | One restore                                                        |
| `PerconaServerMongoDBClusterSync` | `psmdb-clustersync` | Data migration and replication from an external MongoDB deployment |

You install the [CustomResourceDefinitions (CRDs)](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/glossary.html#crd) together with the Operator. Then you describe the database that you want in a `PerconaServerMongoDB` object using the `deploy/cr.yaml` example manifest. The Operator creates and maintains everything that the cluster needs. The Operator manages only the clusters that these objects describe. It doesn’t manage MongoDB deployments created in other ways.

The Operator works as a [reconcile loop](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/glossary.html#reconcile): about every five seconds it compares the Custom Resource with what runs in Kubernetes and in the database, and changes whatever differs. So you [change the cluster through the Custom Resource](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/architecture-responsibilities.html#change-the-cluster-through-the-custom-resource), not through the objects the Operator creates. For what the Operator takes care of and what stays with you, see [Who owns what](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/architecture-responsibilities.html#the-operator). For when it acts and in which order, see [How the Operator reacts to changes](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/architecture-reconciliation.html).

## Percona Server for MongoDB in brief

*Percona Server for MongoDB* is a drop-in replacement for MongoDB Community Edition. It keeps data in [replica sets](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/glossary.html#replica-set). A replica set is a group of `mongod` processes that hold the same data:

- One member is the [primary](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/glossary.html#primary). It accepts all writes and records them in its [oplog](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/glossary.html#oplog).
- The other members are *secondaries*. They copy the primary’s oplog and apply it. Replication is asynchronous, so a secondary can be slightly behind the primary. Drivers read from the primary by default and see the latest data. If an application reads from secondaries with a read preference, it can get slightly older data. The `majority` write concern makes a write wait until most members acknowledge it, but secondaries still apply it on their own schedule.
- If the primary becomes unavailable, the voting members hold an [election](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/glossary.html#election) and promote a secondary. A candidate needs the votes of a majority of the voting members. MongoDB [usually completes an election within about 12 seconds](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/replica-set-elections/) . Drivers retry a failed write once by default, so applications often don’t notice the switch.

A replica set can have up to 50 members, and up to 7 of them can vote. Use an odd number of voting members. With three, the replica set keeps a primary when any one member goes down. With an even number, a network partition can split the voters into two equal halves, and neither half can elect a primary.

By default, the Operator creates replica sets of **three data-bearing members**. You can add [arbiters, non-voting and hidden members](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/arbiter.html) to shape failover and read capacity.

When the data or the write load outgrows one replica set, you turn on [sharding](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/sharding.html):

- Each *shard* is a replica set that holds part of the data.
- The *config server replica set* stores the cluster metadata: which data lives on which shard.
- The `mongos` *query routers* receive client queries and send each one to the shards that hold the data. `mongos` doesn’t store data.

The example manifest `deploy/cr.yaml` creates a sharded cluster with one shard named `rs0`, three config server members and three `mongos` Pods. See [High availability and topology](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/ha-topology.html) to choose between a replica set and a sharded cluster.

## How clients connect

There is no proxy between applications and the database. MongoDB drivers connect to the database Pods and find the members themselves.

- **Sharded cluster.** Applications connect to `mongos` through the `<cluster-name>-mongos` Service on port 27017 (`my-cluster-name-mongos` by default). The Service spreads connections across all `mongos` Pods, and `mongos` routes each query to the right shards.
- **Replica set.** Applications connect to the replica set members directly. The driver reads the list of members from the replica set configuration, sends writes to the primary, and finds the new primary after an election. Use a `mongodb+srv` connection string: the driver resolves the members from the DNS SRV records of the [headless Service](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/glossary.html#headless-service) `my-cluster-name-rs0`, so you don’t list Pod host names yourself.

The Operator creates a [connection Secret](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/connection-secrets.html) with ready-to-use connection strings for the `databaseAdmin` user and for application users you declare in the Custom Resource. To connect from outside Kubernetes, expose the `mongos` Service or one Service per replica set Pod. To learn more, see [Networking and external access](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/expose.html). [Services and ports](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/services.html) lists every Service, its ports and when it exists.

## The four layers

A running cluster is the combined result of four layers. Most confusion during troubleshooting comes from expecting one layer to do something that belongs to another. The [Who owns what](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/architecture-responsibilities.html) page covers each layer in detail.

```
flowchart TB
  U["<b>User</b><br/>Custom Resource, Secrets,<br/>CRDs and RBAC, node and storage capacity"]
  O["<b>Operator</b><br/>reconcile loop: compares the Custom Resource<br/>with the cluster and corrects differences"]
  K["<b>Kubernetes</b><br/>StatefulSets, scheduling, storage (CSI),<br/>networking and DNS, Pod lifecycle"]
  M["<b>Percona Server for MongoDB and PBM</b><br/>replication, elections, initial sync,<br/>backups and restores"]
  U -- "writes the desired state" --> O
  O -- "creates and updates objects" --> K
  K -- "runs Pods and volumes for" --> M
  O -. "writes the replica set configuration;<br/>sends backup and restore commands" .-> M
```

- **User.** You describe the cluster you want in the `PerconaServerMongoDB` Custom Resource and provide everything the Operator cannot create for you: the CRDs and RBAC, credentials for backup storage, and enough nodes and storage to run the cluster.
- **Operator.** Runs the reconcile loop and the day-2 tasks: replica set membership, ordered restarts, passwords, certificates, backups and restores. See [What the Operator is](#what-the-operator-is) and [The Operator](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/architecture-responsibilities.html#the-operator).
- **Kubernetes.** Kubernetes turns the objects the Operator creates into running Pods. It schedules Pods to nodes, provisions and attaches volumes through the CSI driver, provides Services and DNS, and restarts failed containers.
- **Percona Server for MongoDB and Percona Backup for MongoDB.** Inside the Pods, MongoDB replicates data, holds elections and brings new members up to date with an [initial sync](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/glossary.html#initial-sync). The [PBM](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/glossary.html#pbm) agents in the database Pods make backups and restores.

The Operator does more inside the database than create Pods. It initializes each replica set, writes the replica set configuration, and adds and removes members when the Pods change. Elections and replication stay with MongoDB. See [Replica set membership](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/architecture-workflows.html#replica-set-membership).

## Cluster topology

The following diagrams show a cluster named `my-cluster-name` with backups enabled.

### Replica set

```
flowchart LR
  C[Clients] -. "DNS SRV lookup" .-> S["Headless Service<br/>my-cluster-name-rs0"]
  subgraph RS["Replica set rs0"]
    P0["my-cluster-name-rs0-0<br/>primary"]
    P1["my-cluster-name-rs0-1<br/>secondary"]
    P2["my-cluster-name-rs0-2<br/>secondary"]
  end
  C -- "reads and writes" --> P0
  P0 -- "oplog replication" --> P1
  P0 -- "oplog replication" --> P2
  RS -- "backup-agent containers" --> ST[("Backup storage")]
```

Each `mongod` Pod has its own [PersistentVolumeClaim](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/glossary.html#pvc) for the data directory and, when backups are enabled, a `backup-agent` sidecar container with the PBM agent. Any data-bearing voting member can become the primary. The diagram shows `my-cluster-name-rs0-0` as the primary only as an example.

### Sharded cluster

```
flowchart LR
  C[Clients] --> S["Service<br/>my-cluster-name-mongos"]
  S --> M["mongos Pods"]
  subgraph CFG["Config server replica set"]
    CF["my-cluster-name-cfg-0, -1, -2"]
  end
  subgraph SH["Shard rs0"]
    R0["my-cluster-name-rs0-0, -1, -2"]
  end
  M -- "reads metadata" --> CFG
  M -- "routes queries" --> SH
  CFG -- "backup-agent" --> ST[("Backup storage")]
  SH -- "backup-agent" --> ST
```

Here is how a client request reaches the data in a sharded cluster:

1. A client connects to the `my-cluster-name-mongos` Service on port 27017. The Service forwards the connection to one of the `mongos` Pods.
1. `mongos` uses the metadata from the config server replica set to find the shards that hold the requested data.
1. `mongos` sends the query to the primary of each shard involved, or to a secondary if the client asked for it with a read preference.
1. The shard primary applies a write and replicates it to its secondaries.

Members find each other by host name, not through the Kubernetes API. The Operator writes each member into the replica set configuration with a stable DNS name, such as `my-cluster-name-rs0-0.my-cluster-name-rs0.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local:27017`. If you expose the replica set, the Operator can write the address of the per-Pod Service instead. See [Controlling hostnames in replset configuration](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/expose.html#controlling-hostnames-in-replset-configuration). `mongos` gets the config server members from its start-up arguments, and learns the shards from the metadata.

### What differs between the two topologies

|                                   | Replica set                                                                 | Sharded cluster                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| --------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| StatefulSets                      | One for each replica set                                                    | One for each shard, one for the config server replica set `my-cluster-name-cfg`, and one for `mongos`                                                                                                       |
| Client entry point                | The replica set members, through the headless Service `my-cluster-name-rs0` | `mongos`, through the `my-cluster-name-mongos` Service                                                                                                                                                      |
| Cluster endpoint in `status.host` | The headless Service of the replica set                                     | The `mongos` Service, or the list of per-Pod `mongos` Services                                                                                                                                              |
| Extra Operator tasks              | None                                                                        | Adds and removes shards, and turns the balancer on and off. See [Shards and the balancer](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/architecture-workflows.html#shards-and-the-balancer) |
| Smart Update order                | Secondaries, then the primary                                               | The config server replica set first, then the shards, then `mongos`                                                                                                                                         |
| Restore                           | Clients stay connected during a logical restore                             | The Operator stops `mongos` first, so clients can’t connect                                                                                                                                                 |
| Pause and deletion                | Members stop one at a time                                                  | `mongos` stops first, then the replica sets                                                                                                                                                                 |

Optional components run beside the members:

- **Point-in-time recovery** doesn’t add Pods. When it’s on, a PBM agent uploads the oplog to backup storage in short slices. See [Point-in-time recovery](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/architecture-workflows.html#point-in-time-recovery).
- **Percona Search for MongoDB** runs a `mongot` StatefulSet for each data-bearing replica set or shard. `mongod` or `mongos` forwards search queries to it. Applications don’t connect to `mongot`. See [About full-text and vector search](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/search-overview.html).
- **Percona ClusterSync for MongoDB (PCSM)** runs as a separate Deployment when you create a `PerconaServerMongoDBClusterSync` object. It copies data from an external MongoDB deployment into the cluster. See [Real-time replication with PCSM](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/clustersync.html).
- **Sidecar containers** such as the PMM Client for [monitoring](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/monitoring.html), the log collector for [persistent logging](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/persistent-logging.html) and your own [sidecars](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/sidecar.html) run in the database and `mongos` Pods. See [Containers in each Pod](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/objects-created.html#containers-in-each-pod).

The [Key workflows](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/architecture-workflows.html) page describes replica set membership, backups, restores and recovery step by step.

### Scheduling and storage

To survive a node failure, the Operator places the members of each replica set on separate Kubernetes nodes with [Pod anti-affinity](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/assign-pod-node/#affinity-and-anti-affinity) . By default, this rule is *required* and uses the `kubernetes.io/hostname` topology key: with three members you need at least three schedulable nodes, or a Pod stays `Pending`. See [Control Pod scheduling](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/constraints.html) to change it.

If a Kubernetes node fails, Kubernetes can recreate the Pod on another node, but for a [StatefulSet](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/glossary.html#statefulset) Pod it does so only after the failed Node object is removed or the stuck Pod is force-deleted. The Operator does neither. Meanwhile, MongoDB elects a new primary if the lost member was the primary, and the replica set keeps working with the remaining members.

The Pod’s data lives in a PersistentVolume, so the storage must be able to follow the Pod. The Container Storage Interface (CSI) driver and StorageClass must support attaching the volume on a different node. A volume that can attach only in one zone keeps the Pod in that zone. For local disks, see [Local storage support](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/storage.html).

## What gets created

For a cluster named `my-cluster-name`, the Operator creates a StatefulSet for each replica set, for the config server replica set and for `mongos`, together with Services, Secrets, ConfigMaps, [PodDisruptionBudgets](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/glossary.html#pdb) and PVCs. Arbiter, non-voting and hidden members get StatefulSets of their own. The Operator creates no Kubernetes Jobs or CronJobs: the PBM agents make the backups, and the Operator keeps the backup schedules itself. PVCs and Secrets are not owned by the Custom Resource, so deleting the cluster doesn’t delete them unless you set the finalizers.

- [Services and ports](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/services.html) lists every Service, its ports, and when it exists.
- [Objects the Operator creates](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/objects-created.html) lists all other objects, the [finalizers](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/glossary.html#finalizer) that clean them up, and the containers in each Pod.

# Who owns what

When something happens in the cluster, the question is which layer reacts: the Operator, Percona Server for MongoDB, Kubernetes, or you. This page answers it at a glance. For the detail of what you do and what the Operator does in each area, and for what never to change by hand, see [Operator responsibilities by area](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/operator-boundaries.html). For an overview of the layers, see [Design and architecture](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/architecture.html#the-four-layers).

Two rules explain most of the behavior:

- **You change the cluster only through the [Custom Resource](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/glossary.html#custom-resource) and the user Secrets.** The Operator turns them into Kubernetes objects and into the replica set configuration, and reverts manual changes to the fields it manages.
- **Each layer keeps its own part alive.** Kubernetes keeps Pods running, MongoDB keeps a primary and replicates the data, and the Operator keeps the objects, the replica set membership and the day-2 tasks matching the Custom Resource.

## Who reacts when something happens

The table lists failures from the smallest to the largest scope first, then changes, then events that come with time and capacity. The bold text at the start of each answer names who acts.

| Event                                                           | Who reacts                                                                                                                                                                                         | Where it is explained                                                                                                                                   |
| --------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| A container crashes or fails its liveness probe                 | **Kubernetes.** The kubelet restarts the container                                                                                                                                                 | [Health checks and probes](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/architecture-probes.html)                                       |
| A Pod is deleted or evicted                                     | **Kubernetes.** The StatefulSet controller recreates it, and the member rejoins the replica set with the same host name. The Operator isn’t involved                                               | [Replica set membership](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/architecture-workflows.html#replica-set-membership)               |
| A `mongos` Pod fails                                            | **Kubernetes.** It restarts the Pod, and the `my-cluster-name-mongos` Service sends new connections to the other `mongos` Pods. The Operator isn’t involved                                        | [Health checks and probes](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/architecture-probes.html#mongos-pods)                           |
| A Kubernetes node fails                                         | **Kubernetes, then you.** Kubernetes recreates a StatefulSet Pod elsewhere only after the Node object is removed or the stuck Pod is force-deleted, which is up to you or your platform            | [Kubernetes](#kubernetes)                                                                                                                               |
| A member falls behind or starts with an empty volume            | **MongoDB.** The member catches up from the oplog of another member, or runs an initial sync                                                                                                       | [Percona Server for MongoDB](#percona-server-for-mongodb)                                                                                               |
| The primary becomes unavailable                                 | **MongoDB.** The voting members elect a new primary, usually within seconds                                                                                                                        | [Primary failover](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/architecture-workflows.html#primary-failover)                           |
| The config server replica set loses its primary                 | **MongoDB.** The config server replica set elects a new primary like any replica set. Until it does, the cluster metadata can’t change                                                             | [Primary failover](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/architecture-workflows.html#primary-failover)                           |
| A replica set has no primary and can’t elect one                | **MongoDB, then the Operator.** Without a majority of voting members, MongoDB can’t elect a primary. The Operator rewrites the replica set configuration from a ready member                       | [Replica set without a primary](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/architecture-workflows.html#replica-set-without-a-primary) |
| You edit the Custom Resource                                    | **The Operator.** It reconciles the change                                                                                                                                                         | [How the Operator reacts to changes](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/architecture-reconciliation.html)                     |
| A Pod is added or removed, for example when you change the size | **The Operator.** It adds or removes the member in the replica set configuration, and adjusts the votes                                                                                            | [Replica set membership](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/architecture-workflows.html#replica-set-membership)               |
| You remove a shard from the CR                                  | **You, then the Operator.** You move or drop the databases on the shard first. The Operator checks that the shard holds no user databases, drains it through `mongos`, and deletes its StatefulSet | [Shards and the balancer](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/architecture-workflows.html#shards-and-the-balancer)             |
| Someone edits an object the Operator manages                    | **The Operator.** It reverts the fields it manages                                                                                                                                                 | [Change the cluster through the Custom Resource](#change-the-cluster-through-the-custom-resource)                                                       |
| A scheduled backup is due                                       | **The Operator.** It creates the backup object, and a PBM agent makes the backup                                                                                                                   | [Scheduled backups](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/architecture-workflows.html#scheduled-backups)                         |
| A TLS certificate gets close to its expiry date                 | **cert-manager, or you.** cert-manager renews the certificates it issued. You renew the certificates you supplied. Operator-generated certificates are valid until the year 9999                   | [Manage certificates](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/operator-boundaries.html#manage-certificates)                        |
| A disk fills up                                                 | **You, or the Operator.** You resize the storage. With storage autoscaling on, the Operator grows the volume                                                                                       | [Resize storage](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/scaling-storage-resize.html#automatic-storage-resizing)                   |

When something fails and you don’t know which layer to start with, see [Which layer is it?](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/debug.html#which-layer-is-it) in Initial troubleshooting.

## Change the cluster through the Custom Resource

A [Custom Resource](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/extend-kubernetes/api-extension/custom-resources/) (CR) is the Kubernetes object that describes the cluster you want. It is a blueprint that the Operator uses to deploy and manage your cluster.

**The Custom Resource is the source of truth. Change the cluster by editing the CR.**

The Operator compares the CR against what is running about every five seconds and corrects any difference it finds. A change you make directly to a [StatefulSet](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/glossary.html#statefulset), a Service, a Pod, a managed Secret or the replica set configuration is drift. The Operator overwrites it, usually within seconds. If a change survives, the Operator doesn’t manage that field yet. This doesn’t mean the change was accepted.

- **Edits to the fields the Operator manages do not persist.** The Operator reverts them and doesn’t raise an event.
- **Edits outside the CR can still cause damage before they are reverted.** For example, a member you remove with `rs.remove()` is added back on the next pass, and a vote or priority you change with `rs.reconfig()` is set back.

## Review responsibilities at a glance

The following table shows what the Operator handles and what stays with you. Select an area for the details and the list of manual actions to avoid.

| Area                                                                                                                                                           | Operator                                                                                                                                                                 | You                                                                                        | Don’t do manually                                                                                          |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| [Cluster lifecycle](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/operator-boundaries.html#cluster-lifecycle)                                   | - Creates and heals StatefulSets, Services and PodDisruptionBudgets. - Initializes replica sets and manages their membership. - Rolls out changes with ordered restarts. | - Choose the topology and sizes. - Decide when to pause. - Plan maintenance windows.       | - Scale or edit the StatefulSets. - Reconfigure the replica set with `rs.reconfig()`. - Remove finalizers. |
| [Backups](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/operator-boundaries.html#back-up-the-database)                                          | - Creates scheduled backups and applies retention. - Runs one backup at a time. - Waits for a healthy cluster before it starts a backup.                                 | - Verify that backups restore. - Set retention. - Keep copies outside the cluster storage. | - Run `pbm` commands against the cluster. - Delete backup files from storage by hand.                      |
| [Restore and point-in-time recovery](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/operator-boundaries.html#restore-and-point-in-time-recovery) | - Prepares the cluster, starts the restore through PBM, and brings the cluster back. - Turns off oplog uploads during a restore.                                         | - Pick the restore target. - Take a new full backup after the restore.                     | - Edit the cluster CR during a restore. - Start a restore with the PBM CLI.                                |

| [Users and Secrets](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/operator-boundaries.html#users-and-secrets)                                   | - Creates the system users. - Applies the passwords you change in the users Secret. - Creates application users declared in the CR.                                      | - Set passwords in the users Secret. - Delete application users you no longer need.        | - Change a system user password with `db.changeUserPassword()`. - Edit the `internal-` Secret.             |

## The Operator

The Operator keeps the cluster matching the Custom Resource with its [reconcile loop](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/architecture.html#what-the-operator-is). Beyond creating and updating Kubernetes objects, it runs these day-2 tasks:

- Replica set initialization and membership: it adds and removes members, sets their votes, and adds shards to a sharded cluster. See [Replica set membership](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/architecture-workflows.html#replica-set-membership).
- Ordered restarts with [Smart Update](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/architecture-reconciliation.html#update-strategies).
- System user passwords, application users and roles, certificates, storage resizing, backup schedules and retention, restores, and the PBM configuration.
- Sharding operations: it adds and removes shards, keeps the balancer on or off as `sharding.balancer.enabled` says, and stops the balancer during a config server restart.

**The Operator does not:**

- Run elections or replication. MongoDB chooses the primary and replicates the data. The Operator only writes the replica set configuration and asks the primary to step down before it restarts it.
- Handle Kubernetes node failures. It doesn’t force-delete Pods stuck on a failed node or react to node taints. Kubernetes recreates a Pod from an unreachable node elsewhere only after the Node object is removed or the stuck Pod is force-deleted.
- Validate MongoDB options. The `configuration` sections of the CR go into ConfigMaps as they are. The one exception is the TLS mode: the Operator rejects it in `configuration` and expects it in `tls.mode`.
- Install or upgrade CRDs and RBAC.
- Drop database users that you remove from `spec.users`.
- Make or move backup data itself. The PBM agents do this.
- Fail over between sites in a multi-cluster deployment.
- Report problems as Kubernetes events. The cluster controller emits no events. Problems show in the Operator logs and in the Custom Resource status. The backup, restore and ClusterSync controllers emit events only when a ClusterSync blocks them or fails over.

For each area in detail, see [Operator responsibilities by area](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/operator-boundaries.html). For the objects the Operator creates, see [Objects the Operator creates](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/objects-created.html) and [Services and ports](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/services.html).

## Percona Server for MongoDB

**MongoDB does:**

- Elect a primary among the voting members, and elect a new one when the primary is lost. A candidate needs a majority of the votes.
- Replicate writes from the primary’s oplog to the secondaries.
- Bring a member up to date: from the oplog of another member if it is still there, or with a full [initial sync](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/glossary.html#initial-sync) otherwise, for example when the member starts with an empty volume.
- Acknowledge writes according to the write concern. The `defaultRWConcern` section of the CR sets the cluster-wide default.
- In a sharded cluster, route queries through `mongos` and balance chunks between shards.

**What the Operator sets up for MongoDB:**

- The replica set configuration: members, host names, [split horizons](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/expose.html#exposing-replica-set-with-split-horizon-dns), and member votes and priorities. At most 7 members vote. If the number of voting members would be even, the Operator takes the vote away from one member, starting with hidden members. The exception is a two-member replica set with an arbiter, which you allow with `unsafeFlags.replsetSize`. Starting with version 1.24.0, it changes the vote of only one member per reconfiguration, and never takes the vote from the primary.
- The `mongod` and `mongos` configuration from the CR, merged with the options the Operator needs, such as TLS and the keyfile or certificate for internal authentication.
- The system users that the Operator, the probes and the PBM agents use. See [System users](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/system-users.html).
- The shards of a sharded cluster, and the default read and write concern when you set `defaultRWConcern`.

**Health as the Pod probes see it:**

- A `mongod` Pod is *ready* when its member is `PRIMARY`, `SECONDARY` or `ARBITER`. A member in `STARTUP2`, `RECOVERING` or `ROLLBACK` is not ready.
- The liveness probe tolerates a member that is recovering, rolling back or running an initial sync. It fails when the member is `DOWN`, `REMOVED` or unknown, or when the probe can’t connect to `mongod`.
- See [Health checks and probes](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/architecture-probes.html) for what the probes check and who acts on their result.

**What this means in practice:**

- A Pod that is `Running` but not `Ready` usually means the member is still catching up: it runs an initial sync, or it is `RECOVERING` because it fell too far behind.
- A member that fell behind the oldest entry in the other members’ oplogs stays `RECOVERING` until it gets a full copy of the data. See [Exec into the containers](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/debug-shell.html) to inspect it.
- A bad option in `configuration` shows up as `mongod` failing to start, in the `mongod` container logs.

## Kubernetes

**Kubernetes does:**

- **Schedule Pods.** The Operator only writes the affinity rules, node selectors, tolerations, priority class and topology spread constraints you specify. The default anti-affinity is *required* on `kubernetes.io/hostname`: three members of a replica set need three schedulable nodes. Otherwise a Pod stays `Pending`, and after about a minute the Custom Resource status shows the scheduler’s message.
- **Provide storage.** The CSI driver and StorageClass provision volumes, bind them to zones, and expand file systems. A ReadWriteOnce volume ties the Pod to the node or zone where the volume can attach.
- **Run the network and DNS.** Drivers find the replica set members through the DNS records of the [headless Services](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/glossary.html#headless-service), and members reach each other by these names. If DNS is broken, members can’t reach each other, elections fail, and clients can’t resolve the members.
- **Provision load balancers.** For `LoadBalancer` Services, the cloud provider creates the load balancer. Firewalls and source ranges are yours and the provider’s to manage.
- **Manage the Pod lifecycle.** Run probes, restart failed containers, and enforce [PodDisruptionBudgets](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/glossary.html#pdb) during node drains.
- **Collect garbage.** Delete objects owned by the Custom Resource when you delete it.

**Kubernetes does not:**

- Know anything about MongoDB beyond the [probes](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/architecture-probes.html). A native StatefulSet rolling update waits for each Pod to become ready, but it doesn’t restart the primary last, doesn’t ask it to step down, and doesn’t pause for a running backup.
- Expand a volume whose StorageClass doesn’t allow it, or beyond your storage quota.

## You, the user

The Operator keeps the cluster matching the Custom Resource. Everything it cannot create or decide for you stays with you:

- Install and upgrade the CRDs and RBAC, which the Operator never applies. See [Upgrade the Operator and CRD](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/update-operator.html).
- Provide capacity: enough schedulable nodes for the anti-affinity rules, and a StorageClass that allows volume expansion. See [Cluster lifecycle](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/operator-boundaries.html#cluster-lifecycle) and [Storage](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/operator-boundaries.html#storage).
- Provide credentials: the passwords in the users Secret, the backup storage credentials, and the PMM token. See [Users and Secrets](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/operator-boundaries.html#users-and-secrets).
- Renew certificates you supplied yourself. See [Manage certificates](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/operator-boundaries.html#manage-certificates).
- Verify that backups restore, set retention, and keep copies outside the cluster storage. See [Back up the database](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/operator-boundaries.html#back-up-the-database).
- Run and fail over multi-cluster deployments. See [Multi-cluster deployments](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/operator-boundaries.html#multi-cluster-deployments).
- Decide when to pause, upgrade, and restore. See [Database upgrades](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/operator-boundaries.html#database-upgrades) and [Restore and point-in-time recovery](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/operator-boundaries.html#restore-and-point-in-time-recovery).

## Unsafe configurations

The Operator refuses configurations that put availability or data at risk, such as a replica set with fewer than three members, an even number of members without an arbiter, or a cluster without TLS. See [Stay inside safe operating limits](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/operator-boundaries.html#stay-inside-safe-operating-limits). To use one anyway, you opt in with a flag in the `spec.unsafeFlags` subsection. See [Override a safety check](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/operator-boundaries.html#override-a-safety-check).

# Operator responsibilities by area

For each area, this page lists what the Operator does, what you still do, and which manual actions can damage a running cluster. For the layers, the events that trigger each one, and a table of all areas, see [Who owns what](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/architecture-responsibilities.html).

The Custom Resource is the source of truth: change the cluster only by editing it. See [Change the cluster through the Custom Resource](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/architecture-responsibilities.html#change-the-cluster-through-the-custom-resource).

## Cluster lifecycle

Change the topology, sizes, pause state and deletion through the CR. Direct edits to the StatefulSets or to the replica set configuration fight the next reconcile.

**What the Operator does:**

- Creates and reconciles a StatefulSet for each replica set, for the config server replica set, for `mongos`, and for arbiter, non-voting and hidden members. It also creates their Services and a PodDisruptionBudget for each StatefulSet.
- Initializes each replica set, adds new Pods to the replica set configuration, removes members whose Pods are gone, and sets member votes. See [Replica set membership](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/architecture-workflows.html#replica-set-membership).
- In a sharded cluster, adds each replica set as a shard, removes a shard you delete from the CR if it holds no user databases, and keeps the balancer as `sharding.balancer.enabled` says. See [Shards and the balancer](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/architecture-workflows.html#shards-and-the-balancer).
- Scales a replica set down by one Pod per pass, and removes the members whose Pods are gone from the replica set configuration.
- Leaves restarting failed Pods and containers to Kubernetes, and elections and initial sync to MongoDB.
- Shuts the cluster down in order when you set `spec.pause: true`, and brings it back when you set it to `false`. Data is retained. See [What happens during a pause](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/pause.html#what-happens-during-a-pause).
- Deletes Pods in a safe order on cluster deletion, using finalizers. See [Delete the database cluster](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/delete.html#delete-the-database-cluster).

**What you still do:**

- Choose the topology and the sizes. Stay inside the limits in [Stay inside safe operating limits](#stay-inside-safe-operating-limits).
- Decide when to pause a cluster, and for how long.
- Plan capacity, node size and maintenance windows for any change that restarts Pods. Provide enough schedulable nodes for the Pod anti-affinity rules: by default, three members of a replica set need three nodes. See [Control Pod scheduling](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/constraints.html).
- Check and tune MongoDB options before you put them in a `configuration` section. The Operator doesn’t validate them.
- Before you remove a shard, move or drop the databases on it. The Operator refuses to remove a shard that holds user databases.
- Decide whether to set the `percona.com/delete-psmdb-pvc` finalizer. Without it, PVCs and Secrets remain after you delete the cluster, and you delete them yourself. See [Clean up resources](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/delete.html#clean-up-resources).

**Never do this manually:**

| Do not                                                                          | What goes wrong                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 | Do this instead                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Run `kubectl scale` or `kubectl edit` on a StatefulSet                          | The next reconcile reverts the change. If it takes effect first, several members can go away at once, and the replica set can lose the majority it needs to elect a primary                                                                                     | Change `size` in the CR. The Operator removes one Pod per pass                                                                                                                                               |
| Run `rs.add()`, `rs.remove()` or `rs.reconfig()`                                | The Operator rewrites the members, host names, votes and priorities on its next pass. A configuration that fights the Operator can trigger extra elections                                                                                                      | Change the CR. For priorities, use `replsetOverrides` or `primaryPreferTagSelector`. For external members, use `externalNodes`                                                                               |
| Run `removeShard`, `sh.stopBalancer()` or `sh.startBalancer()` through `mongos` | The Operator still has the shard in its replica set list, and sets the balancer back to the CR value on the next pass                                                                                                                                           | Remove the replica set from `replsets`. Set `sharding.balancer.enabled`                                                                                                                                      |
| Remove a finalizer to finish a stuck delete                                     | Finalizers shut down the Pods in order and clean up PVCs, Secrets and oplog chunks. The `percona.com/delete-backup` finalizer on a backup removes the backup files from storage. Removing a finalizer abandons that cleanup and can orphan data or backup files | Find out why the finalizer is blocked. See [Objects the Operator creates](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/objects-created.html#finalizers) for every finalizer and what it does |
| Run `kubectl delete psmdb` to reset a misbehaving cluster                       | With the `percona.com/delete-psmdb-pvc` finalizer set, this deletes the PVCs, the data on them and the users Secret                                                                                                                                             | Pause the cluster and investigate                                                                                                                                                                            |

## Back up the database

Create backups through a schedule in the cluster CR or through a `PerconaServerMongoDBBackup` resource. See [Backup and restore](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/backups.html).

**What the Operator does:**

- Creates scheduled backups from `backup.tasks`, and passes on-demand backups from `PerconaServerMongoDBBackup` resources to PBM.
- Starting with version 1.24.0, creates one catch-up backup when it starts and finds that a scheduled run was missed while it was stopped. See [Scheduled backups](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/architecture-workflows.html#scheduled-backups).
- Applies retention policy to scheduled backups. With `retention` set, it deletes the oldest backups of the task beyond the configured count. Retention counts incremental base backups but ignores subsequent increments. When retention deletes a base backup from storage, PBM also deletes its dependent increments.
- **Runs one backup at a time.** It holds a lock for each running backup. Other backups wait in the `waiting` state.
- **Waits for a healthy cluster.** A backup doesn’t start until the cluster is `ready`, unless you set `unsafeFlags.backupIfUnhealthy`. With `startingDeadlineSeconds` set, a backup that doesn’t start in time fails.
- Writes the PBM configuration from the `backup` section of the CR, and keeps it in sync.
- Uploads the oplog for point-in-time recovery when `backup.pitr.enabled` is `true`. See [Enable point-in-time recovery](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/backups-pitr.html).

**What you still do:**

- **Verify that your backups restore.** The Operator confirms that PBM completed a backup. It doesn’t confirm that the backup is usable. Test restores on a schedule. See [Restore from a backup](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/backups-restore.html).
- Set retention, and keep copies outside the cluster storage target.
- Manage credentials and lifecycle policies on the bucket, and provide the storage credentials in Secrets or through an IAM role.
- Take a new full backup after a restore, so that point-in-time recovery has a base to start from.
- Decide whether a backup during a degraded window is worth the risk.

**Never do this manually:**

| Do not                                                                        | What goes wrong                                                                                                                                                           | Do this instead                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Run `pbm backup`, `pbm restore` or `pbm config` in a `backup-agent` container | The Operator doesn’t know about the operation. A manual backup or restore can overlap with an Operator one. A manual configuration change is overwritten on the next pass | Create a `PerconaServerMongoDBBackup` or `PerconaServerMongoDBRestore` resource, and change the `backup` section of the CR                                                                          |
| Set `unsafeFlags.backupIfUnhealthy` to get a backup from a broken cluster     | A backup from a cluster that is not healthy may be inconsistent and may not restore                                                                                       | Repair the cluster, then back up. If you must take the backup, treat the result as best effort only                                                                                                 |
| Delete objects from the backup storage by hand                                | The point-in-time recovery chain between a full backup and its oplog breaks. An incremental chain breaks, too                                                             | Delete the `PerconaServerMongoDBBackup` resource and let the finalizer clean up. See [Delete the unneeded backup](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/backups-delete.html) |

## Restore and point-in-time recovery

**What the Operator does:**

- Waits until no backup or other restore runs, and checks that PBM knows the backup. If PBM doesn’t have the backup in its metadata, the Operator asks PBM to resync the storage.
- Prepares the cluster: it stops `mongos`, and for physical and snapshot restores, it also stops the arbiters and runs PBM inside the `mongod` containers. Then it starts the restore through PBM and brings the cluster back to its normal configuration. See [How backup and restore work](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/backups.html#how-backup-and-restore-work).
- Turns off oplog uploads for point-in-time recovery right before the restore, and keeps them off while the restore runs.
- Restores to a point in time, and restores selected namespaces from a logical backup.

**What you still do:**

- Choose the restore target, and accept the loss of the data written after it.
- Plan the maintenance window. A sharded cluster is unavailable for clients while `mongos` is stopped, and a physical restore restarts every member.
- Take a new full backup after the restore.

**Never do this manually:**

| Do not                                               | What goes wrong                                                                                                                                                                    | Do this instead                                                                                                                                          |
| ---------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Edit the cluster CR while a restore is running       | A physical restore changes the StatefulSets and restarts the members several times. An edit in that window is applied to a cluster that doesn’t match the restore’s expected state | Wait until the restore is finished                                                                                                                       |
| Start a second restore because the first looks stuck | The Operator queues it in the `waiting` state. It doesn’t speed up the first one                                                                                                   | Check the first restore. See [Troubleshoot backups and restores](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/debug-backup-restore.html) |
| Delete the restore resource mid-flight               | The Operator stops tracking the restore, and the cluster can stay in the restore configuration                                                                                     | Let the restore finish, then delete the resource                                                                                                         |

## Manage certificates

How certificates are renewed depends on who created them. See [Transport Layer Security (TLS)](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/TLS.html).

**What the Operator does:**

- Issues certificates when the cluster is created, if the TLS Secrets don’t exist: through cert-manager when it is installed, and self-signed otherwise. With backups enabled, it also issues the PBM client certificate starting with version 1.24.0.
- Lets cert-manager renew the certificates it manages.
- Watches the contents of the TLS Secrets and restarts the Pods with Smart Update when they change.
- With `tls.certManagementPolicy: userProvidedOnly`, doesn’t create missing certificates and reports the `TLSSecretsReady` condition instead. See [Configure the TLS certificate management policy](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/tls-cert-management-policy.html).

**What you still do:**

- **Renew certificates you supplied yourself.** The Operator doesn’t renew them. Self-signed certificates the Operator generated are long-term. Renew them yourself if you need.
- Choose the certificate management policy that fits your workflow.

**Never do this manually:**

| Do not                                      | What goes wrong                                                                                                           | Do this instead                                                                                            |
| ------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Replace the CA in a TLS Secret in one step  | Members that have the old CA and members that have the new one stop trusting each other, and replication breaks           | Follow [Update certificates](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/tls-update.html) |
| Delete a TLS Secret to get new certificates | With the default policy, the Operator creates a new CA. All Pods restart, and clients that trust the old CA can’t connect | Follow [Update certificates](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/tls-update.html) |

## Users and Secrets

**What the Operator does:**

- Creates the users Secret with random passwords if it doesn’t exist, and creates the system users in MongoDB. See [System users](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/system-users.html).
- **Applies password changes.** When you change a password in the users Secret, the Operator changes it in MongoDB and then copies the Secret to the internal Secret `internal-<cluster-name>-users`. It restarts only the containers that use the changed credentials: the `backup-agent` containers for the backup user, and the `pmm-client` containers for the PMM token.
- Creates and updates the application users and roles declared in `spec.users` and `spec.roles`, once the cluster is `ready`. See [Application-level users](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/app-users.html).
- Keeps the [connection Secrets](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/connection-secrets.html) up to date.

**What you still do:**

- Set and rotate passwords in the users Secret.
- Delete application users that you remove from `spec.users`. The Operator doesn’t drop them. See [Delete users and roles](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/app-users.html#delete-users-and-roles).
- Keep application users separate from system users.

**Never do this manually:**

| Do not                                                       | What goes wrong                                                                                                                                                                                                                   | Do this instead                                               |
| ------------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Change a system user password with `db.changeUserPassword()` | The Secret and the database disagree. The probes and the Operator use the `clusterMonitor` and `clusterAdmin` users: if they can’t log in, the liveness probe fails on every member and the Operator can’t manage the replica set | Change the password in the users Secret                       |
| Edit or delete the `internal-<cluster-name>-users` Secret    | The Operator compares the users Secret with this one to detect changes. An edit can hide a change or trigger an unneeded one                                                                                                      | Leave it to the Operator                                      |
| Drop or lock a system user                                   | The probes, the backups or the Operator stop working, depending on the user                                                                                                                                                       | Keep the system users. Create separate users for applications |

## Storage

**What the Operator does:**

- Grows the PVCs when you raise the storage size in the CR, if `storageScaling.enableVolumeScaling` is `true`. With `storageScaling.autoscaling`, it grows them automatically when they fill up. See [Resize storage](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/scaling-storage-resize.html).
- Starting with version 1.24.0, shrinks the PVCs when you lower the storage size and `storageScaling.enableVolumeShrink` is `true`. It replaces each PVC with a smaller one, one member at a time, and the member gets its data back through an initial sync.
- Keeps the cluster in `initializing` while a resize runs, and delays Smart Update until it finishes.

**What you still do:**

- Pick a StorageClass that supports volume expansion.
- Watch capacity, and set limits for autoscaling.

**Never do this manually:**

| Do not                               | What goes wrong                                                                                                                   | Do this instead                                                                                                                 |
| ------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Resize a PVC with `kubectl edit pvc` | The StatefulSet and the CR still ask for the old size. The Operator and the next StatefulSet update don’t know about the change   | Change the size in the CR                                                                                                       |
| Delete a PVC to free space           | The member loses its data and needs a full initial sync. If more members lose data at once, the replica set can lose the majority | Use storage shrinking, or contact [Percona Support](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/get-help.html) |

## Multi-cluster deployments

In a [multi-cluster deployment](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/replication.html), one replica set spans several Kubernetes clusters. The Main site runs a managed cluster. The Replica sites run clusters with `unmanaged: true`.

**What the Operator does:**

- On the Main site, adds the members you list in `externalNodes` to the replica set configuration with the votes and priorities you define.
- On a Replica site, creates the Pods and Services, but doesn’t initialize the replica set or change its configuration. It also doesn’t create the users Secret: it expects the one you copied from the Main site.
- With [Multi-Cluster Services](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/replication-mcs.html) enabled, creates the ServiceExport objects and waits until the Services are imported.

**What you still do:**

- Copy the Secrets and certificates from the Main site to the Replica sites, and make the members reachable across sites.
- Fail over between sites. If the Main site is lost, you turn a Replica site into the new Main site. See [Fail over services to the Replica site](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/replication-failover.html).
- Monitor replication across sites.

**Never do this manually:**

| Do not                                               | What goes wrong                                                                                           | Do this instead               |
| ---------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------- |
| Add the Replica site members with `rs.add()`         | The Operator on the Main site removes members that are neither its own Pods nor listed in `externalNodes` | List them in `externalNodes`  |
| Run two clusters as managed for the same replica set | Both Operators rewrite the replica set configuration                                                      | Keep exactly one managed site |

## Database upgrades

**What the Operator does:**

- Upgrades the database member by member with Smart Update (default strategy): secondaries first, the primary last after a step-down. In a sharded cluster, it upgrades the config server replica set first, then the shards, then `mongos`. See [How Smart Update works](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/architecture-reconciliation.html#how-smart-update-works).
- With `upgradeOptions.apply`, checks the Version Service on the `upgradeOptions.schedule` and applies new images. The check runs only when the cluster is `ready`. See [Automatic minor upgrade](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/update-minor-automatic.html).
- With `upgradeOptions.setFCV: true`, sets the feature compatibility version to the new major version after every Pod runs the new image.

**What you still do:**

- Decide when to upgrade, and test the upgrade on a staging cluster first.
- Upgrade the Operator and the CRDs before you raise `spec.crVersion`. See [Upgrade the Operator and CRD](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/update-operator.html).
- Upgrade one major version at a time. See [Major version upgrades](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/update-major.html).

**Never do this manually:**

| Do not                                                                         | What goes wrong                                                                                             | Do this instead                                                                            |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Edit image tags to skip a major version                                        | MongoDB supports upgrades only from the previous major version. Members can fail to start on the data files | Upgrade one major version at a time                                                        |
| Set the feature compatibility version before every member runs the new version | Older members can’t apply the changes, and you lose the option to downgrade                                 | Let the Operator set it with `upgradeOptions.setFCV`, or set it after the upgrade finishes |
| Use `updateStrategy: RollingUpdate` and expect a MongoDB-aware rollout         | Kubernetes restarts the Pods in reverse order without a step-down, and doesn’t wait for running backups     | Keep `SmartUpdate`                                                                         |

## Stay inside safe operating limits

The Operator rejects a CR that breaks these limits. The cluster goes to the `error` state, and the status message names the check.

| Setting                              | Safe limit                                         | Why                                                                                                         |
| ------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `replsets[].size` without an arbiter | At least 3, and an odd number                      | A replica set needs a majority of voting members to elect a primary. Three members tolerate the loss of one |
| `replsets[].size` with an arbiter    | An even number, at least 4, with `arbiter.size: 1` | The arbiter makes the number of voting members odd                                                          |
| `tls.mode`                           | Anything but `disabled`                            | Replication and client traffic are otherwise unencrypted                                                    |
| `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`      | At least 30                                        | `mongod` needs time to shut down cleanly                                                                    |

You can turn each check off individually under `spec.unsafeFlags`. See [Override a safety check](#override-a-safety-check). Do not turn a check off to clear an error message.

## Override a safety check

`spec.unsafeFlags` turns off individual safety checks. Each check exists because turning it off can lose data or availability. Field details are in the [Unsafe flags section](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/operator.html#operator-unsafeflags-section).

| Flag                                 | Enables                                                                                                      | What you give up                                                                   |
| ------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `unsafeFlags.replsetSize`            | Replica sets with one or two members, an even number of members without an arbiter, or other arbiter layouts | Election guarantees. A replica set with one or two members is not highly available |
| `unsafeFlags.tls`                    | Running without TLS                                                                                          | Encryption of replication and client traffic                                       |
| `unsafeFlags.terminationGracePeriod` | A termination grace period shorter than 30 seconds                                                           | A clean shutdown. `mongod` can be killed while it writes                           |
| `unsafeFlags.backupIfUnhealthy`      | Backups from a cluster that is not `ready`                                                                   | Confidence that the backup is consistent and restorable                            |

The older `allowUnsafeConfigurations` option turns on all the flags at once.

Use these flags for a development cluster, a local test, or a deliberate single-member setup for continuous integration. On a production cluster, an Operator rejection describes a real risk in the configuration you asked for.

## Check before you intervene

When a manual change looks necessary, do the following:

1. Check whether the CR already exposes what you want. Most requests for manual changes are covered by a field.
1. Reproduce the change on a non-production cluster first.
1. Capture the Operator logs and the resource status before you change anything. See [Check the logs](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/debug-logs.html).
1. Contact [Percona Support](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/get-help.html) when in doubt before you act on a production cluster.

Manual intervention on a running database cluster is recoverable far less often than it looks from the outside.
