# How the Operator reacts to changes

This page explains what the Operator does after you change the [Custom Resource](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/glossary.html#custom-resource): when it acts, in which order, which changes restart Pods, and what the cluster status tells you while the change is applied.

## What a reconcile is

The `PerconaServerMongoDB` Custom Resource describes the *desired state* of the cluster. A *reconcile* is one pass of the Operator over the cluster: it reads the Custom Resource, compares it with the *actual state* of the Kubernetes objects and the database, and changes whatever differs. Reconciles repeat continuously, so the cluster converges to the Custom Resource even if a single pass cannot finish the job.

## What triggers a reconcile

- **A change to the Custom Resource.**
- **A periodic re-check.** After each successful pass, the Operator reconciles the cluster again 5 seconds later. Set a longer interval with the [`RECONCILE_INTERVAL`](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/env-vars-operator.html#reconcile_interval) environment variable of the Operator Deployment. Because of the periodic re-check, manual edits to the objects the Operator manages, such as a [StatefulSet](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/glossary.html#statefulset) or a Service, are reverted within seconds. A change to the users Secret is also picked up by the next periodic pass, because the Operator doesn’t watch Secrets.
- **A retry after an error.** If a pass fails, the Operator retries it with an increasing delay.

Why the Operator seems to do nothing after an error

After a failed pass, the Operator doesn’t re-check the cluster every 5 seconds. It retries with an exponential backoff: the delay starts at a few milliseconds and doubles with each consecutive failure, up to about 16 minutes. The delay resets only after a successful pass. So if a reconcile has been failing for a while and you then fix the cause, for example create a missing Secret, the Operator may not notice it for several minutes.

Passes in which the Operator only waits, for example for Pods to start or for a backup to finish, are not errors: the Operator still checks again on its regular interval, 5 seconds by default.

Any change to the Custom Resource starts a new pass immediately. To trigger one without changing the configuration, add or update an annotation:

```
kubectl annotate psmdb my-cluster-name percona.com/reconcile-trigger="$(date +%s)" --overwrite
```

The annotation name is arbitrary, and the Operator doesn’t read it. Restarting the Operator Pod also resets the backoff.

Only one Operator Pod is active at a time. If you run several replicas, they elect a leader. The Operator watches the namespaces listed in the `WATCH_NAMESPACE` environment variable, or all namespaces if it is empty. See [Install the Operator in multi-namespace mode](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/cluster-wide.html).

The `MAX_CONCURRENT_RECONCILES` environment variable sets how many objects of each kind the Operator reconciles in parallel. It applies separately to clusters, backups, restores and ClusterSync objects. The default is `1`: the Operator reconciles one cluster at a time, and other clusters wait in the queue. A pass can take long, because a [Smart Update](#how-smart-update-works) waits inside the pass for each restarted Pod. If you run many clusters with one Operator, raise this value. See [Configure concurrency for a cluster reconciliation](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/reconciliation-concurrency.html).

Backups and restores have reconcile loops of their own. The Operator rechecks a backup or a restore only while it’s in progress, every 5 seconds by default. Starting with version 1.24.0, you can make these intervals longer with the `BACKUP_RECONCILE_INTERVAL` and `RESTORE_RECONCILE_INTERVAL` environment variables. A longer interval means fewer Kubernetes API requests, but the backup or restore status updates later, and restores take longer. See [Configure the reconciliation interval](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/reconciliation-concurrency.html#configure-the-reconciliation-interval).

## Order of operations

Each reconcile runs the same steps in the same order. Knowing the order helps you understand why one change waits for another: for example, a storage resize in progress holds back the Smart Update of that replica set.

```
flowchart TD
  A["Apply defaults to the Custom Resource"] --> B{"Cluster being<br/>deleted?"}
  B -- "yes" --> B1["Run finalizers"]
  B -- "no" --> C["Pause or resume,<br/>sharding on or off"]
  C --> D["Check the configuration,<br/>limit a downscale to one Pod"]
  D --> E["Users Secret, ConfigMaps,<br/>system user passwords"]
  E --> F["Remove deleted replica sets"]
  F --> G["TLS certificates, keyfile,<br/>encryption key"]
  G --> H["Backup schedules"]
  H --> I["Per replica set: Services, StatefulSets,<br/>storage resize, PodDisruptionBudgets,<br/>Smart Update"]
  I --> J["Per replica set: initialize,<br/>update members and votes, add shards"]
  J --> K["mongos: StatefulSet,<br/>Smart Update, balancer"]
  K --> L["Feature compatibility version,<br/>application users, PBM configuration"]
  L --> M["Update status, re-check in 5 s"]
```

## What happens when I change a field

| Field                                                                       | What the Operator does                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      | Restart?                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `replsets[].size`, `sharding.configsvrReplSet.size`, `sharding.mongos.size` | Changes the number of Pods. On scale-up, it adds the new members to the replica set configuration. On scale-down, it removes one Pod per pass, and then removes the member from the configuration. With the `percona.com/delete-psmdb-pvc` finalizer set, it also deletes the PVCs of the removed Pods. The new size must pass the [safety checks](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/operator-boundaries.html#stay-inside-safe-operating-limits) | No                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| A replica set removed from `replsets`                                       | In a sharded cluster, checks that it holds no user databases, removes the shard through `mongos`, and deletes the StatefulSet. See [Shards and the balancer](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/architecture-workflows.html#shards-and-the-balancer)                                                                                                                                                                                              | Its Pods stop                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| `sharding.balancer.enabled`                                                 | Turns the balancer on or off through `mongos`                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               | No                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| `arbiter`, `nonvoting` or `hidden` sections                                 | Creates or deletes the StatefulSet for these members, and adds or removes them in the replica set configuration                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             | No                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| Image, resources, environment variables, affinity, sidecars, probes         | Updates the Pod template                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    | Yes, a rolling restart in the [Smart Update](#how-smart-update-works) order. Starting with version 1.24.0, a resources change can be applied in place, without a restart, when [`vpa.inPlaceResize`](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/operator.html) is on |
| A `configuration` section                                                   | Updates the ConfigMap. The `percona.com/configuration-hash` annotation on the Pods changes                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  | Yes                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| The contents of the TLS Secrets                                             | The `percona.com/ssl-hash` and `percona.com/ssl-internal-hash` annotations on the Pods change                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               | Yes                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| A system user password in the users Secret                                  | Changes the password in the database, then restarts only the containers that use this user: `backup-agent` for the backup user, `pmm-client` for the PMM token. See [System users](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/system-users.html)                                                                                                                                                                                                          | Selected containers only                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| Storage size, larger                                                        | Patches the PVCs and recreates the StatefulSet without deleting its Pods. Requires `storageScaling.enableVolumeScaling`. See [Resize storage](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/scaling-storage-resize.html)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     | No                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| Storage size, smaller                                                       | Starting with version 1.24.0, with `storageScaling.enableVolumeShrink` on, replaces each PVC with a smaller one, one member at a time. Each member gets its data back through an initial sync                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               | Yes, one member at a time                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| `sharding.enabled`                                                          | With backups enabled, pauses the cluster, changes the topology, and starts it again. With backups disabled, restarts the members one by one. See [Turning sharding on and off](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/sharding.html#turning-sharding-on-and-off)                                                                                                                                                                                      | Yes. With backups enabled, a full stop and start                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| `pause: true`                                                               | Waits for running backups, then stops all Pods in a safe order. Data is kept. See [What happens during a pause](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/pause.html#what-happens-during-a-pause)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        | Pods stop                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| `upgradeOptions.apply`                                                      | On the `upgradeOptions.schedule`, checks for new versions and writes new images into the Custom Resource, which triggers a Smart Update                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     | Yes, when a new version is applied                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |

## Update strategies

When a change requires restarting Pods, the `updateStrategy` option decides how it happens. There are the following update strategies available: `SmartUpdate` (the default), `RollingUpdate` or `OnDelete`. For what each strategy does, see [Update strategies](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/update.html#update-strategies). This section explains how Smart Update works in detail.

### How Smart Update works

```
sequenceDiagram
  participant O as Operator
  participant P2 as my-cluster-name-rs0-2
  participant P1 as my-cluster-name-rs0-1
  participant P0 as my-cluster-name-rs0-0 (primary)
  Note over O: Pods run an outdated revision.<br/>A backup or restore running? Then wait.
  O->>P2: delete Pod
  P2-->>O: recreated and ready
  O->>P1: delete Pod
  P1-->>O: recreated and ready
  O->>P0: step down
  Note over P0,P1: an election picks a new primary
  O->>P0: delete Pod
  P0-->>O: recreated and ready, now a secondary
  Note over O: rollout complete
```

1. The Operator starts only when every Pod of the StatefulSet is ready. It waits while a backup is running or a PBM operation such as a restore is in progress. A backup in the `waiting` state doesn’t hold the rollout back.
1. In a sharded cluster, it updates the config server replica set first and stops the balancer for that time. The shards follow. `mongos` is updated last, from the lowest Pod number up, once every replica set runs the new revision. When a certificate change requires it, the Operator updates `mongos` first instead.
1. It finds the primary and restarts the other Pods first, from the highest number down.
1. After each restart, it waits until the Pod runs the new revision and its `mongod` container is ready. The [readiness probe](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/architecture-probes.html#what-the-probes-check) passes only when the member is `PRIMARY`, `SECONDARY` or `ARBITER`.
1. It asks the primary to step down, waits for the election, and restarts the former primary last. Hidden and non-voting members are never primary, so their StatefulSets update without a step-down.

The Operator waits for each Pod for as many seconds as the liveness probe’s `initialDelaySeconds`, 90 by default. If a Pod isn’t ready by then, the pass fails with the `reach pod wait limit` error, and the next pass continues the rollout from where it stopped. While it waits, the Operator logs show what it is waiting for.

The balancer is turned back on when every StatefulSet runs the current revision and no backup or restore is running.

### Automatic upgrades

With `upgradeOptions.apply` set to `Recommended`, `Latest` or a specific version, the Operator checks the Percona Version Service on the `upgradeOptions.schedule` and, if a new version is available, writes the new images into the Custom Resource. The Smart Update then rolls them out. The check runs only when the cluster is `ready`. The default value `disabled` turns automatic upgrades off. See [Automatic minor upgrade](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/update-minor-automatic.html).

Upgrade the Operator itself and its CRDs before you raise `spec.crVersion`. See [Upgrade the Operator and CRD](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/update-operator.html).

## Status

The `status.state` field of the Custom Resource shows where the cluster is: `initializing`, `ready`, `paused`, `stopping` or `error`. The Operator sets it at the end of every pass. When a pass fails, the state is `error`, and the reason is in `status.message` and in a condition with the reason `ErrorReconcile`.

- For the conditions the cluster must meet to be `ready`, see [What `ready` means](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/cr-statuses.html#what-ready-means).
- If the cluster stays in `initializing`, see [Cluster stays in `initializing`](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/troubleshoot-operator.html#cluster-stays-in-initializing).
- For all status fields and conditions, see [Custom resource statuses](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/cr-statuses.html#perconaservermongodb-status).

The status doesn’t show everything. If the state looks wrong but there is no message, read the Operator logs. See [Which layer is it?](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/debug.html#which-layer-is-it).

# Key workflows

This page describes the main workflows of the Operator step by step: how it builds and maintains the replica sets, what happens when a primary fails, and how backups, point-in-time recovery and restores work. Each section ends with the objects and fields to check when the workflow fails.

The examples use a cluster named `my-cluster-name`.

## Replica set membership

The Operator turns the Pods of a StatefulSet into a replica set and keeps the replica set configuration matching the Pods.

```
sequenceDiagram
  participant O as Operator
  participant K as Kubernetes
  participant P0 as my-cluster-name-rs0-0
  participant P1 as my-cluster-name-rs0-1
  O->>K: create StatefulSet my-cluster-name-rs0
  K->>P0: start Pod
  K->>P1: start Pod when rs0-0 is ready
  Note over O: all Pods of the replica set exist
  O->>P0: rs.initiate(), create system users
  Note over P0: becomes the primary
  O->>P0: write the configuration: add rs0-1 and rs0-2
  P1->>P0: initial sync
  Note over O: every pass: compare members with Pods,<br/>fix host names, votes, priorities
```

**What happens:**

1. **Initialization.** The Operator waits until every Pod of the replica set exists. A Pod in `CrashLoopBackOff` puts the cluster in the `error` state. Then it runs `rs.initiate()` on one member and creates the [system users](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/system-users.html). In a sharded cluster, it initializes the config server replica set and each shard the same way.
1. **Shards.** In a sharded cluster, once `mongos` runs, the Operator adds each replica set as a shard through `mongos`. It also sets the default read and write concern from the `defaultRWConcern` section, if you set it.
1. **Members.** On every pass, the Operator builds the list of members it wants from the Pods and from the `externalNodes` you listed, and compares it with the replica set configuration. When they differ, it writes a new configuration. It fixes member host names, stepping the primary down first if its own host name changes. It updates member settings, removes members whose Pods are gone, and adds members for new Pods. A new member starts with an empty volume and copies the data with an [initial sync](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/glossary.html#initial-sync).
1. **Votes.** At most 7 members vote. If the number of voting members would be even, the Operator takes a vote away, starting with hidden members, so that elections always have a clear majority. It changes the vote of only one member per configuration change and never takes the vote from the primary, so that the replica set keeps its fault tolerance while votes move.
1. **Priorities.** Members get the default priority. Members you match with `primaryPreferTagSelector` get a higher priority, and you can set a priority for one Pod with `replsetOverrides`. Arbiter, non-voting and hidden members have priority 0 and never become primary.

With `unmanaged: true`, the Operator skips all of this. It creates the Pods, but you or a managed cluster on another site own the replica set configuration. See [Multi-cluster deployments](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/operator-boundaries.html#multi-cluster-deployments).

**Where to look if it fails:**

- `kubectl get psmdb my-cluster-name -o yaml`: `status.replsets.<name>.initialized`, the `ready` and `size` counts, and the member list.
- Operator logs: `Adding new nodes`, `Removing old nodes`, `Fixing hostname of member` and `Configuring member votes and priorities` show each change to the configuration.
- `rs.status()` and `rs.conf()` in `mongosh` as the `clusterAdmin` user show what MongoDB sees. See [Exec into the containers](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/debug-shell.html).
- More symptoms and the layer that owns each: [Initial troubleshooting](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/debug.html#where-to-look-first).

## Shards and the balancer

This section applies to sharded clusters only.

**Adding a shard.** When you add a replica set to `replsets`, the Operator creates its StatefulSet and initializes the replica set. Then it adds the replica set as a shard through `mongos`, and the balancer starts moving chunks to it.

**Removing a shard.** When you remove a replica set from `replsets`, the Operator does the following:

1. It connects to the replica set and lists its databases. If the replica set holds any database other than the system databases, the Operator stops. The cluster goes to the `error` state with the message `non system db found: <database>`. Move or drop those databases first.
1. It runs `removeShard` through `mongos`, and repeats it every 10 seconds until MongoDB reports that the shard is drained and removed. The pass waits for this to finish.
1. It deletes the StatefulSet. The PVCs of the removed replica set stay. Delete them yourself when you no longer need the data.

**`mongos`.** The Operator creates and updates the `mongos` StatefulSet only when every other StatefulSet of the cluster runs its current revision, and never while a restore runs. So a pending rollout of a replica set also holds back a `mongos` change.

**The balancer.** The Operator keeps the balancer in the state `sharding.balancer.enabled` asks for, `true` by default. It stops the balancer while it restarts the config server replica set. It turns the balancer back on only when every StatefulSet runs its current revision, no backup or restore is running, no storage shrink is in progress, and the cluster isn’t paused. A balancer you stop or start with `sh.stopBalancer()` or `sh.startBalancer()` is set back on the next pass, so use the CR option.

**Where to look if it fails:**

- `kubectl get psmdb my-cluster-name -o yaml`: `status.message` for the `non system db found` error.
- Operator logs: the `removeShard` progress messages, and the balancer changes.
- `sh.status()` in `mongosh` through `mongos`: the shards, the balancer state and the chunk distribution.
- More symptoms and the layer that owns each: [Initial troubleshooting](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/debug.html#where-to-look-first).

## Primary failover

When the primary fails or is unavailable, MongoDB elects a new one. The Operator isn’t involved.

```
sequenceDiagram
  participant C as Client
  participant P0 as my-cluster-name-rs0-0 (primary)
  participant P1 as my-cluster-name-rs0-1
  participant P2 as my-cluster-name-rs0-2
  C->>P0: writes
  Note over P0: fails
  P1->>P2: heartbeats time out, request votes
  P2-->>P1: vote
  Note over P1: becomes the primary
  C->>P1: the driver finds the new primary and retries
  Note over P0: Kubernetes restarts the Pod
  P0->>P1: rejoins as a secondary, catches up from the oplog
```

**What happens:**

- The secondaries notice the missing heartbeats and hold an election. A secondary that gets the votes of a majority of the voting members becomes the primary.
- Drivers find the new primary from the replica set and send new writes there. Writes in flight during the election fail, and drivers retry them once by default.
- In a sharded cluster, `mongos` finds the new primary of the shard the same way. Clients stay connected to `mongos`.
- The config server replica set fails over the same way. Until it has a primary, the cluster metadata can’t change: no chunk migrations, no new databases or collections. Reads and writes to the shards continue. See [Config server availability](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/sharded-cluster-config-servers/#config-server-availability) .
- When the failed member comes back with the same host name and its data, it rejoins as a secondary and catches up from the primary’s oplog. If it was down for longer than the oplog covers, it stays `RECOVERING` and needs a full copy of the data.
- Writes that the old primary accepted but didn’t replicate to a majority are rolled back when it rejoins. Use the `majority` write concern for data you can’t lose.

**Where to look if it fails:**

- `kubectl get pods`: a member that stays not ready, and its restart count.
- `kubectl logs my-cluster-name-rs0-0 -c mongod`: election and rollback messages.
- [Troubleshoot connection issues](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/troubleshoot-connection.html) for drivers that don’t find the new primary.
- More symptoms and the layer that owns each: [Initial troubleshooting](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/debug.html#where-to-look-first).

## Replica set without a primary

An election needs a majority of the voting members. If more members are lost than the replica set can tolerate, for example two of three, the remaining members stay secondaries and the replica set accepts no writes.

**What happens:**

1. The Operator can’t connect to a primary. Starting with version 1.24.0, it retries for about 80 seconds first, so that a normal election doesn’t trigger the next step.
1. It logs `FULL CLUSTER CRASH` and connects to the first ready `mongod` Pod of the replica set directly, as the `clusterAdmin` user.
1. It reads the replica set configuration from that member and writes it back as a *forced reconfiguration*. Starting with version 1.24.0, it first removes the members that have no Pod and are not listed in `externalNodes`, so that missing members no longer count toward the majority.
1. With enough voting members left, the remaining members elect a primary.

If no `mongod` Pod is ready, the Operator waits. Members whose Pods still exist stay in the configuration, even if they are down. In that case, the replica set elects a primary only when enough of them come back.

A forced reconfiguration can lose writes

A forced reconfiguration lets the remaining members elect a primary without the members that are gone. Writes that only the lost members had are not on the new primary. If the lost members come back, MongoDB rolls those writes back. Check the [rollback files](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/replica-set-rollbacks/) after such an event.

**Where to look if it fails:**

- Operator logs: `FULL CLUSTER CRASH` and the errors that follow.
- `kubectl get pods`: whether any `mongod` Pod of the replica set is ready.
- `rs.status()` on a remaining member: its state and the members it sees.
- More symptoms and the layer that owns each: [Initial troubleshooting](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/debug.html#where-to-look-first).

## On-demand backup

The PBM agents in the `backup-agent` containers make the backups. The Operator decides when a backup may start and tells PBM to run it.

```
sequenceDiagram
  participant U as User
  participant O as Operator
  participant L as Lease psmdb-my-cluster-name-backup-lock
  participant A as pbm-agent on a secondary
  participant S as Storage
  U->>O: create PerconaServerMongoDBBackup "backup1"
  O->>O: is the cluster ready? another backup or restore running?
  O->>L: take the lock
  O->>A: send the backup command through PBM
  Note over O: state requested
  A->>S: copy and upload the data
  Note over O: state running
  A-->>O: PBM reports the backup done
  O->>L: release the lock
  O->>U: state ready
```

**What happens:**

1. You create a `PerconaServerMongoDBBackup` object. See [Make on-demand backups](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/backups-ondemand.html).
1. The Operator waits until the cluster is `ready`. To back up a cluster that isn’t `ready`, set `unsafeFlags.backupIfUnhealthy`. Even then, every replica set needs at least one ready member.
1. If another backup or a restore is running, or a ClusterSync replicates into the cluster, the backup goes to the `waiting` state.
1. The Operator takes the `psmdb-my-cluster-name-backup-lock` [Lease](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/glossary.html#lease), so that only one backup runs at a time. Backups that don’t get the lock stay `waiting`.
1. It sends the backup command to PBM. A PBM agent on one member of each replica set copies the data and uploads it to the storage. PBM chooses the member by priority: by default, hidden members first, then secondaries, and the primary last. Before version 1.24.0, the Operator also wrote PBM priorities that kept backups off the primary and off external members. Starting with version 1.24.0, it leaves the choice to PBM. See [How backup and restore work](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/backups.html#how-backup-and-restore-work) for what each backup type copies.
1. The Operator follows the progress in PBM, sets the state to `ready` or `error`, and releases the lock.

The backup goes through these states: empty while the Operator hasn’t processed it, `waiting`, `requested`, `running`, and `ready` or `error`. See [Backup state values](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/cr-statuses.html#backup-state-values).

`startingDeadlineSeconds` limits how long a new backup may wait before it starts. If it is omitted from the backup resource, the Operator uses `backup.startingDeadlineSeconds` from the cluster Custom Resource, or defaults to 120 seconds. When the deadline is exceeded, the backup fails.

When you delete a backup object, the `percona.com/delete-backup` [finalizer](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/glossary.html#finalizer) removes the backup files from the storage first.

**Where to look if it fails:**

- `kubectl get psmdb-backup backup1 -o yaml`: the state, `status.error`, and `status.pbmPods`, which names the member that made the backup.
- `kubectl logs <pod> -c backup-agent` on that member: errors from PBM, such as wrong storage credentials or an unreachable endpoint.
- Operator logs: `Cluster is not ready for backup`, `Waiting to finish another backup/restore` and `Another backup is holding the lock` show why a backup waits.
- See [Troubleshoot backups and restores](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/debug-backup-restore.html).
- More symptoms and the layer that owns each: [Initial troubleshooting](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/debug.html#where-to-look-first).

## Scheduled backups

Scheduled backups are not Kubernetes CronJobs. The Operator keeps the schedules from `backup.tasks` in its own memory and, when a run is due, creates a regular backup object named `cron-<cluster-name>-<timestamp>-<suffix>`, with the cluster name cut to 16 characters. The `percona.com/backup-ancestor` label holds the task name. From there, the backup follows the [on-demand workflow](#on-demand-backup).

- **The Operator creates the backup object even if the cluster isn’t `ready`.** The backup then waits until the cluster is `ready`, or until its `startingDeadlineSeconds` runs out.
- **The schedule runs only while the Operator runs.** Starting with version 1.24.0, when the Operator starts and finds that a task missed a run, it creates one catch-up backup right away. See [Making scheduled backups](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/backups-scheduled.html).
- **Retention.** With `retention` set, the Operator deletes the oldest backups of the task beyond the configured count. Retention doesn’t apply to incremental backups. See [Delete the unneeded backup](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/backups-delete.html).

**Where to look if it fails:**

- `kubectl get psmdb-backup -l percona.com/backup-ancestor=<task-name>`: the backups of one task and their states.
- Operator logs: errors creating backups and the backups deleted for retention.
- More symptoms and the layer that owns each: [Initial troubleshooting](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/debug.html#where-to-look-first).

## Point-in-time recovery

```
flowchart LR
  P["Member of each replica set"] -- "oplog slices" --> A["pbm-agent<br/>in backup-agent"]
  A -- "upload every oplogSpanMin minutes" --> S[("Main backup storage")]
  O["Operator"] -- "latestRestorableTime" --> B["Backup objects"]
```

**What happens:**

- When you set `backup.pitr.enabled` to `true`, the Operator turns on oplog slicing in the PBM configuration. No extra Pods are created.
- A PBM agent in each replica set uploads the oplog to the main backup storage in slices, every `backup.pitr.oplogSpanMin` minutes.
- PBM uploads the oplog only after a full backup exists. Take a full backup for a new cluster and after every restore.
- The `status.latestRestorableTime` field of a backup shows the latest point you can restore to.
- The Operator turns oplog slicing off right before a restore. PVC snapshot backups don’t support point-in-time recovery.

See [Enable point-in-time recovery](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/backups-pitr.html).

**Where to look if it fails:**

- `kubectl get psmdb-backup <backup> -o yaml`: `latestRestorableTime`.
- `kubectl logs <pod> -c backup-agent`: oplog upload errors, such as storage access problems.
- More symptoms and the layer that owns each: [Initial troubleshooting](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/debug.html#where-to-look-first).

## Restore

A restore replaces the data of the whole cluster, or of selected namespaces for a selective restore. You start it by creating a `PerconaServerMongoDBRestore` object. See [Restore from a backup](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/backups-restore.html).

```
stateDiagram-v2
  state "waiting" as Waiting
  state "requested" as Requested
  state "running" as Running
  [*] --> Waiting: checks, locks, PBM resync
  Waiting --> Requested: cluster prepared,<br/>restore sent to PBM
  Requested --> Running
  Running --> ready: PBM done,<br/>cluster restored to normal
  Waiting --> error
  Requested --> error
  Running --> error
  ready --> [*]
  error --> [*]
```

**What happens:**

1. **Checks.** The Operator checks the backup: with `backupName`, the backup object must be `ready`. It also checks that no backup, restore or ClusterSync holds the cluster, and that the PBM agents are up. If PBM doesn’t know the backup, the Operator asks PBM to resync the storage first. The restore stays `waiting` meanwhile.
1. **Preparation.** What the Operator does depends on the topology and the restore type. In a sharded cluster, it stops `mongos` for every restore type, so clients can’t connect. For a physical, incremental or PVC snapshot restore, it also stops the arbiters, runs PBM inside the `mongod` containers and restarts the members. A logical restore of a replica set leaves the members running, and clients stay connected, so stop your applications first. Oplog slicing for point-in-time recovery is turned off. For the downtime of each restore type, see [Downtime to expect](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/backups-restore.html#downtime-to-expect).
1. **Restore.** PBM restores the data, and for point-in-time recovery, replays the oplog up to the target.
1. **Return to normal.** The Operator brings back `mongos`, the arbiters and the regular StatefulSet configuration, and sets the state to `ready`. A restore that fails sets the state to `error`, with the reason in `status.error`.

The step-by-step flows for each backup type are in [How backup and restore work](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/backups.html#how-backup-and-restore-work).

A restore overwrites data

The data written after the backup or the point-in-time target is lost. A sharded cluster is unavailable to clients while `mongos` is stopped, and a physical restore restarts every member. After a failed restore, the Operator can’t guarantee data consistency. Take a new full backup after every restore.

**Where to look if it fails:**

- `kubectl get psmdb-restore <restore> -o yaml`: the `state`, the waiting reason, and the error in `status.error`.
- `kubectl logs <pod> -c backup-agent` for a logical restore, or the `mongod` container logs for a physical restore. See [View restore logs](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/debug-backup-restore.html#view-restore-logs).
- Operator logs.
- More symptoms and the layer that owns each: [Initial troubleshooting](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/debug.html#where-to-look-first).

# Health checks and probes

Kubernetes decides whether a container is healthy by running *probes*: small checks it runs on a schedule. It acts on the results without asking the Operator or MongoDB:

- The **readiness probe** decides whether a Pod is *ready*. Only a ready Pod receives traffic through a Service: Kubernetes adds it to the endpoints of the Services that select it and removes it when the probe fails. Ready Pods also count as available and let the next Pod of a [StatefulSet](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/glossary.html#statefulset) start.
- The **liveness probe** decides whether a container is *alive*. When it fails, the kubelet restarts the container.

What is the kubelet

The kubelet is the Kubernetes agent that runs on every node. It starts and stops the containers of the Pods scheduled to its node, runs their probes, and reports their state to the Kubernetes API. The kubelet acts on probe results locally, without involving the Operator.

For a database, this means Kubernetes keeps its own opinion about which members are healthy, and it restarts `mongod` when that opinion says so. Many behaviors that look surprising, such as a member that restarts in a loop, a node drain that never finishes, or a cluster stuck in `initializing`, come from the probes. This page explains what the probes check and who acts on their result.

The examples use a cluster named `my-cluster-name`.

## What the probes check

The Operator sets the probes for the `mongod` and `mongos` containers. Both run the `mongodb-healthcheck` tool from the Operator image. The tool connects to the local server as the `clusterMonitor` [system user](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/system-users.html) and runs a command.

### `mongod` Pods

**Readiness.** The probe first opens a TCP connection to the `mongod` port. Then it logs in and reads the member state with `replSetGetStatus`. The Pod is ready when the member is:

- `PRIMARY`, `SECONDARY` or `ARBITER`.

The Pod is not ready when the member is `STARTUP`, `STARTUP2`, `RECOVERING`, `ROLLBACK`, `DOWN`, `REMOVED` or in an unknown state.

Two exceptions keep a new cluster from blocking itself. If the probe can open the port but can’t log in, for example before the Operator has created the system users, the Pod counts as ready. The same happens when the replica set configuration is invalid, so that the Operator can fix it.

**Liveness.** The probe connects to `mongod` and reads the member state. It fails when it can’t connect. It passes when the member:

- is `PRIMARY`, `SECONDARY` or `ARBITER`;
- has no replica set configuration yet, which is normal before the Operator initializes the replica set;
- is `RECOVERING` or `ROLLBACK`: the member is busy, and a restart wouldn’t help;
- is `STARTUP` or `STARTUP2` and runs an initial sync, for as long as the sync takes.

A member that is `STARTUP` or `STARTUP2` without an initial sync gets 30 seconds plus 60 seconds for every GB of its oplog. After that, the probe fails. The probe also fails when the member is `DOWN`, `REMOVED` or in an unknown state.

**Special cases.** Two files in the container make both probes pass, whatever the state:

| File                               | Readiness | Liveness | Why                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| ---------------------------------- | --------- | -------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `/opt/percona/restore-in-progress` | Passes    | Passes   | A physical restore stops and starts `mongod` several times. The restore must not be interrupted by restarts                                                                                                                      |
| `/data/db/sleep-forever`           | Passes    | Passes   | Lets you keep the container running without `mongod` for [manual repair](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/debug-shell.html#avoid-the-restart-on-fail-loop-for-percona-server-for-mongodb-containers) |

Arbiter, non-voting and hidden members use the same checks. The `startupDelaySeconds` option of the liveness probe is deprecated, and the probe ignores it.

### `mongos` Pods

**Readiness.** The probe logs in to `mongos` and runs `listDatabases` for the `admin` database.

**Liveness.** The probe checks that the server answers and reports itself as `mongos`.

### Other containers

The `backup-agent` container has no probes by default. Starting with version 1.23.0, you can set them with `backup.livenessProbe` and `backup.readinessProbe`. The probes of the `pmm-client` and `mongot` containers are described in the [Custom Resource options](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/operator.html).

## Default timings

| Container                           | Probe     | First check after | Period | Timeout | Failures before acting | Time to act                                      |
| ----------------------------------- | --------- | ----------------- | ------ | ------- | ---------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ |
| `mongod`, data replica sets         | Readiness | 10 s              | 3 s    | 2 s     | 8                      | about 25 seconds                                 |
| `mongod`, config server replica set | Readiness | 10 s              | 3 s    | 2 s     | 3                      | about 10 seconds                                 |
| `mongod`                            | Liveness  | 90 s              | 10 s   | 5 s     | 12                     | about 2 minutes, counted after the initial delay |
| `mongos`                            | Readiness | 10 s              | 1 s    | 1 s     | 3                      | about 3 seconds                                  |
| `mongos`                            | Liveness  | 90 s              | 10 s   | 5 s     | 12                     | about 2 minutes, counted after the initial delay |

Non-voting and hidden members inherit the settings of their replica set unless you set their own.

## Who acts on readiness

A Pod’s readiness is read by several parties, each for its own purpose:

```
flowchart LR
  probe["readiness probe<br/>PRIMARY, SECONDARY or ARBITER?"] --> ready(["Pod ready"])
  ready --> svc["Headless Service<br/>DNS records of ready Pods"]
  svc --> drv["Drivers using<br/>mongodb+srv"]
  ready --> sts["StatefulSet<br/>start the next Pod"]
  ready --> pdb["PodDisruptionBudget<br/>allow an eviction"]
  ready --> op["Operator<br/>cluster status, Smart Update"]
```

### Services and DNS

The headless Service of a replica set, such as `my-cluster-name-rs0`, publishes DNS records only for ready Pods. A driver that uses a `mongodb+srv` connection string gets its first list of members from these records. After it connects, the driver uses the member list from the replica set configuration.

The `my-cluster-name-mongos` Service sends new connections only to ready `mongos` Pods.

The per-Pod Services that the Operator creates when you [expose the replica set](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/expose.html#accessing-replica-set-pods) publish the address of a Pod whether it is ready or not.

### Ordered start

Pods of a StatefulSet start in order: `my-cluster-name-rs0-1` is created only after `my-cluster-name-rs0-0` is running and ready, and so on. As a result:

- On cluster creation and scale-up, a member that can’t become ready blocks every Pod after it. This is why the readiness probe lets a Pod pass before the replica set exists.
- If `my-cluster-name-rs0-1` stays `RECOVERING`, and `my-cluster-name-rs0-2` is missing, Kubernetes doesn’t recreate `my-cluster-name-rs0-2` until `my-cluster-name-rs0-1` is ready.
- With `updateStrategy: SmartUpdate`, the Operator restarts the next Pod only when the previous one is ready.

### Node drains

The default [PodDisruptionBudget](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/glossary.html#pdb) of each StatefulSet allows one Pod to be unavailable. A Pod that is not ready counts as unavailable. While one member of a replica set is not ready, for example during a long initial sync, Kubernetes refuses to evict another one of the same StatefulSet: `kubectl drain` keeps retrying, and managed node pool upgrades wait. Some cloud providers evict the Pod anyway after their own timeout.

### The Operator

The Operator reads Pod readiness, too:

- **Cluster status.** The cluster is `ready` only when every Pod has all containers ready. When one Pod becomes not ready, the cluster goes back to `initializing`, and everything that waits for a `ready` cluster waits as well: new backups, the creation of application users, and automatic upgrades. See [What `ready` means](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/cr-statuses.html#what-ready-means).
- **[Smart Update](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/glossary.html#smart-update).** After it restarts a Pod, the Operator waits until the Pod runs the new revision and its `mongod` container is ready, for up to the liveness probe’s `initialDelaySeconds` in seconds. See [How Smart Update works](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/architecture-reconciliation.html#how-smart-update-works).
- **Database connections.** To initialize a replica set, or to rewrite its configuration when there is [no primary](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/architecture-workflows.html#replica-set-without-a-primary), the Operator connects to a ready `mongod` Pod.

## Who acts on liveness

Only the kubelet. When the liveness probe fails, the kubelet stops the container, with the termination grace period, and starts it again. After repeated restarts, the Pod goes into `CrashLoopBackOff`, and the kubelet waits longer before each next start, up to 5 minutes.

A restarted member keeps its data and host name. It rejoins the replica set and catches up from the oplog of another member. If it was down for longer than the oplog covers, it stays `RECOVERING`.

## What this means for users

The probes act on their own, and they don’t know what you are doing on the member. Keep them in mind in these situations:

- **A long initial sync.** The liveness probe tolerates an initial sync of any length. The member stays not ready until the sync completes, so it blocks node drains and the Smart Update meanwhile.
- **A member that fell too far behind.** It stays `RECOVERING`. The liveness probe passes, so Kubernetes doesn’t restart it, but it stays not ready. It blocks node drains, the start of the Pods after it, and the Smart Update until it gets a full copy of the data.
- **A network partition.** A member that loses contact with the majority becomes a secondary, which is still ready and alive. Kubernetes doesn’t restart it, and it rejoins when the network comes back.
- **A slow or stalled server.** If `mongod` doesn’t answer the liveness probe within 5 seconds, 12 times in a row, the container is restarted. Common causes are a stalled disk, CPU throttling by the container’s CPU limit, and an overloaded server. Check the Pod events for `Liveness probe failed` before you look for a crash in the `mongod` log.
- **The `clusterMonitor` user.** Every probe logs in as `clusterMonitor`. If you change its password directly in MongoDB instead of in the users Secret, drop it, or lock it, the liveness probe fails on every data-bearing member. The kubelets restart containers independently, potentially at the same time, which can make the replica set unavailable. Change system user passwords only through the Secret. See [System users](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/system-users.html).
- **Manual maintenance on a running member.** If you stop `mongod` or remove the member from the replica set, the liveness probe fails within about 2 minutes and the container restarts. To work on a member without `mongod` running, use the `sleep-forever` file. See [Avoid the restart-on-fail loop](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/debug-shell.html#avoid-the-restart-on-fail-loop-for-percona-server-for-mongodb-containers).
- **A Pod that stays not ready.** It blocks node drains, the start of the Pods after it, the Smart Update, and everything that waits for a `ready` cluster.

## Tune the probes

Change the probe settings in the [Custom Resource](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/glossary.html#custom-resource) with the `livenessProbe` and `readinessProbe` subsections of `replsets`, `replsets.nonvoting`, `replsets.hidden`, `sharding.configsvrReplSet` and `sharding.mongos`. See [Custom Resource options](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/operator.html#replsetslivenessprobefailurethreshold).

- Probe settings are part of the Pod template. Changing them restarts the Pods with your [update strategy](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/architecture-reconciliation.html#update-strategies).
- If heavy load makes the liveness probe time out, raise `livenessProbe.timeoutSeconds` or `failureThreshold` rather than turning the probe off.
- `livenessProbe.initialDelaySeconds` also limits how long the Smart Update waits for each restarted Pod. Raise it if your members need more than 90 seconds to start and become ready.

## Where to look if probes fail

- `kubectl describe pod my-cluster-name-rs0-0` shows the probe settings and, under `Events`, the `Readiness probe failed` and `Liveness probe failed` messages with the reason the tool reported.
- `kubectl get pod my-cluster-name-rs0-0` shows the restart count. If the events contain `Container mongod failed liveness probe, will be restarted`, the kubelet restarted the container; it was not a `mongod` crash.
- `kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | grep -i probe` lists probe failures across the cluster.
- `kubectl get endpoints my-cluster-name-rs0` shows which members are ready.
- `kubectl get pdb` shows how many disruptions each PodDisruptionBudget allows right now.
- More symptoms and the layer that owns each: [Initial troubleshooting](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/debug.html#where-to-look-first).

# Compare various solutions to deploy MongoDB in Kubernetes

There are multiple ways to deploy and manage MongoDB in Kubernetes. Here we will focus on comparing the following open source solutions:

- [Bitnami Helm chart](https://github.com/bitnami/charts/tree/master/bitnami/mongodb)
- [KubeDB](https://github.com/kubedb)
- [MongoDB Controllers for Kubernetes (MCK)](https://github.com/mongodb/mongodb-kubernetes)
- [Percona Operator for MongoDB](https://github.com/percona/percona-server-mongodb-operator/)

## Generic

Here is the review of generic features, such as supported MongoDB versions, open source models and more.

| Feature/Product        | Percona Operator for MongoDB           | Bitnami Helm Chart | KubeDB for MongoDB                         | MongoDB Controllers for Kubernetes (MCK)                                                                                  |
| ---------------------- | -------------------------------------- | ------------------ | ------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Open source model      | Apache 2.0                             | Apache 2.0         | Open core                                  | Open core                                                                                                                 |

| Web-based GUI          | [OpenEverest](https://openeverest.io/) |                    | [kubedb-ui](https://kubedb.com/datasheet/) | [Ops Manager / Cloud Manager](https://www.mongodb.com/products/self-managed/enterprise-advanced/ops-manager) (Enterprise) |

\* Percona Operator relies on [Percona Server for MongoDB](https://www.percona.com/mongodb/software/percona-server-for-mongodb) - a free, enhanced, fully compatible MongoDB software alternative for MongoDB Community Server with enterprise-grade features.

# Known limitations

This page describes known limitations of Percona Operator for MongoDB. Understanding these constraints helps you plan deployments and avoid unexpected behavior.

## Hardware and CPU requirements

### x86-64-v3 CPU microarchitecture (Operator 1.22.0 and later)

Starting with Operator version [1.22.0](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/RN/Kubernetes-Operator-for-PSMONGODB-RN1.22.0.html), the Operator image is based on [Red Hat Universal Base Image (UBI) 10](https://catalog.redhat.com/software/base-images) . RHEL 10 / UBI 10 requires the **x86-64-v3** CPU microarchitecture on `amd64` hosts. That level includes AVX2, BMI1, BMI2, and FMA (roughly Intel Haswell 2013 or newer, or AMD Excavator 2015 or newer).

This requirement is stricter than the [AVX requirement for MongoDB 5.0 and later](https://docs.percona.com/percona-server-for-mongodb/8.0/system-requirements.html) . Older hosts such as Sandy Bridge-class CPUs may meet the MongoDB AVX requirement but still fail with UBI 10.

## Backups and restores

- Point-in-time recovery and selective restore are not available for [PVC snapshot backups](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/backups-pvc-snapshots.html) (type `external`).
- When you delete an incremental base backup, Percona Backup for MongoDB also deletes all increments that derived from it from the backup storage. The `percona.com/delete-backup` finalizer applies to the base backup and is ignored for increments. This means that the Operator deletes the Backup resource for the base incremental backup but the Backup resources for increments remain because the Operator doesn’t control their deletion.
- Restoring a collection under a different name is supported only on replica set clusters for unsharded collections from a full logical backup. It is not supported on sharded clusters. See [Restore a collection under a different name](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/backups-restore-new-name.html#limitations).
- Selective restores have additional constraints in Percona Backup for MongoDB. See the [selective restore limitations](https://docs.percona.com/percona-backup-mongodb/features/known-limitations.html#selective-backups-and-restores) .
- After a failed restore, the Operator cannot guarantee data consistency because it does not know at which stage the failure happened. See [Restore from a backup](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/backups-restore.html).

## Multi-cluster and multi-region deployments

- The Operator cannot place MongoDB Pods in other data centers by itself. Cross-site topologies need an Operator deployment on each site, with unmanaged clusters registered as `externalNodes` on the Main site. Setup and scaling require manual operations. See [Splitting a replica set across multiple data centers](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/replication-multi-dc.html).
- Backups are supported on the Main site only, not on Replica sites in a multi-datacenter replica set split.
- Multi-cluster Services (MCS) can add cloud-provider limits. For example, on GKE all participating Pods must be in the same project. Avoid exporting Services from the `default` and `kube-system` namespaces. See [Multi-cluster Services](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/replication-mcs.html).
- Setting `clusterServiceDNSMode` to `ServiceMesh` supersedes multi-cluster settings. You cannot combine `ServiceMesh` DNS mode with multi-cluster Services. See the [Custom Resource options](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/operator.html#clusterservicednsmode).

## Networking and exposure

Split horizon DNS has these MongoDB constraints:

- You cannot duplicate domain names in horizons
- You cannot use IP addresses in horizons
- You must set horizons for all Pods of a replica set, or for none of them

See [Exposing the cluster](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/expose.html).

## Search and vector search

Percona Search for MongoDB is in the tech preview stage. Notable limits include:

- a single search Pod per replica set or shard,
- no automated embedding,
- no migration from externally managed `mongot`, and
- search index data is not included in backups.

See [Limitations](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/search-overview.html#limitations) in the search overview.

## Real-time replication with Percona ClusterSync for MongoDB

PCSM follows upstream [known issues and limitations](https://docs.percona.com/percona-clustersync-for-mongodb/limitations.html) .

Notable constraints:

- Source and target run the same major MongoDB version, or one of the supported upgrade paths. See [Supported MongoDB deployments](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/clustersync.html#supported-mongodb-deployments).
- Single source / single target pair only.
- Reverse synchronization is not supported.
- The initial clone is **not resumable**, even with high availability. If it’s interrupted, start a new sync. A failover during the clone stops the sync with the error `initial clone interrupted by failover and is not resumable`. See [Status shows `failed`](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/clustersync-setup.html#status-shows-failed).
- With high availability, the Operator replaces the PCSM Pods in no fixed order during an update, so the active role can move more than once.
- PCSM connects to the **primary** only; `directConnection` to secondaries is ignored.
- Users, roles, and `system.*` collections are not synchronized.
- Unsupported types include timeseries, queryable encryption, Percona Memory Engine, and several sharding admin commands during replication.
- External authentication (LDAP, Kerberos, AWS IAM) is not supported for PCSM connections.

[Get started](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/quickstart.html)
# Features

# Features

The Percona Operator for MongoDB is a Kubernetes-native controller that automatically manages the full lifecycle of Percona Server for MongoDB clusters. The Operator offloads your teams from manual day-to-day database management so you can focus on building applications and running the platform.

## Core capabilities

Here is what the Operator brings to your infrastructure:

### High availability and failover

**MongoDB’s built-in high availability** — Replica sets and sharding give you data redundancy and automatic failover at the database layer. A [replica set](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/architecture.html#replica-set) uses elections to promote a new primary when the current one fails, with no manual intervention. With [sharding](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/sharding.html), data is distributed across shards (each shard is a replica set), and mongos routes traffic. Both topologies are designed for availability and scale.

**What the Operator adds** — The Operator runs these topologies reliably in Kubernetes:

- **Pod distribution** — Use [anti-affinity rules](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/constraints.html) to spread replica set members (and optionally arbiters) across nodes so a single node failure does not take down multiple members.
- **Health and rescheduling** — If a node or Pod fails, Kubernetes reschedules the workload; the replica set reconnects and continues serving traffic.
- **Rolling upgrades** — [Upgrade the Operator](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/update-operator.html) and [Percona Server for MongoDB](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/update-db.html) with minimal or no downtime.
- **Multi-cluster and multi-region** — Use [multi-cluster or multi-region deployments](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/replication.html) (including [Multi-cluster Services (MCS)](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/replication-mcs.html) where supported) for disaster recovery, cross-site replication, and migration. You can replicate data across clusters or regions so that if one site fails, another can serve traffic.

### Backup and restore

Protect your data with Percona Backup for MongoDB, which runs as a sidecar in your database Pods. The [Backup and restore](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/backups.html) overview covers types, storages, restores, and point-in-time recovery. When you are ready to set things up, follow [Configure backups](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/backups-configure.html).

- **Scheduled and on-demand backups** — [Run backups on a schedule](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/backups-scheduled.html) or [create one when you need it](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/backups-ondemand.html).
- **Logical, physical, incremental, and PVC snapshots** — See [backup types](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/backups.html#backup-types) to pick the right one.
- **Point-in-time recovery** — Roll back the database to a specific time.
- **Restore** — [Restore on the same cluster or a new cluster](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/backups-restore.html).

### Automated scaling and resource management

Scale your database infrastructure as demand grows:

- **Horizontal scaling** — [Add replica set members](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/scaling.html) or scale [shards and mongos](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/sharding.html) when sharding is enabled.
- **Vertical scaling** — Adjust CPU and memory limits in the PerconaServerMongoDB custom resource.
- **Storage expansion** — Expand PersistentVolumeClaims for database volumes when your storage class supports it.
- **Pod placement** — Use [affinity and anti-affinity](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/constraints.html) to control which nodes run MongoDB Pods, arbiters, or mongos.

### Security and compliance

Keep your data and backups secure with built-in options:

- **Transport encryption** — [Enable TLS](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/TLS.html) for client and server; use [cert-manager](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/tls-cert-manager.html) or [custom certificates](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/tls-manual.html).
- **Data-at-rest encryption** — [Encrypt MongoDB data on disk](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/encryption.html).
- **Users and roles** — Manage [application users](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/app-users.html) and [system users](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/system-users.html); optionally use [Vault](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/system-users-vault.html) for system user credentials.
- **Backup encryption** — [Encrypt backups](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/backups-encryption.html) in object storage.

### Monitoring and observability

Gain visibility into your database and cluster:

- **Percona Monitoring and Management (PMM)** — [Integrate PMM](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/monitoring.html) via sidecar for metrics, query analysis, and dashboards.
- **Kubernetes monitoring** — [Monitor the Kubernetes layer](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/monitor-kubernetes.html) alongside the database.
- **Logging** — Configure [persistent logging](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/persistent-logging.html) and [log rotation](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/logrotate.html).
- **Custom options** — [Tune MongoDB options](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/options.html) and [PBM options](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/options-pbm.html) via the custom resource.
- **Sidecars** — Add [sidecar containers](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/sidecar.html) (e.g. custom exporters or tools) to replica set, config server, or mongos Pods.

## Understand how it works

The [Design and architecture](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/architecture.html) pages explain the controller model, the components the Operator manages, and what stays with you.
