## Setting labels and annotations in the Custom Resource

You can define both Labels and Annotations as `key-value` pairs in the metadata section of a YAML manifest for a specific resource.

### Set labels and annotations for Pods

To specify labels and annotations for Percona Server for MongoDB Pods, use the `replsets.<name>.annotations` /`replsets.<name>.labels`, `sharding.configsvrReplSet.annotations` / `sharding.configsvrReplSet.labels` and `sharding.mongos.annotations` / `sharding.mongos.labels` options in the `deploy/cr.yaml` Custom Resource. The example configuration for Percona Server for MongoDB database instances looks as follows:

```
apiVersion: psmdb.percona.com/v1
kind: PerconaServerMongoDB
spec:
  replsets:
  - name: rs0
    annotations:
      iam.amazonaws.com/role: role-arn
    labels:
      rack: rack-22 
    ...
```

### Set labels and annotations for Services

To annotate Services, use the `replsets.<name>.expose.annotations` / `replsets.<name>.expose.labels`, `sharding.configsvrReplSet.expose.annotations` / `sharding.configsvrReplSet.expose.labels` and `sharding.mongos.expose.annotations` / `sharding.mongos.expose.labels` options in the `deploy/cr.yaml` Custom Resource. The example configuration for `mongos` is:

```
spec:
  sharding:
    mongos:
      expose:
        annotations:
          service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-backend-protocol: http
        labels:
          rack: rack-22
```

## Querying labels and annotations

To check which **labels** are attached to a specific object, use the additional `--show-labels` option of the `kubectl get` command.

For example, to see the Operator version associated with a Custom Resource Definition, use the following command:

```
kubectl get crd perconaservermongodbs.psmdb.percona.com --show-labels
```

Sample output

```
NAME                                      CREATED AT             LABELS
perconaservermongodbs.psmdb.percona.com   2025-09-18T08:27:53Z   app.kubernetes.io/component=crd,app.kubernetes.io/name=percona-server-mongodb,app.kubernetes.io/part-of=percona-server-mongodb-operator,app.kubernetes.io/version=v1.23.1
```

To check **annotations** associated with an object, use the following command:

```
kubectl get <resource> <resource-name> -o jsonpath='{.metadata.annotations}'
```

For example:

```
kubectl get pod my-cluster-name-rs0-0 -o jsonpath='{.metadata.annotations}'
```

## Specifying labels and annotations ignored by the Operator

Sometimes various Kubernetes flavors can add their own annotations to the Services managed by the Operator.

The Operator keeps track of all changes to its objects and can remove annotations that it didn’t create.

If there are no annotations or labels in the Custom Resource `expose.*` subsections, the Operator does nothing if a new label or annotation is added to the Service object.

If the [Service per Pod](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/expose.html#service-per-pod) mode is not used, the Operator **won’t remove any annotations and labels** from any Services related to *this expose subsection*. Though, it is still possible to add annotations and labels via the Custom Resource in this case. Use the appropriate `expose.serviceAnnotations` and `expose.serviceLabels` fields.

Else, if the [Service per Pod](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/expose.html#service-per-pod) mode is active, the Operator removes unknown annotations and labels from Services *created by the Operator for Pods*.

Yet it is still possible to specify which annotations and labels the Operator should keep. It is useful if a cloud provider adds own labels and annotations. Or you may have custom automation tools that add own labels or annotations and you need to keep them.

List these labels and annotations in the `spec.ignoreAnnotations` or `spec.ignoreLabels` fields of the `deploy/cr.yaml`, as follows:

```
spec:
  ignoreAnnotations:
    - some.custom.cloud.annotation/smth
  ignoreLabels:
    - some.custom.cloud.label/smth
...
```

The label and annotation values must exactly match the ones defined for the Service to be kept.

External DNS annotations follow separate ownership rules. The Operator manages `external-dns.alpha.kubernetes.io/hostname` and `/ttl` only on Services marked with `percona.com/external-dns-managed`. Manual External DNS annotations on unmarked Services, and other External DNS keys such as `/target` or `/alias`, are preserved and do not need to be listed in `ignoreAnnotations`. See [How the Operator manages External DNS annotations](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/expose.html#how-the-operator-manages-external-dns-annotations) for details.

# Configure concurrency for a cluster reconciliation

Reconciliation is the process by which the Operator continuously compares the desired state with the actual state of the cluster. The desired state is defined in a Kubernetes custom resource, like PerconaServerMongoDB.

If the actual state does not match the desired state, the Operator takes actions to bring the system into alignment. This means creating, updating, or deleting Kubernetes resources (Pods, Services, ConfigMaps, etc.) or performing database-specific operations like scaling, backups, or failover.

Reconciliation is triggered by a variety of events, including:

- Changes to the cluster configuration
- Changes to the cluster state
- Changes to the cluster resources

You can tune reconciliation behavior with these environment variables in the `percona-server-mongodb-operator` Deployment:

- `MAX_CONCURRENT_RECONCILES` — how many clusters the Operator can reconcile in parallel
- `RECONCILE_INTERVAL` — how long the Operator waits before re-queuing reconciliation for each cluster
- `BACKUP_RECONCILE_INTERVAL` and `RESTORE_RECONCILE_INTERVAL` — how often the Operator rechecks backups and restores that are in progress.

See [Configure Operator environment variables](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/env-vars-operator.html) for the full list of supported values and defaults.

## Configure concurrent reconciliation workers

By default, the Operator has one reconciliation worker. This means that if you deploy or update 2 clusters at the same time, the Operator will reconcile them sequentially.

The `MAX_CONCURRENT_RECONCILES` environment variable controls the number of concurrent workers that can reconcile resources in Percona Server for MongoDB clusters in parallel.

Thus, to extend the previous example, if you set the number of reconciliation workers to `2`, the Operator will reconcile both clusters in parallel. This also helps you with benchmarking the Operator performance.

The general recommendation is to set the number of concurrent workers equal to the number of Percona Server for MongoDB clusters. When the number of workers is greater, the excessive workers will remain idle.

### Set the number of reconciliation workers

1. Check the index of the `MAX_CONCURRENT_RECONCILES` environment variable using the following command:

   ```
   kubectl get deployment percona-server-mongodb-operator -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].env[?(@.name=="MAX_CONCURRENT_RECONCILES")].value}'
   ```

   Sample output

   ```
   1
   ```

1. To set a new value and verify it’s been updated, run the following command:

   ```
   kubectl patch deployment percona-server-mongodb-operator \
   --type='strategic' \
   -o yaml \
   -p='{
       "spec": {
           "template": {
               "spec": {
                   "containers": [
                       {
                           "name": "percona-server-mongodb-operator",
                           "env": [
                               {
                                   "name": "MAX_CONCURRENT_RECONCILES",
                                   "value": "2"
                               }
                           ]
                       }
                   ]
               }
           }
       }
   }'\
   -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].env[?(@.name=="MAX_CONCURRENT_RECONCILES")].value}'
   ```

The command does the following:

- Patches the deployment to update the `MAX_CONCURRENT_RECONCILES` environment variable
- Sets the value to `2`.
- Outputs the result

You can set the value to any number greater than 0.

Sample output

```
2
```

## Configure the reconciliation interval

After each reconcile loop, the Operator schedules the next one after an interval. Each kind of object has its own interval:

| Environment variable         | What the Operator rechecks                                                                  | Default |
| ---------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------- |
| `RECONCILE_INTERVAL`         | Each cluster                                                                                | `5s`    |
| `BACKUP_RECONCILE_INTERVAL`  | Backups that are waiting, running or being canceled. Available starting with version 1.24.0 | `5s`    |
| `RESTORE_RECONCILE_INTERVAL` | Restores that are in progress. Available starting with version 1.24.0                       | `5s`    |

Increasing a value reduces Kubernetes API traffic from the Operator. This can be useful in large environments where the default interval generates more requests than needed. For example, raise `BACKUP_RECONCILE_INTERVAL` if you run many backups and want cluster changes to stay fast.

A longer interval also means that the Operator notices changes later. Backup and restore status updates arrive up to one interval late. A restore goes through several steps, so a long `RESTORE_RECONCILE_INTERVAL` can make restores take noticeably longer.

All three variables accept a Go duration string, such as `30s` or `1m`. Values below `5s`, zero, negative, or invalid duration strings fall back to `5s`.

### Set the reconciliation interval

1. Check the current value:

   ```
   kubectl -n <namespace> get deployment percona-server-mongodb-operator -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].env[?(@.name=="RECONCILE_INTERVAL")].value}'
   ```

   Sample output

   ```
   5s
   ```

1. To set a new value and verify it’s been updated, run the following command:

   ```
   kubectl -n <namespace> patch deployment percona-server-mongodb-operator \
   --type='strategic' \
   -o yaml \
   -p='{
       "spec": {
           "template": {
               "spec": {
                   "containers": [
                       {
                           "name": "percona-server-mongodb-operator",
                           "env": [
                               {
                                   "name": "RECONCILE_INTERVAL",
                                   "value": "30s"
                               }
                           ]
                       }
                   ]
               }
           }
       }
   }'\
   -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].env[?(@.name=="RECONCILE_INTERVAL")].value}'
   ```

The command does the following:

- Patches the deployment to update the `RECONCILE_INTERVAL` environment variable
- Sets the value to `30s`
- Outputs the result

To change `BACKUP_RECONCILE_INTERVAL` or `RESTORE_RECONCILE_INTERVAL`, use the same command with that variable name. Changing the Deployment restarts the Operator Pod, and the new value applies from then on.

Sample output

```
30s
```

# Use Docker images from a custom registry

Using images from a private Docker registry may required for privacy, security or other reasons. In these cases, Percona Operator for MongoDB allows the use of a custom registry This following example of the Operator deployed in the OpenShift environment demonstrates the process:

1. Log into the OpenShift and create a project.

   ```
   oc login
   ```

   Expected output

   ```
   Authentication required for https://192.168.1.100:8443 (openshift)
   Username: admin
   Password:
   Login successful.
   ```

   ```
   oc new-project psmdb
   ```

   Expected output

   ```
   Now using project "psmdb" on server "https://192.168.1.100:8443".
   ```

1. You need obtain the following objects to configure your custom registry access:

   - A user token
   - the registry IP address

   You can view the token with the following command:

   ```
   oc whoami -t
   ```

   Expected output

   ```
   ADO8CqCDappWR4hxjfDqwijEHei31yXAvWg61Jg210s
   ```

   The following command returns the registry IP address:

   ```
   kubectl get services/docker-registry -n default
   ```

   Expected output

   ```
   NAME              TYPE        CLUSTER-IP       EXTERNAL-IP   PORT(S)    AGE
   docker-registry   ClusterIP   172.30.162.173   <none>        5000/TCP   1d
   ```

1. Use the user token and the registry IP address to login to the registry:

   ```
   docker login -u admin -p ADO8CqCDappWR4hxjfDqwijEHei31yXAvWg61Jg210s 172.30.162.173:5000
   ```

   Expected output

   ```
   Login Succeeded
   ```

1. Use the Docker commands to pull the needed image by its SHA digest:

   ```
   docker pull docker.io/perconalab/percona-server-mongodb@sha256:991d6049059e5eb1a74981290d829a5fb4ab0554993748fde1e67b2f46f26bf0
   ```

   Expected output

   ```
   Trying to pull repository docker.io/perconalab/percona-server-mongodb ...
   sha256:991d6049059e5eb1a74981290d829a5fb4ab0554993748fde1e67b2f46f26bf0: Pulling from docker.io/perconalab/percona-server-mongodb
   Digest: sha256:991d6049059e5eb1a74981290d829a5fb4ab0554993748fde1e67b2f46f26bf0
   Status: Image is up to date for docker.io/perconalab/percona-server-mongodb@sha256:991d6049059e5eb1a74981290d829a5fb4ab0554993748fde1e67b2f46f26bf0
   ```

   You can find correct names and SHA digests in the [current list of the Operator-related images officially certified by Percona](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/images.html).

1. The following method can push an image to the custom registry for the example OpenShift `psmdb` project:

   ```
   docker tag \
       docker.io/perconalab/percona-server-mongodb@sha256:991d6049059e5eb1a74981290d829a5fb4ab0554993748fde1e67b2f46f26bf0 \
       172.30.162.173:5000/psmdb/percona-server-mongodb:7.0.43-23
   docker push 172.30.162.173:5000/psmdb/percona-server-mongodb:7.0.43-23
   ```

1. Verify the image is available in the OpenShift registry with the following command:

   ```
   oc get is
   ```

   Expected output

   ```
   NAME                              DOCKER REPO                                                             TAGS             UPDATED
   percona-server-mongodb            docker-registry.default.svc:5000/psmdb/percona-server-mongodb  7.0.43-23  2 hours ago
   ```

1. When the custom registry image is available, edit the the `image:` option in `deploy/operator.yaml` configuration file with a Docker Repo + Tag string (it should look like `docker-registry.default.svc:5000/psmdb/percona-server-mongodb:7.0.43-23`)

   Note

   If the registry requires authentication, you can specify the `imagePullSecrets` option for all images.

1. Repeat steps 3-5 for other images, and update corresponding options in the `deploy/cr.yaml` file.

   Note

   Don’t forget to set [upgradeoptions.apply](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/operator.html#upgradeoptionsapply) option to `Disabled`. Otherwise [Smart Upgrade functionality](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/update.html#update-strategies) will try using the image recommended by the Version Service instead of the custom one.

   Note

   If a cluster’s `crVersion` is older than the Operator and you don’t set `initImage`, the Operator pulls the Operator image tag that matches `crVersion` for the init container. For example, Operator 1.23.1 running a cluster with `crVersion: 1.22.0` uses the `1.22.0` tag. Push that tag to your registry too, or set `initImage` explicitly. See [Init image](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/update-crversion.html#init-image).

1. Now follow the standard Percona Operator for MongoDB [installation instruction](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/System-Requirements.html#installation-guidelines).

## See also

- [What `crVersion` does](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/update-crversion.html#what-crversion-does)
- [Troubleshooting](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/debug.html) - environment variables, reconciliation concurrency, and hook scripts are exactly what gets tuned in response to an observed problem

# Pause and resume the cluster

Pausing stops all database Pods and keeps the data. Clients can’t connect while the cluster is paused. Pause the cluster when you need it down for a while, for example during maintenance of the Kubernetes infrastructure or to [update expired TLS certificates](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/tls-update.html#update-certificates-with-downtime). To remove the cluster for good, [delete it](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/delete.html#delete-the-database-cluster) instead.

## Before you start

- Check that no backup is running. The Operator doesn’t pause the cluster until running backups finish:

  ```
  kubectl get psmdb-backup -n <namespace>
  ```

  Backups in the `ready`, `error` or `waiting` state don’t delay the pause.

- Stop the applications that write to the cluster, or make sure they can handle the outage.

## Pause the cluster

Set `spec.pause` to `true`. Replace `my-cluster-name` with the name of your cluster:

```
kubectl patch psmdb my-cluster-name -n <namespace> --type=merge --patch '{"spec": {"pause": true}}'
```

You can also set `pause: true` in your `deploy/cr.yaml` file and apply it with `kubectl apply -f deploy/cr.yaml -n <namespace>`.

## What happens during a pause

The Operator stops the cluster in an order that keeps the data consistent:

1. If a backup is running, the Operator waits until it finishes. Until then, the cluster stays `ready`, and the Operator logs `cluster will pause after all backups finished`.
1. In a sharded cluster, the Operator stops the `mongos` Pods first, so clients can’t connect during the shutdown.
1. It stops the `mongot` search Pods, and the arbiter, non-voting and hidden members.
1. In each replica set, it makes the Pod with the index 0, for example `my-cluster-name-rs0-0`, the primary. It then stops the other members one Pod at a time. The primary stops last, so the member that starts first on resume has the latest data.
1. In a sharded cluster, the config server replica set stops after all shards.

While the cluster is paused:

- PVCs and the data on them stay in place.
- The Operator doesn’t run Smart Updates, change the backup configuration, or manage the balancer.
- The `status.state` field is `stopping` while Pods shut down, and `paused` when all of them have stopped.

The Operator also pauses the cluster by itself when you turn sharding on or off with backups enabled. See [Turning sharding on and off](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/sharding.html#turning-sharding-on-and-off).

## Verify the pause

1. Check the cluster state:

   ```
   kubectl get psmdb -n <namespace>
   ```

   The `STATUS` column shows `paused`.

1. Check that no database Pods are left:

   ```
   kubectl get pods -n <namespace> -l app.kubernetes.io/instance=my-cluster-name
   ```

   The output has no `mongod`, `mongos` or `mongot` Pods.

## Resume the cluster

Set `spec.pause` back to `false`:

```
kubectl patch psmdb my-cluster-name -n <namespace> --type=merge --patch '{"spec": {"pause": false}}'
```

The Operator starts the Pods again with their existing PVCs. The state changes to `initializing`, and then to `ready` when all members are up and the [conditions for `ready`](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/cr-statuses.html#what-ready-means) are met.

## Troubleshooting

**Symptom:** The cluster stays `ready` after you set `pause: true`.

**Cause:** A backup is running. The Operator waits for it to finish.

**Fix:**

1. Check the Operator logs for `cluster will pause after all backups finished`.
1. Run `kubectl get psmdb-backup -n <namespace>` and wait until the backup reaches the `ready` or `error` state. The pause then starts on its own.

**Symptom:** The cluster stays in `stopping`.

**Cause:** A Pod doesn’t terminate, or the Operator can’t make the Pod with the index 0 the primary. The Operator logs `deleting rs pods` with the replica set name and the reason, for example `waiting first pod to become primary`.

**Fix:**

1. Check which Pods are still running with `kubectl get pods -n <namespace>`.
1. Check the Operator logs for the `deleting rs pods` messages.
1. If a Pod is stuck in `Terminating`, check its events with `kubectl describe pod <pod-name> -n <namespace>`.

For other problems, see [Initial troubleshooting](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/debug.html).

## See also

- [Update certificates with downtime](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/tls-update.html#update-certificates-with-downtime) uses a pause to replace expired TLS certificates.
- [Custom Resource statuses](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/cr-statuses.html) explains every value of `status.state` and the conditions behind it.
- [How the Operator reacts to changes](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/architecture-reconciliation.html#what-happens-when-i-change-a-field) shows how other Custom Resource changes affect the Pods.
# Troubleshooting

# Initial troubleshooting

Use this page when something is wrong and you don’t know the cause yet. For example, the cluster doesn’t reach the `ready` state, Pods restart or don’t start, or clients can’t connect. Start with the quick health check, find which layer the problem is in, then use the symptom tables to reach the page with the fix.

## Before you start

- You need `kubectl` access to the namespace of the cluster and to the namespace of the Operator. They are the same namespace unless you run the Operator in the [cluster-wide mode](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/cluster-wide.html).
- The examples use the cluster name `my-cluster-name`. Replace it and `<namespace>` with your values.

## Quick health check

Run these three checks first. Together they take a minute and show which part of the system needs a closer look.

### Check the cluster status

```
kubectl get psmdb -n <namespace>
```

Expected output

```
NAME              ENDPOINT                                           STATUS   AGE
my-cluster-name   my-cluster-name-mongos.default.svc.cluster.local   ready    5m26s
```

A healthy cluster is `ready`. The cluster is `initializing` while it is created and while it applies a change. If it stays there, see [Cluster stays in `initializing`](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/troubleshoot-operator.html#cluster-stays-in-initializing). For an `error` state, the reason is in the `status.message` field:

```
kubectl get psmdb my-cluster-name -n <namespace> -o yaml
```

For what each state means and what the cluster must meet to be `ready`, see [Custom Resource statuses](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/cr-statuses.html#what-ready-means).

### Check the Pods

```
kubectl get pods -n <namespace>
```

Expected output

```
NAME                                               READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
my-cluster-name-cfg-0                              2/2     Running   0          11m
my-cluster-name-cfg-1                              2/2     Running   1          10m
my-cluster-name-cfg-2                              2/2     Running   1          9m
my-cluster-name-mongos-0                           1/1     Running   0          11m
my-cluster-name-mongos-1                           1/1     Running   0          11m
my-cluster-name-mongos-2                           1/1     Running   0          11m
my-cluster-name-rs0-0                              2/2     Running   0          11m
my-cluster-name-rs0-1                              2/2     Running   0          10m
my-cluster-name-rs0-2                              2/2     Running   0          9m
percona-server-mongodb-operator-665cd69f9b-xg5dl   1/1     Running   0          37m
```

In a healthy cluster, every Pod is `Running` and the `READY` column shows all containers ready, such as `2/2`. A database Pod runs the `mongod` container and, depending on your configuration, `backup-agent`, `pmm-client`, `logs` and `logrotate`. See [Containers in each Pod](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/objects-created.html#containers-in-each-pod).

A growing `RESTARTS` count means a container keeps failing. The `STATUS` column points to where to look next:

| `STATUS`                                                                         | What it means                                              | Where to look                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Running`, but `READY` is lower than the number of containers                    | A container started but isn’t ready yet                    | [Check the logs](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/debug-logs.html) of the container that isn’t ready                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| `Pending`                                                                        | Kubernetes hasn’t placed the Pod on a node                 | [Troubleshoot Pod scheduling](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/debug-scheduling.html)                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| `ContainerCreating`                                                              | The Pod is on a node, but a volume or an image isn’t ready | The `Events` section of `kubectl describe pod <pod-name> -n <namespace>`                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| `ImagePullBackOff`, `ErrImagePull`                                               | The node can’t pull the image                              | Check the image name and registry access. See [Use a private registry](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/custom-registry.html)                                                                                                                                                            |
| `CrashLoopBackOff`                                                               | A container starts and exits repeatedly                    | [Check the logs](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/debug-logs.html) with `--previous`, and [stop the restart loop](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/debug-shell.html#avoid-the-restart-on-fail-loop-for-percona-server-for-mongodb-containers) to investigate |
| `OOMKilled`, or `OOMKilled` as the `Last State` reason in `kubectl describe pod` | The container ran out of memory                            | [Troubleshoot out-of-memory errors](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/debug-oom.html)                                                                                                                                                                                                     |

### Check the Operator

Find the Operator Deployment. Its name depends on how you installed the Operator: `percona-server-mongodb-operator` for a `kubectl` installation, and usually a name that ends with `psmdb-operator` for Helm:

```
kubectl get deployments -n <operator-namespace> | grep -E 'percona-server-mongodb-operator|psmdb-operator'
```

Read its recent logs:

```
kubectl logs deployment/<operator-deployment> -n <operator-namespace> --since=30m
```

The Operator Pod should be `Running` with no restarts. The logs show what the Operator is doing and what it waits for. Repeated `ERROR` lines for the same cluster point to the problem.

## Which layer is it?

Problems come from four layers: your configuration, the Operator, Kubernetes, or Percona Server for MongoDB itself. See [Who owns what](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/architecture-responsibilities.html) for what each layer does.

Check these sources in order. Each one narrows down the layer.

1. **Custom Resource status and conditions.** `kubectl get psmdb my-cluster-name -n <namespace> -o yaml` shows the cluster state, the reconcile error message, the state of each replica set and of `mongos`, and scheduling problems. An `error` state with a message about the spec points to your configuration. See [Custom Resource statuses](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/cr-statuses.html#perconaservermongodb-status).

1. **Events.** Kubernetes problems show up here: scheduling, volume attachment and resize, image pulls, probe failures. The Operator itself adds no events for the cluster. To see the events of one Pod:

   ```
   kubectl get events -n <namespace> --sort-by=.lastTimestamp --field-selector involvedObject.name=<pod-name>
   ```

1. **Operator logs.** They show what the Operator is doing or waiting for: a stuck rolling restart, a backup that waits, a change to the replica set configuration. Most Operator problems appear only here. See [Check the Operator](#check-the-operator).

1. **Database logs.** They show MongoDB problems: elections, initial sync, start failures. With the log collector enabled, as in the default `deploy/cr.yaml`, `mongod` writes its log to a file, so read it from the `logs` container: `kubectl logs my-cluster-name-rs0-0 -n <namespace> -c logs`. Without the log collector, use `-c mongod`. For backup and restore problems, read the `backup-agent` logs. See [Check the logs](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/debug-logs.html).

## Where to look first

Find the symptom, check the place in the second column, and follow the link for the fix.

### Cluster and Pods

| Symptom                                                                                                                     | Look here first                                                                                       | Usually owned by                                                                                                                                       | What to do                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Cluster status is `error` with a message that starts with `wrong psmdb options`, such as `replset size must be odd`         | The `status` section of `kubectl get psmdb my-cluster-name -n <namespace> -o yaml`                    | **User**: the Custom Resource breaks a safety check                                                                                                    | Fix the Custom Resource. See [Stay inside safe operating limits](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/operator-boundaries.html#stay-inside-safe-operating-limits)                                                            |
| The cluster stays in `initializing`                                                                                         | The `replsets` and `mongos` status in the Custom Resource, Operator logs                              | **Varies**: a pending rollout, a member that isn’t ready, PBM agent errors, a PVC resize, a missing endpoint, or a Pod that can’t be scheduled         | See [Cluster stays in `initializing`](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/troubleshoot-operator.html#cluster-stays-in-initializing)                                                                                         |
| The cluster doesn’t react to changes in the Custom Resource                                                                 | `kubectl get deployments -A`, Operator logs                                                           | **Operator**: its Pod isn’t running, or it doesn’t watch this namespace                                                                                | See [Check the Operator](#check-the-operator) and [Troubleshoot the Operator installation](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/troubleshoot-operator.html)                                                                  |
| Pod is `Pending`                                                                                                            | The `Events` section of `kubectl describe pod <pod-name> -n <namespace>`                              | **Kubernetes**: not enough resources, nodes or zones for the affinity rules, taints, or a volume that can’t bind                                       | See [Troubleshoot Pod scheduling](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/debug-scheduling.html)                                                                                                                                |
| A container restarts with `OOMKilled`                                                                                       | `Last State` in `kubectl describe pod <pod-name> -n <namespace>`                                      | **User**: the memory limit is too low for the workload or the cache                                                                                    | See [Troubleshoot out-of-memory errors](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/debug-oom.html)                                                                                                                                 |
| `mongod` fails to start after a configuration change                                                                        | `kubectl logs <pod-name> -n <namespace> -c logs`, or `-c mongod --previous` without the log collector | **User**: the Operator doesn’t validate the `configuration` section                                                                                    | Fix the option in the Custom Resource. To inspect the Pod meanwhile, [stop the restart loop](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/debug-shell.html#avoid-the-restart-on-fail-loop-for-percona-server-for-mongodb-containers) |
| `mongod` stops or restarts, and the data volume is full                                                                     | `kubectl exec <pod-name> -n <namespace> -c mongod -- df -h /data/db`                                  | **User**: the storage is too small for the data and the oplog                                                                                          | Increase the storage size. See [Resize storage](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/scaling-storage-resize.html)                                                                                                            |
| Pod is `Running` but not ready; the member is in `STARTUP2` or `RECOVERING`                                                 | `rs.status()`. See [Connect to a member](#connect-to-a-member)                                        | **MongoDB**: the member runs an initial sync or catches up                                                                                             | Wait for the sync to finish. See [Health checks and probes](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/architecture-probes.html#what-this-means-for-users)                                                                         |
| `mongod` container restarts; events show `Liveness probe failed`                                                            | `kubectl describe pod <pod-name> -n <namespace>`                                                      | **Kubernetes**, acting on the probe: the member is `DOWN` or `REMOVED`, or doesn’t answer in time                                                      | See [Health checks and probes](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/architecture-probes.html#where-to-look-if-probes-fail)                                                                                                   |
| No primary; writes fail; Operator logs show `FULL CLUSTER CRASH`                                                            | Operator logs, `rs.status()` on a remaining member                                                    | **MongoDB**: the replica set lost its majority. The Operator rewrites the configuration                                                                | See [Replica set without a primary](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/architecture-workflows.html#replica-set-without-a-primary)                                                                                          |
| A rolling restart is stuck                                                                                                  | Operator logs                                                                                         | **Operator**: waits for a Pod to become ready, or for a backup or restore to finish                                                                    | See [How Smart Update works](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/architecture-reconciliation.html#how-smart-update-works)                                                                                                   |
| Sharded cluster: `mongos` Pods are missing or don’t get the new version; Operator logs show `StatefulSet is not up to date` | Operator logs, the config server and shard Pods                                                       | **Operator**: it creates and updates `mongos` only after every config server and shard StatefulSet runs its current revision, and not during a restore | Fix the replica set that isn’t up to date. See [How Smart Update works](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/architecture-reconciliation.html#how-smart-update-works)                                                        |
| The cluster stays in `stopping` after you set `pause: true`                                                                 | Operator logs: `deleting rs pods`                                                                     | **Kubernetes** or **MongoDB**: a Pod doesn’t terminate, or the first Pod can’t become the primary                                                      | See [Pause and resume the cluster](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/pause.html#troubleshooting)                                                                                                                          |
| Clients can’t resolve member host names                                                                                     | Cluster DNS, the replica set configuration                                                            | **Kubernetes**: networking and DNS, or the exposure settings                                                                                           | See [Troubleshoot connection issues](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/troubleshoot-connection.html)                                                                                                                      |

### Backups and restores

| Symptom                                                                                         | Look here first                                                                                                                                         | Usually owned by                                                                                             | What to do                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| A backup has no state or stays `waiting`                                                        | `kubectl get psmdb-backup <backup-name> -n <namespace> -o yaml`, Operator logs: `Cluster is not ready for backup`, `Another backup is holding the lock` | **Operator**: waits for a healthy cluster, or for another backup, restore or ClusterSync to finish           | Restore cluster health or wait for the other operation. See [On-demand backup](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/architecture-workflows.html#on-demand-backup)                                                       |
| A backup is in the `error` state                                                                | `status.error`, the `backup-agent` logs on the Pod named in `status.pbmPods`                                                                            | **User**: storage credentials or endpoint                                                                    | See [Troubleshoot backups and restores](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/debug-backup-restore.html)                                                                                                                 |
| The cluster stays `initializing` while all Pods are ready; Operator logs show `Agent is not OK` | Operator logs, the `backup-agent` logs                                                                                                                  | **User**: the backup storage is unreachable                                                                  | Fix the storage configuration. See [Configure storage for backups](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/backups-storage.html)                                                                                           |
| A restore is in the `error` state                                                               | `status.error` in `kubectl get psmdb-restore <restore-name> -n <namespace> -o yaml`                                                                     | **Varies**: often the backup source or storage access                                                        | See [Restore](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/architecture-workflows.html#restore) and [Troubleshoot backups and restores](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/debug-backup-restore.html) |
| A backup object is stuck in `Terminating`                                                       | Operator logs                                                                                                                                           | **User**: the backup files can’t be deleted from storage, so the `percona.com/delete-backup` finalizer stays | Check storage access. See [Delete the unneeded backup](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/backups-delete.html)                                                                                                        |

### Storage and TLS

| Symptom                                                               | Look here first                                                                                                                                                                          | Usually owned by                                                                                                                | What to do                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| A storage size change does nothing                                    | The storage size in the Custom Resource compared with the PVC size, PVC events                                                                                                           | **User**, if `storageScaling.enableVolumeScaling` is off. **Kubernetes** or the CSI driver, for resize errors in the PVC events | See [Resize storage](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/scaling-storage-resize.html) and [Troubleshooting storage](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/debug-storage.html) |
| TLS errors after you replaced a certificate                           | The `ca.crt` keys of the TLS Secrets                                                                                                                                                     | **User**: the CA changed in one step                                                                                            | See [Update certificates](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/tls-update.html)                                                                                                                       |
| TLS handshake errors, and the certificates are past their expiry date | The certificate dates. See [Check your certificates for expiration](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/tls-update.html#check-your-certificates-for-expiration) | **User**, for certificates you manage. cert-manager, if it failed to renew them                                                 | See [Update certificates with downtime](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/tls-update.html#update-certificates-with-downtime)                                                                       |

## Connect to a member

To check the replica set yourself, open `mongosh` in the `mongod` container. The container already has the `clusterAdmin` credentials in its environment:

```
kubectl exec -it my-cluster-name-rs0-0 -n <namespace> -c mongod -- \
  bash -c 'mongosh -u "$MONGODB_CLUSTER_ADMIN_USER" -p "$MONGODB_CLUSTER_ADMIN_PASSWORD"'
```

If `tls.mode` is `requireTLS`, add `--tls --tlsCAFile /etc/mongodb-ssl/ca.crt --tlsCertificateKeyFile /tmp/tls.pem --tlsAllowInvalidHostnames` to the `mongosh` command.

Useful commands:

- `rs.status()` shows each member, its state and its health. The short form is `rs.status().members.map(m => ({name: m.name, state: m.stateStr, health: m.health}))`.
- `rs.printSecondaryReplicationInfo()` shows how far each secondary is behind the primary.
- In a sharded cluster, connect to a `mongos` Pod with `-c mongos`, for example `my-cluster-name-mongos-0`, and run `sh.status()`.

If the container keeps restarting, you can’t connect. [Stop the restart loop](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/debug-shell.html#avoid-the-restart-on-fail-loop-for-percona-server-for-mongodb-containers) first. For more about shell access, see [Exec into the containers](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/debug-shell.html).

## Collect diagnostics for support

If you need help from Percona, collect the diagnostic data first. [pt-k8s-debug-collector](https://docs.percona.com/percona-toolkit/pt-k8s-debug-collector.html) gathers the Custom Resources, Pod descriptions, events, logs and other Kubernetes objects into one archive.

Run the tool on the machine where you run `kubectl`, not inside a Pod. It uses your kubeconfig to read the cluster, so it needs `kubectl` in the `PATH` and read access to the cluster’s namespace. The tool is part of [Percona Toolkit](https://docs.percona.com/percona-toolkit/installation.html) , which also installs `pt-mongodb-summary`, used for the database summary.

```
pt-k8s-debug-collector --resource=psmdb --namespace=<namespace> --cluster=my-cluster-name
```

The tool writes a `cluster-dump_<timestamp>.tar.gz` archive to the current directory.

If you can’t run the tool, collect at least:

- `kubectl get psmdb my-cluster-name -n <namespace> -o yaml`
- The Operator logs. See [Check the Operator](#check-the-operator)
- `kubectl describe pods -n <namespace>`
- `kubectl get events -n <namespace> --sort-by=.lastTimestamp`
- The logs of the failing containers, with `--previous` if they restarted

Then see [Get help from Percona](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/get-help.html) for the community forum and support options.

- [Troubleshoot backups and restores](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/debug-backup-restore.html) walks through failed backups and restores step by step.
