# Troubleshoot the Operator

Use this page when the Operator itself is the problem: the installation fails, the Operator Pod doesn’t run, the cluster gets no status or doesn’t react to your changes, or it stays in `initializing`. For problems with the database Pods, backups or connections, start with [Initial troubleshooting](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/debug.html).

## Before you start

- Install `kubectl` and configure it for your Kubernetes cluster.

- Know the namespace of the Operator and of the database cluster. They are the same namespace unless you run the Operator in [cluster-wide mode](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/cluster-wide.html).

- Find the name of the Operator Deployment. It is `percona-server-mongodb-operator` for a `kubectl` installation, and usually ends with `psmdb-operator` for Helm:

  ```
  kubectl get deployments -A | grep -E 'percona-server-mongodb-operator|psmdb-operator'
  ```

## `kubectl` can’t reach the cluster

**Symptom:** `kubectl` commands time out or fail with a connection error, or they show objects from a different cluster.

**Cause:** `kubectl` isn’t configured for this cluster, or the current context in your kubeconfig points to another cluster.

**Fix:**

1. Check the connection:

   ```
   kubectl cluster-info
   ```

   Sample output

   ```
   Kubernetes control plane is running at https://<control-plane-ip>:49475
   CoreDNS is running at https://<control-plane-ip>:49475/api/v1/namespaces/kube-system/services/kube-dns:dns/proxy
   ```

1. If the output shows the wrong cluster, check the current context and switch to the right one:

   ```
   kubectl config current-context
   kubectl config use-context <context-name>
   ```

1. Run `kubectl cluster-info` again. If it still fails, ask your Kubernetes cluster administrator to check your access.

## The installation fails

### Missing privileges

**Symptom:** `kubectl apply` fails with `forbidden` errors, for example `cannot create resource "customresourcedefinitions"`.

**Cause:** Installing the Operator creates cluster-scoped CustomResourceDefinitions and namespaced RBAC objects. Your account lacks the rights for some of them.

**Fix:**

1. Check your privileges with the privileges check script. It reports what’s missing for each Percona Operator:

   ```
   bash <(curl -s https://gist.githubusercontent.com/cshiv/6048bdd0174275b48f633549c69d0844/raw/fd547b783a30b827362ee9f9ec03436f9bc79524/check_priviliges.sh)
   ```

   Sample output

   ```
   Checking privileges to install Percona Operators in kubernetes cluster...
   Warning: Unable to check the privileges for resource 'issuers', check if the resource 'issuers' is present in the cluster
   Warning: Unable to check the privileges for resource 'certificates', check if the resource 'certificates' is present in the cluster

   Warning: Some resources are not found in the kubernetes cluster.Check the Warning messages before you proceed
   ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
   GOOD TO INSTALL: Percona Operator for PostgreSQL
   https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-postgresql/index.html
   ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
   GOOD TO INSTALL: Percona Operator for MySQL based on Percona XtraDB Cluster
   https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mysql/pxc/index.html
   ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
   GOOD TO INSTALL: Percona Operator for MongoDB
   https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/index.html
   ```

   If your security policy doesn’t allow running a downloaded script, check the privileges with `kubectl auth can-i` instead. Each command prints `yes` or `no`:

   ```
   kubectl auth can-i create customresourcedefinitions
   kubectl auth can-i create serviceaccounts -n <namespace>
   kubectl auth can-i create roles -n <namespace>
   kubectl auth can-i create rolebindings -n <namespace>
   kubectl auth can-i create deployments -n <namespace>
   ```

   For [cluster-wide mode](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/cluster-wide.html), check `clusterroles` and `clusterrolebindings` instead of `roles` and `rolebindings`.

1. If any check fails, ask your Kubernetes cluster administrator to grant the missing privileges or to install the CustomResourceDefinitions for you.

### The CustomResourceDefinition is too long

**Symptom:** `kubectl apply` fails with `metadata.annotations: Too long: must have at most 262144 bytes` for `perconaservermongodbs.psmdb.percona.com`.

**Cause:** A client-side `kubectl apply` stores the whole object in an annotation. The `PerconaServerMongoDB` CustomResourceDefinition is larger than the annotation limit.

**Fix:** Apply the file with server-side apply, as the [installation guides](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/kubectl.html) do:

```
kubectl apply --server-side -f deploy/bundle.yaml -n <namespace>
```

## The Operator Pod isn’t running

**Symptom:** The Operator Pod is in `ImagePullBackOff`, `ErrImagePull` or `CrashLoopBackOff`, or its `RESTARTS` count keeps growing.

**Cause:** The node can’t pull the Operator image, the CustomResourceDefinitions are missing, or the Operator’s service account lacks the RBAC rights it needs.

**Fix:**

1. Check the Pod state and events:

   ```
   kubectl describe pod -l app.kubernetes.io/component=operator -n <operator-namespace>
   ```

   For a Helm installation, use `kubectl get pods -n <operator-namespace>` to find the Pod name.

1. For an image pull error, check the image name and your registry access. See [Use a private registry](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/custom-registry.html).

1. Read the Operator log. For a crash, `--previous` shows the log of the last run:

   ```
   kubectl logs deployment/<operator-deployment> -n <operator-namespace> --previous
   ```

   - A `no matches for kind` error means the CustomResourceDefinitions aren’t installed. Apply them with `kubectl apply --server-side -f deploy/crd.yaml`.
   - A `forbidden` error means the Operator’s service account lacks a privilege. Check that the Role or ClusterRole and its binding from the bundle were applied in the right namespace.

## The cluster has no status or doesn’t react to changes

**Symptom:** `kubectl get psmdb -n <namespace>` shows the cluster with empty `STATUS` and `ENDPOINT` columns, no Pods appear, or changes to the Custom Resource have no effect.

**Cause:** No Operator reconciles this cluster. Either the Operator isn’t running, or it doesn’t watch the cluster’s namespace. An Operator installed with `deploy/bundle.yaml` watches only its own namespace. In cluster-wide mode, the `WATCH_NAMESPACE` environment variable lists the watched namespaces, and an empty value means all namespaces.

**Fix:**

1. Check that the Operator Pod is running. See [The Operator Pod isn’t running](#the-operator-pod-isnt-running).

1. Check which namespaces the Operator watches:

   ```
   kubectl get deployment <operator-deployment> -n <operator-namespace> \
     -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].env[?(@.name=="WATCH_NAMESPACE")]}'
   ```

   A `fieldRef` to `metadata.namespace` means the Operator watches only its own namespace.

1. Create the cluster in a watched namespace, or reinstall the Operator in [cluster-wide mode](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/cluster-wide.html) with the cluster’s namespace in `WATCH_NAMESPACE`. See [Single-namespace and multi-namespace deployment modes](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/namespace-mode.html).

## Options are missing after an Operator upgrade

**Symptom:** After you upgrade the Operator, `kubectl apply` of the Custom Resource prints `unknown field` warnings, and the new options don’t stay in the Custom Resource.

**Cause:** The CustomResourceDefinitions are older than the Operator. Kubernetes drops the fields that the installed CustomResourceDefinition doesn’t define.

**Fix:** Upgrade the CustomResourceDefinitions to the Operator’s version before you use new options. See [Upgrade the Operator and CRD](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/update-operator.html).

## Cluster stays in `initializing`

The cluster reports `initializing` while any of the conditions in [What `ready` means](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/cr-statuses.html#what-ready-means) is not met. First find the affected component. Compare `ready` with `size` for each replica set and for `mongos`:

```
kubectl get psmdb <cluster-name> -n <namespace> -o jsonpath='{.status.replsets}{"\n"}{.status.mongos}{"\n"}'
```

Then find the matching entry.

### A rollout is pending

**Symptom:** Some Pods still run the previous revision. The Operator logs show `can't start 'SmartUpdate': waiting for running backups to be finished` or `waiting for active jobs to be finished`.

**Cause:** A Smart Update doesn’t restart Pods while a backup or restore runs.

**Fix:**

1. List the backups and restores: `kubectl get psmdb-backup,psmdb-restore -n <namespace>`.
1. Wait until they finish. If one is stuck, see [Troubleshoot backups and restores](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/debug-backup-restore.html).

### A member isn’t ready

**Symptom:** A `mongod` Pod is `Running` but not `Ready`, and the replica set reports fewer ready Pods than its size.

**Cause:** The member runs an initial sync, or it is `RECOVERING` because it fell too far behind the other members.

**Fix:**

1. Check the member state in the database log. See [Check the logs](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/debug-logs.html).
1. For an initial sync, wait. It can take hours for large data sets.
1. For a member that stays `RECOVERING`, see [Health checks and probes](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/architecture-probes.html#what-this-means-for-users) for why Kubernetes doesn’t restart it and what it blocks.

### The PBM agents report an error

**Symptom:** All Pods are ready, but the cluster stays in `initializing`. The Operator logs show `Agent is not OK` with the node, the replica set and the error.

**Cause:** With backups enabled, the cluster is `ready` only when every PBM agent is healthy and can reach the backup storage. Wrong storage credentials or an unreachable endpoint keep it in `initializing`.

**Fix:**

1. Check the error in the `backup-agent` container logs: `kubectl logs <pod-name> -n <namespace> -c backup-agent`.
1. Fix the storage configuration. See [Configure storage for backups](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/backups-storage.html).

### A PVC resize is in progress

**Symptom:** A replica set stays in `initializing` after you changed the storage size.

**Cause:** The replica set reports `initializing` until the resize of all its PVCs finishes.

**Fix:**

1. Check the PVC events: `kubectl describe pvc <pvc-name> -n <namespace>`.
1. If the resize fails, see [Troubleshooting storage](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/debug-storage.html).

### No endpoint is assigned

**Symptom:** All Pods are ready, and `status.host` is empty.

**Cause:** The `LoadBalancer` Service of `mongos` or of the exposed replica set waits for the cloud provider to assign an address.

**Fix:**

1. Check the Service: `kubectl get svc -n <namespace>`. An `EXTERNAL-IP` of `<pending>` means no address yet.
1. Check the Service events and your cloud provider’s load balancer quota.

### A Pod can’t be scheduled

**Symptom:** A Pod stays `Pending`. After a minute, the replica set status shows `error` and the scheduler’s message in `status.replsets.<name>.message`.

**Cause:** No node meets the Pod’s requirements: the required anti-affinity, the resource requests, or a volume bound to another zone.

**Fix:**

1. Read the reason: `kubectl describe pod <pod-name> -n <namespace>`.
1. Add nodes or relax the scheduling rules. See [Troubleshoot Pod scheduling](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/debug-scheduling.html).

If the problem started after an upgrade or a `crVersion` change, see [Troubleshoot upgrades and `crVersion`](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/debug-upgrade.html).

## See also

- [Initial troubleshooting](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/debug.html) for problems with the database Pods, a quick health check and a symptom table for every layer.
- [System requirements](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/System-Requirements.html) for the supported platforms and the resources the cluster needs.
- [Upgrade the Operator and CRD](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/update-operator.html) for the order to follow when you upgrade.

# Troubleshoot Pod scheduling

Use this page when `kubectl get pods` shows `Pending` for one or more database Pods.

A database Pod stays `Pending` and never starts. Kubernetes has not chosen a node for it, so the cluster does not become ready. The Operator has already created the Pod. The Kubernetes scheduler is what selects a node, so restarting the Operator leaves the Pod `Pending`.

The Pod’s events name every node the scheduler rejected, and why. Fix that reason in the Custom Resource or in the cluster.

Refer to the sections below for the steps.

For other Pod states, see [Check the Pods](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/debug.html#check-the-pods).

## Find the reason

1. List the Pods and note which ones are `Pending`:

   ```
   kubectl get pods -n <namespace> -o wide
   ```

   Sample output

   ```
   NAME                    READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE   NODE
   my-cluster-name-rs0-0   4/4     Running   0          12m   node-1
   my-cluster-name-rs0-1   4/4     Running   0          11m   node-2
   my-cluster-name-rs0-2   0/4     Pending   0          10m   <none>
   ```

   A `Pending` Pod has `<none>` in the `NODE` column. The `READY` count depends on the enabled sidecars, such as the backup agent and the log collector.

1. Read the events of the `Pending` Pod:

   ```
   kubectl describe pod <pod-name> -n <namespace>
   ```

   Look at the `Events` section at the bottom. The scheduler records a `FailedScheduling` event with the reason:

   Sample output

   ```
   Events:
     Type     Reason            Age   From               Message
     ----     ------            ----  ----               -------
     Warning  FailedScheduling  25s   default-scheduler  0/4 nodes are available: 4 Insufficient memory. no new claims to deallocate, preemption: 0/4 nodes are available: 4 Preemption is not helpful for scheduling.
   ```

   The exact wording depends on the Kubernetes version. Newer versions add a clause about preemption (`preemption: ...`) at the end. You can ignore it. The reason is in the part before it.

1. Read the whole message. It lists every node and groups the nodes by the reason each was rejected. The number before each reason is how many nodes it applies to, and different nodes can fail for different reasons:

   ```
   0/4 nodes are available: 2 node(s) didn't match pod topology spread constraints, 2 node(s) were unschedulable.
   ```

   To place the Pod, you must fix the reason for at least one node.

1. Check the Custom Resource. While a Pod is `Pending`, `kubectl get psmdb` reports the state `initializing`. The scheduler’s message is in the status of the replica set, after the next reconcile:

   ```
   kubectl get psmdb <cluster-name> -n <namespace> -o jsonpath='{.status.replsets.rs0.message}'
   ```

   Replace `rs0` with the name of the replica set that the Pod belongs to.

Note

If the `Events` section is empty, the events have expired (Kubernetes keeps them for about an hour by default). Delete the `Pending` Pod. The StatefulSet recreates it, and the scheduler records a fresh event.

Each component is scheduled with its own settings. A change under `replsets` doesn’t affect the config server or `mongos` Pods. Apply the fix to the section that the `Pending` Pod belongs to.

## Event messages at a glance

| The event says                                                                                                                                                                                                          | What it means                                                                 | Go to                                                                                   |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Insufficient cpu` or `Insufficient memory`                                                                                                                                                                             | No node has enough unreserved CPU or memory for the Pod’s requests            | [Not enough CPU or memory](#not-enough-cpu-or-memory)                                   |
| `didn't match pod anti-affinity rules` or `didn't satisfy existing pods anti-affinity rules`                                                                                                                            | There are fewer nodes (or zones) than replica set members                     | [Not enough nodes or zones](#not-enough-nodes-or-zones-for-anti-affinity)               |
| `had untolerated taint(s)`                                                                                                                                                                                              | The nodes are tainted and the Pod has no matching toleration                  | [Taints, labels, or selectors block the Pod](#taints-labels-or-selectors-block-the-pod) |
| `didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector`                                                                                                                                                                             | No node has the labels the Pod requires                                       | [Taints, labels, or selectors block the Pod](#taints-labels-or-selectors-block-the-pod) |
| `didn't match pod topology spread constraints`                                                                                                                                                                          | A `DoNotSchedule` spread constraint can’t be met                              | [Taints, labels, or selectors block the Pod](#taints-labels-or-selectors-block-the-pod) |
| `were unschedulable`                                                                                                                                                                                                    | The node is cordoned                                                          | [A node is cordoned](#a-node-is-cordoned)                                               |
| `pod has unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims`, `didn't find available persistent volumes to bind`, `persistentvolumeclaim "<name>" not found`, `is being deleted`, or `binding volumes: context deadline exceeded` | The Pod’s volume claim doesn’t exist, can’t get a volume, or is being deleted | [PVC is missing or unbound](#pvc-is-missing-or-unbound)                                 |
| `didn't match PersistentVolume's node affinity` (older Kubernetes versions: `had volume node affinity conflict`)                                                                                                        | The volume is pinned to a node or zone where the Pod can’t run                | [Volume node affinity conflict](#volume-node-affinity-conflict)                         |
| `Pod didn't trigger scale-up` (reason `NotTriggerScaleUp`)                                                                                                                                                              | The cluster autoscaler has no node group that would fit the Pod               | [The autoscaler does not add a node](#the-autoscaler-does-not-add-a-node)               |

## Apply the fix

How the Pod picks up a fix depends on where you make it.

- **A fix in the Kubernetes cluster** (uncordon a node, remove a taint, add a node or a label) is picked up by the scheduler on its own. The `Pending` Pod schedules within seconds.

- **A fix in the Custom Resource** (requests, affinity, tolerations, `nodeSelector`, storage) changes the StatefulSet, but not the Pod that is already `Pending`. [Smart Update](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/update.html#smart-update) waits for all Pods to be ready before it replaces any of them, and a `Pending` Pod never becomes ready. Apply the change, then delete the `Pending` Pod:

  ```
  kubectl apply -f deploy/cr.yaml -n <namespace>
  ```

  Before deleting the Pod, inspect its StatefulSet with `kubectl get statefulset <statefulset-name> -n <namespace> -o yaml`. Wait until `spec.template` contains the corrected requests or scheduling constraints. Then delete the Pod:

  ```
  kubectl delete pod <pending-pod> -n <namespace>
  ```

  The StatefulSet recreates the Pod with the new settings. Delete only the `Pending` Pod. It never started, so no data is lost.

## Not enough CPU or memory

**Meaning.** The scheduler compares the Pod’s resource *requests* with what is still unreserved on each node. It adds up the requests of all containers in the Pod, including sidecars such as the log collector, and ignores `limits` and the current load. A node can be idle and still be full on paper.

**Fix.**

1. Compare the requests with the free capacity. In the output, check the `Allocatable` and `Allocated resources` sections. The `Non-terminated Pods` table shows the requests of every Pod on the node:

   ```
   kubectl describe node <node-name>
   ```

1. Do one of the following:

   - Add a node, or use larger nodes.

   - Lower the requests in the Custom Resource. Check what your cluster can afford before you do, as the database needs enough memory to run:

     ```
     spec:
       replsets:
       - name: rs0
         resources:
           requests:
             cpu: 300m
             memory: 1Gi
     ```

1. Apply the change and delete the `Pending` Pod, as described in [Apply the fix](#apply-the-fix).

If other workloads should give way to the database Pods, you can also set `priorityClassName`. See [Priority Classes](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/constraints.html#priority-classes). For sizing, see [Scaling](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/scaling.html).

## Not enough nodes or zones for anti-affinity

**Meaning.** By default, the Operator keeps replica set members on different nodes (`antiAffinityTopologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname`). When every schedulable node already runs a member, the next Pod has nowhere to go. In the following example, two of four nodes are cordoned, and the other two already run members:

```
0/4 nodes are available: 2 node(s) didn't match pod anti-affinity rules, 2 node(s) were unschedulable.
```

With `topology.kubernetes.io/zone`, each member needs a node in its own zone, so three members need nodes in three zones.

If you set `affinity.advanced`, the Operator ignores `antiAffinityTopologyKey`. Check the rules under `advanced` instead. Only `required...` rules can keep a Pod `Pending`. A `preferred...` rule never does.

**Fix.**

1. Add a node (or a zone) so that every member gets its own. This is the right fix for production, because the spread is what lets the replica set survive the loss of one node.

1. For a test cluster that has to run on fewer nodes, turn the rule off in `deploy/cr.yaml`:

   ```
   spec:
     replsets:
     - name: rs0
       affinity:
         antiAffinityTopologyKey: "none"
   ```

   Apply the full `cr.yaml`, then delete the `Pending` Pod, as described in [Apply the fix](#apply-the-fix). A merge patch with this snippet replaces the whole `replsets` list, and the API server rejects it.

   Don’t use `none` in production. Several members can then land on the same node, and one node failure can take down the majority of the replica set.

See [Affinity and anti-affinity](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/constraints.html#affinity-and-anti-affinity) for all valid values.

## Taints, labels, or selectors block the Pod

**Meaning.** The scheduler rejected the nodes for one or more of these reasons:

- The node is tainted, and the Pod has no toleration for the taint.
- The Pod asks for a node label (`nodeSelector` or node affinity) that no node has.
- A `DoNotSchedule` spread constraint can’t be met.

**Fix.**

1. Check the taints and labels of the nodes. Newer Kubernetes versions print only `had untolerated taint(s)` in the event, without the key and the value, so list the taints from the nodes:

   ```
   kubectl get nodes -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,TAINTS:.spec.taints
   kubectl get nodes --show-labels
   ```

   Sample output

   ```
   NAME     TAINTS
   node-1   [map[effect:NoSchedule key:dedicated value:mongodb]]
   node-2   <none>
   ```

1. Compare them with the Custom Resource:

   ```
   kubectl get psmdb <cluster-name> -n <namespace> -o yaml
   ```

   Check `nodeSelector`, `affinity`, `tolerations` and `topologySpreadConstraints` under the section that the Pod belongs to.

1. Either label or untaint the node, or change the Custom Resource so that the Pod matches. For example, add a toleration for a dedicated node pool. A change to the node needs no further steps. A change to the Custom Resource needs the Pod to be deleted, as described in [Apply the fix](#apply-the-fix). See [Tolerations](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/constraints.html#tolerations), [Node selector](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/constraints.html#node-selector) and [Topology Spread Constraints](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/constraints.html#topology-spread-constraints).

## A node is cordoned

**Meaning.** A cordoned node accepts no new Pods. It is marked `SchedulingDisabled`. It’s normal during a node drain or upgrade. However, it becomes a problem if the node was cordoned and forgotten. The message usually combines `were unschedulable` with other reasons, as in the examples above.

**Fix.**

1. Find the cordoned nodes:

   ```
   kubectl get nodes
   ```

1. If no maintenance is running on the node, make it schedulable again:

   ```
   kubectl uncordon <node-name>
   ```

   The `Pending` Pod schedules on its own. If a drain is still in progress, wait for it to finish.

## Storage problems

Database Pods keep their data on PersistentVolumeClaims (PVCs). If the volume can’t be provided, or is in a place the Pod can’t reach, the Pod stays `Pending`.

### PVC is missing or unbound

**Meaning.** The scheduler can’t place a Pod whose PVC doesn’t exist or can’t get a volume. The event of the Pod names the claim, but not the cause:

| The event says                                     | What it means                                                                              |
| -------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `pod has unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims` | The PVC has no volume yet and its StorageClass binds immediately                           |
| `didn't find available persistent volumes to bind` | No free volume matches the claim. For example, the StorageClass has no provisioner         |
| `persistentvolumeclaim "<name>" not found`         | The PVC isn’t in the Pod’s namespace                                                       |
| `persistentvolumeclaim "<name>" is being deleted`  | The PVC is being replaced, for example when you recreate a member. This state is temporary |
| `binding volumes: context deadline exceeded`       | The provisioner didn’t create the volume in time                                           |

**Fix.**

1. Check the claims. The cause is in the events of the PVC, not in the events of the Pod:

   ```
   kubectl get pvc -n <namespace>
   kubectl describe pvc <pvc-name> -n <namespace>
   ```

   The PVC of a member is named `mongod-data-<pod-name>`, for example `mongod-data-my-cluster-name-rs0-2`. Look for a `ProvisioningFailed` event:

   Sample output

   ```
   Warning  ProvisioningFailed  storageclass.storage.k8s.io "does-not-exist" not found
   ```

1. Fix what the PVC events report: the StorageClass name (`kubectl get sc` lists the existing ones), the default StorageClass, the provisioner, or the namespace quota.

A PVC with a StorageClass that waits for the first consumer stays `Pending` until the Pod is scheduled. That alone isn’t an error. Changing `storageClassName` in the Custom Resource doesn’t change PVCs that already exist.

See [Troubleshooting storage](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/debug-storage.html) for quota and CSI issues.

### Volume node affinity conflict

**Meaning.** A PersistentVolume is pinned to certain nodes, and the Pod can only run where the volume can be attached. The Pod waits when the place where the volume lives is not available:

- Local storage (local-path, hostPath, OpenEBS hostpath, local CSI drivers) is pinned to the node that created the volume. The Pod waits if that node is cordoned, drained, or gone.
- Cloud disks are pinned to a zone. The Pod waits if no schedulable node is available in that zone.

The event looks like this:

```
0/4 nodes are available: 1 node(s) were unschedulable, 3 node(s) didn't match PersistentVolume's node affinity.
```

Older Kubernetes versions say `had volume node affinity conflict`.

The PVC still shows `Bound`, so look at the volume instead:

```
kubectl get pvc mongod-data-<pod-name> -n <namespace>
kubectl describe pv <pv-name>
```

Sample output

```
Node Affinity:
  Required Terms:
    Term 0:        kubernetes.io/hostname in [node-1]
```

**Fix.**

1. If the node or zone can come back, bring it back: uncordon the node, finish the drain, or add a node in that zone. The Pod schedules on its own and keeps its data.

1. If the node or zone is gone for good, recreate the member. The Operator creates a new, empty volume on an available node, and the member runs an initial sync from the other members. **Do this for one member at a time, and only while the rest of the replica set is healthy and keeps a majority.** This applies to config server members too. The data on the member’s volume is deleted:

   ```
   kubectl delete pvc mongod-data-<pod-name> -n <namespace> --wait=false
   kubectl delete pod <pod-name> -n <namespace>
   ```

   The `--wait=false` option keeps the first command from blocking while a running Pod still uses the claim. If the Pod is already `Pending`, deleting the claim can be enough: the StatefulSet recreates it, and the Pod schedules on its own.

1. Wait until the new member is `SECONDARY` before you touch another one. Open [mongosh](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/connection-secrets.html#open-an-interactive-shell-with-mongosh), connecting to the affected shard or config server replica set (`cfg`), not through `mongos`. Authenticate as a user authorized to run `replSetGetStatus`, then run `rs.status()` to check the recreated member. `kubectl get psmdb` can show `ready` before the initial sync finishes. If you recreate two members of a three-member replica set at once, there is no majority: the primary steps down, and writes fail until one of the members finishes the sync.

## The autoscaler does not add a node

**Meaning.** The Pod stays `Pending` although the cluster has a cluster autoscaler. The autoscaler adds a node only if some node group would fit the Pod. Look for the event:

```
kubectl get events -n <namespace> --field-selector reason=NotTriggerScaleUp
```

The message starts with `Pod didn't trigger scale-up:` and gives the reason why a new node would not help, for example `max node group size reached`. On some platforms, such as GKE, the reason after the colon can be empty. Check the status or the logs of the cluster autoscaler for the reason.

**Fix.** Check that at least one node group has the labels, taints and zone that the Pod requires, that its machine size is large enough for the Pod’s requests, and that it hasn’t reached its maximum size. Then fix the node group, or the Pod’s constraints, as described above.

## Verify recovery

1. Check that the Pod is scheduled and running:

   ```
   kubectl get pods -n <namespace> -o wide
   ```

   The `STATUS` is `Running`, the `READY` column is full (for example `4/4`), and `NODE` shows a node name.

1. Check the cluster state:

   ```
   kubectl get psmdb -n <namespace>
   ```

   The `STATUS` changes from `initializing` to `ready`. For a recreated member, also check `rs.status()` in [mongosh](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/connection-secrets.html#open-an-interactive-shell-with-mongosh): the member must be `SECONDARY` or `PRIMARY`, because `ready` can appear before the initial sync finishes.

1. Check that no new `FailedScheduling` events appear:

   ```
   kubectl get events -n <namespace> --field-selector reason=FailedScheduling
   ```

## See also

- [Control Pod scheduling](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/constraints.html)
- [Troubleshoot the Operator installation issues](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/troubleshoot-operator.html)
- [Troubleshooting storage](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/debug-storage.html)

# Troubleshoot out-of-memory errors

Use this page when a container restarts with `OOMKilled`, or when the `RESTARTS` count of a Pod keeps growing and you suspect memory.

A container that uses more memory than is defined in its `resources.limits.memory` is killed by the Linux kernel. Kubernetes records the restart, but it doesn’t choose or prevent it. The Pod keeps its data and restarts in place. Every kill drops the connections to that container, and if the killed container is `mongod` on the primary, the replica set holds an election.

The fix depends on which container was killed, so find that out first.

## Find the container that was killed

1. List the Pods. A killed container shows `OOMKilled` in the `STATUS` column for a moment, `READY` is lower than the number of containers, and `RESTARTS` grows:

   ```
   kubectl get pods -n <namespace>
   ```

   Sample output

   ```
   NAME                    READY   STATUS      RESTARTS      AGE
   my-cluster-name-rs0-0   3/3     Running     0             2m54s
   my-cluster-name-rs0-1   2/3     OOMKilled   1 (9s ago)    2m23s
   my-cluster-name-rs0-2   3/3     Running     1 (76s ago)   3m24s
   ```

1. Show the reason for the last restart of every container in the Pod. The columns are the container name, the restart count, the reason and the exit code:

   ```
   kubectl get pod <pod-name> -n <namespace> -o jsonpath='{range .status.containerStatuses[*]}{.name}{"\t"}{.restartCount}{"\t"}{.lastState.terminated.reason}{"\t"}{.lastState.terminated.exitCode}{"\n"}{end}'
   ```

   Sample output

   ```
   logrotate   0
   logs        0
   mongod      2   OOMKilled   137
   ```

   Kubernetes lists the containers in alphabetical order, not in the order of the Pod spec. In scripts, select a container by name, for example `{.status.containerStatuses[?(@.name=="mongod")].lastState.terminated.reason}`.

1. To see the same information with more detail, describe the Pod and look at `Last State` under the container:

   ```
   kubectl describe pod <pod-name> -n <namespace>
   ```

   Sample output

   ```
   Last State:     Terminated
     Reason:       OOMKilled
     Exit Code:    137
   ```

Kubernetes doesn’t post an `OOMKilled` event, so `kubectl get events` doesn’t show the kill. The Operator doesn’t flag it either: `kubectl get psmdb` reports `initializing`. After a long crash loop, the status becomes `error` with a message such as `Error: pod my-cluster-name-cfg-0 is in CrashLoopBackOff state`.

An `OOMKilled` reason can also result from node-wide memory exhaustion. Check node/kernel diagnostics and the affected container’s cgroup memory counters to distinguish node pressure from a container-limit OOM before increasing limits.

Use the container name to choose the next step:

| What you see                                         | What it means                                                                                                | Go to                                                                                    |
| ---------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `mongod` in a replica set Pod                        | The database container was OOM-killed; check its memory limit and node memory pressure                       | [mongod is killed](#mongod-is-killed)                                                    |
| `mongos`, or `mongod` in a config server Pod         | A router or config server was OOM-killed; check its memory limit and node memory pressure                    | [mongos and config server Pods](#mongos-and-config-server-pods)                          |
| `backup-agent`, `pmm-client`, `logs`, or `logrotate` | A sidecar was OOM-killed; check its memory limit and node memory pressure                                    | [Sidecar containers](#sidecar-containers)                                                |
| The Operator Pod                                     | The Operator was OOM-killed; check its memory limit and node memory pressure                                 | [The Operator is killed](#the-operator-is-killed)                                        |
| Exit code `137` without `OOMKilled`                  | The process got `SIGKILL` for another reason, such as a failed liveness probe or a node shutdown             | Check the Pod events and the node, not the memory limit                                  |
| The Pod is `Evicted`                                 | The node ran short of memory and the kubelet evicted the Pod. This is node pressure, not the container limit | Check `kubectl describe node <node-name>` and the requests of the other Pods on the node |

## mongod is killed

**Meaning.** The memory limit of the `mongod` container has to hold two things: the WiredTiger cache, and everything else. The cache has a fixed size that the Operator calculates from the limit. Everything else is connections, query and aggregation memory, index builds, and memory that the allocator hasn’t returned to the system. It isn’t capped by the cache size, and it is what usually pushes the container over its limit.

After the restart, the log of the new `mongod` process shows that the previous one didn’t shut down cleanly. The killed process writes nothing, because a kernel kill can’t be logged. With the log collector enabled (the default), `mongod` writes its log to a file, and the log of the `mongod` container is almost empty. Read the log from the `logs` container instead. See [Check logs](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/debug-logs.html) for more.

```
kubectl logs <pod-name> -n <namespace> -c logs | grep "Detected unclean shutdown"
```

Sample output

```
"msg":"Detected unclean shutdown - Lock file is not empty
```

### Check the memory settings

Connect directly to the affected `mongod` member with [mongosh](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/connection-secrets.html#open-an-interactive-shell-with-mongosh). Use a `mongodb://` URI with that Pod’s hostname and port as the only host, and add `directConnection=true`, retaining the authentication and TLS settings from the connection guide. Check how much memory `mongod` sees and how large its cache is:

```
db.hostInfo().system.memLimitMB
db.serverStatus().wiredTiger.cache["maximum bytes configured"] / 1024 / 1024
```

`memLimitMB` must match the `resources.limits.memory` of the container. If it shows the memory of the node, the component has no memory limit. In that case, the Operator doesn’t set the cache size, and `mongod` sizes the cache from the memory of the whole node, which is more than the Pod’s share of it. Set `resources.limits.memory` for the component.

### How the Operator sizes the cache

The Operator starts `mongod` with a WiredTiger cache of `(memory limit − 1 GiB) × cacheSizeRatio`, with a minimum of 256 MiB. The [`cacheSizeRatio`](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/operator.html#replsetsstoragewiredtigerengineconfigcachesizeratio) option is set for each replica set and defaults to `0.5`. Whatever the cache doesn’t take is all the room that `mongod` has for everything else:

| Memory limit | `cacheSizeRatio` | WiredTiger cache  | Left for everything else |
| ------------ | ---------------- | ----------------- | ------------------------ |
| 1Gi          | 0.5              | 256 MiB (minimum) | about 0.75 GiB           |
| 5Gi          | 0.5              | 2 GiB             | 3 GiB                    |
| 5Gi          | 0.8              | 3.2 GiB           | 1.8 GiB                  |
| 8Gi          | 0.5              | 3.5 GiB           | 4.5 GiB                  |
| 8Gi          | 0.8              | 5.6 GiB           | 2.4 GiB                  |

A high `cacheSizeRatio` on a small limit leaves little room for connections and queries.

The in-memory engine is different. Its size is `memory limit ×`[`inMemorySizeRatio`](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/operator.html#replsetsstorageinmemoryengineconfiginmemorysizeratio), which defaults to `0.9`, and the Operator doesn’t subtract 1 GiB. The data lives in that memory, and with a 1Gi limit only about 100 MiB is left for everything else.

### Find what uses the memory

The configured cache size does not cap the total memory used by `mongod`. An OOM kill alone does not tell you whether cache or non-cache memory grew. Compare the two in `mongosh`, ideally several times while the memory rises:

```
const s = db.serverStatus();
const GiB = x => (Number(x) / 1073741824).toFixed(2);
print("allocated     " + GiB(s.tcmalloc.generic.current_allocated_bytes));
print("wt cache      " + GiB(s.wiredTiger.cache["bytes currently in the cache"]));
print("connections   " + s.connections.current);
print("open cursors  " + s.metrics.cursor.open.total);
```

The `allocated` value minus the `wt cache` value is a rough estimate of live heap allocations outside the cache. It excludes free memory retained by the allocator and other memory charged to the container. Also compare `db.serverStatus().mem.resident` (in MiB) with the container’s cgroup memory usage. If live allocations grow while the cache stays flat, look at what the workload is doing. These are the patterns that occur most often:

- **Abandoned cursors.** A client reads one batch and never iterates or closes the cursor. If the query needed an in-memory sort, the cursor holds the sorted result outside the cache. List the idle cursors with:

  ```
  db.getSiblingDB("admin").aggregate([
    { $currentOp: { allUsers: true, idleCursors: true } },
    { $match: { type: "idleCursor" } }
  ])
  ```

- **Blocking sorts and collection scans.** A sort that no index supports, or a `COLLSCAN` in the slow query log, uses memory for each query. Many of them at once add up. Drivers retry reads, so the same query can run again and kill `mongod` right after the restart.

- **Connection spikes.** Each connection uses memory. A jump in `connections.current` that lines up with the kills points at the clients or their connection pools.

- **Change streams.** Many open change streams, especially on the primary, are a common source of growth. A `fullDocument` lookup adds work and memory.

If you don’t have PMM, the `diagnostic.data` directory in the data directory of `mongod` records `serverStatus` every second and covers the minutes before the kill.

If the container keeps being killed after you raise the limit, the cause is almost always one of these workload patterns, not the size of the limit.

### Fix the cause

1. Fix the workload first. A larger limit only delays the next kill when the memory outside the cache keeps growing:

   - Make the application exhaust or close its cursors. Use a real `limit(n)` instead of a very large one, and add an index that supports the sort. As a stopgap, kill idle cursors with `killCursors`. This stops the growth, and `mongod` reuses the freed memory, but the memory use that Kubernetes reports may not drop at once.
   - Add indexes for the queries that show `COLLSCAN` or an in-memory sort.
   - Cap the connection pools in the application drivers.
   - Open change streams on as few collections as possible, and avoid `fullDocument` lookups that you don’t need.

1. Give `mongod` more room outside the cache. Raise the limit, lower `cacheSizeRatio`, or both. Keep `requests.memory` equal to `limits.memory`, so the scheduler places the Pod only on a node that has that memory:

   ```
   spec:
     replsets:
     - name: rs0
       resources:
         limits:
           memory: "8Gi"
         requests:
           memory: "8Gi"
       storage:
         wiredTiger:
           engineConfig:
             cacheSizeRatio: 0.5
   ```

1. Apply the change:

   ```
   kubectl apply -f deploy/cr.yaml -n <namespace>
   ```

   With the default `SmartUpdate` strategy, the Operator restarts the members one at a time: the secondaries first and the primary last, after a step-down. `RollingUpdate` uses the StatefulSet controller’s update order; `OnDelete` requires you to delete and recreate each Pod manually. See [Update strategies](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/update.html#update-strategies) and [Upgrade manually](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/update-manually.html). Once a member has restarted with the new settings, its cache size follows the new limit. Check the new values with the `mongosh` commands from [Check the memory settings](#check-the-memory-settings).

Note

If a Pod that is crash-looping or `Pending` still has the old resource settings, confirm that the StatefulSet’s Pod template has the new settings before deleting that Pod. Delete one Pod at a time and wait for it to become ready before proceeding. If a `Pending` Pod already has the new request and its scheduling events report insufficient memory, add node capacity or revise the requested resources; deleting it won’t resolve that capacity shortage.

For the settings of the limits, see [`replsets.resources.limits.memory`](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/operator.html#replsetsresourceslimitsmemory). For sizing, see [Scaling](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/scaling.html).

## mongos and config server Pods

**Meaning.** In a sharded cluster, the `mongos` Pods and the config server replica set have their own limits. A limit of a few MiB is too small, and the container is killed or starved under load. That shows up as failures on the shards too. An idle `mongos` used about 40 MiB in a test, before it handled any load. A killed `mongos` shows `CrashLoopBackOff` in `kubectl get pods`, and its message is in `.status.mongos.message`. The other `mongos` Pods keep serving, so the cluster stays available.

**Fix.**

1. Raise the limit of the component that was killed:

   ```
   spec:
     sharding:
       mongos:
         resources:
           limits:
             memory: "1Gi"
           requests:
             memory: "1Gi"
       configsvrReplSet:
         resources:
           limits:
             memory: "1Gi"
           requests:
             memory: "1Gi"
   ```

   Size them like any other `mongod` or router, not to a token value. See [`sharding.mongos.resources.limits.memory`](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/operator.html#shardingmongosresourceslimitsmemory) and [`sharding.configsvrReplSet.resources.limits.memory`](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/operator.html#shardingconfigsvrreplsetresourceslimitsmemory).

1. Apply the change with `kubectl apply -f deploy/cr.yaml -n <namespace>`. Delete any Pod that is still crash-looping, one at a time, so that it starts with the new settings.

## Sidecar containers

**Meaning.** Each sidecar has its own limit. When a sidecar is killed, `mongod` in the same Pod keeps running and stays a member of the replica set. Find the key for the container that was killed:

| Container                  | Limit is set in                                                                                                              |
| -------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `mongod`                   | `replsets[].resources`                                                                                                       |
| `backup-agent`             | [`backup.resources`](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/operator.html#backupresourceslimitsmemory) |
| `pmm-client`               | [`pmm.resources`](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/operator.html#pmmresourceslimitsmemory)       |
| `logs` (the log collector) | `logcollector.resources`                                                                                                     |
| `logrotate`                | `logcollector.resources` (shared with `logs`)                                                                                |

A restore needs much more memory in `backup-agent` than a backup does. To find the peak that a sidecar reaches, read the memory counters of its cgroup while a backup or a restore runs. This example is for nodes that use cgroup v2:

```
kubectl exec <pod-name> -n <namespace> -c backup-agent -- sh -c 'cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.current /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.peak /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.max; grep oom_kill /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.events'
```

Sample output

```
17555456
17887232
25165824
oom_kill 0
```

The lines are the current use, the peak, and the limit, all in bytes, followed by the number of OOM kills in the cgroup. On nodes that use cgroup v1, the files are `/sys/fs/cgroup/memory/memory.usage_in_bytes` and `/sys/fs/cgroup/memory/memory.limit_in_bytes`.

**Fix.**

1. Set the limit with a margin above the peak that you measured. Removing the limit also stops the kills, but then the sidecar can take memory that the node needs for `mongod`.
1. Apply the change with `kubectl apply -f deploy/cr.yaml -n <namespace>`.
1. Delete the Pods that are still crash-looping, one at a time. A Pod in a crash loop keeps the old limit until the StatefulSet recreates it.

## The Operator is killed

**Meaning.** The default Operator Deployment has no resource requests or limits, and an idle Operator uses about 40 MiB. If you set a limit that the Operator exceeds, its container is killed and restarts.

The database keeps running, but nothing reconciles while the Operator is down: changes to the Custom Resource, Smart Update, backups and status updates all wait. `kubectl get psmdb` keeps showing the last status, `ready`, so a stale status is a sign of a dead Operator. The log of the previous container ends normally, without an error line, because the process was killed.

**Fix.**

1. Check the Operator Pod for restarts and for `OOMKilled`:

   ```
   kubectl get pods -n <namespace> -l app.kubernetes.io/name=percona-server-mongodb-operator
   kubectl describe pod <operator-pod-name> -n <namespace>
   ```

1. Raise the memory limit of the Operator container in the Deployment of the Operator, or remove the limit that you set.

## Verify recovery

1. Check that the Pods are running and that the restart count stops growing while the workload runs:

   ```
   kubectl get pods -n <namespace>
   ```

1. Check the cluster state. The `STATUS` returns to `ready`:

   ```
   kubectl get psmdb -n <namespace>
   ```

1. For `mongod`, check that `memLimitMB` and the cache match the new limit. See [Check the memory settings](#check-the-memory-settings).

1. If the metrics server is installed, watch the memory use of the containers and confirm that it stays below the limit:

   ```
   kubectl top pod <pod-name> -n <namespace> --containers
   ```
