# Objects the Operator creates

This page lists what the Operator creates in your Kubernetes cluster for Percona Server for MongoDB, and which containers run in each Pod. Use it to size quotas, plan RBAC and storage, and to find an object when you troubleshoot.

## Kubernetes objects

For a cluster named `my-cluster-name` with a replica set named `rs0`, the Operator creates and manages the following Kubernetes objects. Some exist only when the related feature is turned on.

| Kind                       | Name                                                                                                           | Purpose                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| -------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| StatefulSet                | `my-cluster-name-rs0`, one for each replica set                                                                | Data-bearing members                                                                                                                                                                        |
| StatefulSet                | `my-cluster-name-rs0-arbiter`, `my-cluster-name-rs0-nv`, `my-cluster-name-rs0-hidden`                          | [Arbiter, non-voting and hidden members](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/arbiter.html), when you turn them on                                                  |
| StatefulSet                | `my-cluster-name-cfg`                                                                                          | Config server replica set, when sharding is on                                                                                                                                              |
| StatefulSet                | `my-cluster-name-mongos`                                                                                       | `mongos` query routers, when sharding is on                                                                                                                                                 |
| StatefulSet                | `my-cluster-name-rs0-search`                                                                                   | `mongot` for [search](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/search-overview.html), when search is on                                                                 |
| Service                    | `my-cluster-name-rs0`, `my-cluster-name-mongos`, and more                                                      | Headless Services for the members, client entry points, and optional per-Pod Services. See [Services and ports](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/services.html) |
| Secret                     | The name in `secrets.users`. The example manifest uses `my-cluster-name-secrets`                               | Passwords of the system users. The Operator creates it with random passwords if it doesn’t exist. Edit it to change passwords                                                               |
| Secret                     | `internal-my-cluster-name-users`                                                                               | Passwords the Operator has actually applied to the database. Do not edit it                                                                                                                 |
| Secret                     | `my-cluster-name-databaseadmin-conn-str`, and one for each application user Secret                             | Ready-to-use connection strings. See [Connection secrets](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/connection-secrets.html)                                             |
| Secret                     | `my-cluster-name-ssl`, `my-cluster-name-ssl-internal`                                                          | TLS certificates for client and internal traffic                                                                                                                                            |
| Secret                     | `my-cluster-name-pbm`                                                                                          | TLS client certificate of the PBM agents. Starting with version 1.24.0, when backups are enabled                                                                                            |
| Secret                     | `my-cluster-name-mongodb-keyfile`                                                                              | Key for internal authentication between members, when the cluster uses a keyfile                                                                                                            |
| Secret                     | `my-cluster-name-mongodb-encryption-key`                                                                       | Key for [data-at-rest encryption](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/encryption.html), when you don’t use HashiCorp Vault                                         |
| ConfigMap                  | `my-cluster-name-rs0-mongod`, `my-cluster-name-rs0-nv`, `my-cluster-name-rs0-hidden`, `my-cluster-name-mongos` | Your custom configuration from the `configuration` sections of the CR                                                                                                                       |
| ConfigMap                  | Configuration of the log collector and of `logrotate`, of backup hook scripts, and of `mongot`                 | Created when the related feature is on                                                                                                                                                      |
| PodDisruptionBudget        | One for each StatefulSet                                                                                       | Limits voluntary disruptions, such as node drains, to one Pod of the StatefulSet at a time by default                                                                                       |
| PersistentVolumeClaim      | `mongod-data-my-cluster-name-rs0-N`, `mongod-data-my-cluster-name-cfg-N`                                       | Data volumes, created by the StatefulSets. Arbiters keep no data and use no PVC                                                                                                             |
| PersistentVolumeClaim      | `mongos-logs-my-cluster-name-mongos-N`                                                                         | `mongos` logs, when [persistent logging](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/persistent-logging.html#for-mongos-pods) for `mongos` is on                           |
| PersistentVolumeClaim      | `mongot-data-my-cluster-name-rs0-search-N`                                                                     | Search indexes, when search is on                                                                                                                                                           |
| Lease                      | `psmdb-my-cluster-name-backup-lock`                                                                            | Makes backups run one at a time                                                                                                                                                             |
| PerconaServerMongoDBBackup | `cron-my-cluster-name-<timestamp>-<suffix>`                                                                    | One backup object for each scheduled run. See [Scheduled backups](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/architecture-workflows.html#scheduled-backups)               |
| VolumeSnapshot             | One for each data PVC                                                                                          | Created for each [PVC snapshot backup](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/backups-pvc-snapshots.html)                                                             |
| ServiceExport              | One for each Service                                                                                           | Created when [Multi-Cluster Services](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/replication-mcs.html) are enabled                                                        |

If cert-manager is installed, the Operator also creates cert-manager Issuers and Certificates that produce the TLS Secrets. When you create a `PerconaServerMongoDBClusterSync` object, the Operator creates the Deployment that runs [PCSM](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/clustersync.html) and the `psmdb-my-cluster-name-clustersync-lock` Lease.

Note

The Operator creates no Kubernetes Jobs or CronJobs. The PBM agents make backups and restores, and the Operator keeps the backup schedules itself. See [Scheduled backups](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/architecture-workflows.html#scheduled-backups).

Objects that survive cluster deletion

PVCs and Secrets are not owned by the Custom Resource, so deleting the CR does not delete them. This lets you recreate the cluster with its data and credentials. To delete them together with the cluster, set the `percona.com/delete-psmdb-pvc` finalizer. See [Delete the database cluster](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/delete.html#delete-the-database-cluster).

## Finalizers

A [finalizer](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/glossary.html#finalizer) makes Kubernetes wait for a cleanup step before it deletes an object.

| Finalizer                                | Set on                                     | What it does before deletion                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| ---------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `percona.com/delete-psmdb-pods-in-order` | Cluster. On by default in `deploy/cr.yaml` | Stops `mongos`, then scales each replica set down one Pod at a time, so that the first Pod is the last one to stop                                                                                                |
| `percona.com/delete-psmdb-pvc`           | Cluster. Off by default                    | Deletes the StatefulSets, all PVCs of the cluster, the users Secret, the internal users Secret and the encryption key Secret. While it is set, the Operator also deletes the PVCs of Pods removed by a scale-down |
| `percona.com/delete-pitr-chunks`         | Cluster. Off by default                    | Deletes the oplog chunks saved for point-in-time recovery from the backup storage                                                                                                                                 |
| `percona.com/delete-backup`              | Backup                                     | Deletes the backup files from the storage, or the VolumeSnapshots of a PVC snapshot backup. For an `incremental` backup, it does nothing: its files are deleted together with the base backup of the chain        |
| `internal.percona.com/release-lock`      | Backup                                     | Releases the backup lock if a running backup is deleted. The Operator adds and removes it itself                                                                                                                  |

Don’t remove a finalizer to finish a stuck deletion. Find out why the cleanup is blocked instead. See [Cluster lifecycle](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/operator-boundaries.html#cluster-lifecycle).

## Containers in each Pod

**Replica set and config server Pods** (`my-cluster-name-rs0-N`, `my-cluster-name-cfg-N`):

- `mongo-init`, an init container, copies the Operator’s entrypoint, the `mongodb-healthcheck` tool and other helper files into a shared volume.
- `mongod` runs the database. It listens on port 27017.
- `backup-agent` runs the PBM agent, when backups are enabled.
- Optional sidecars: `pmm-client` for [monitoring](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/monitoring.html), `logs` and `logrotate` for [log collection](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/persistent-logging.html), and your own [sidecar containers](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/sidecar.html).

**Arbiter, non-voting and hidden member Pods** have the same layout. The main container is named `mongod-arbiter`, `mongod-nv` or `mongod-hidden`. The arbiter has no data volume and no `backup-agent` container.

**`mongos` Pods** (`my-cluster-name-mongos-N`):

- `mongo-init`, an init container, as in the replica set Pods.
- `mongos` routes client queries. It listens on port 27017.
- Optional sidecars: `pmm-client`, `logs` and `logrotate`, and your own sidecar containers.

**Search Pods** (`my-cluster-name-rs0-search-N`):

- `mongot` serves full-text and vector search queries for `mongod` and `mongos`.

## See also

- [Services and ports](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/services.html) for every Service, its ports and when it exists
- [Design and architecture](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/architecture.html) for how these objects work together
- [Operator responsibilities by area](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/operator-boundaries.html) for what the Operator does and doesn’t do with them

# Manage clusters with the Kubernetes API

Percona Operator for MongoDB extends the [Kubernetes API](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/extend-kubernetes/api-extension/custom-resources/) with Custom Resources (CRs). You manage database clusters the same way you manage other Kubernetes objects:

- with `kubectl`
- with Kubernetes client libraries in your programming language
- with HTTPS requests to the Kubernetes API server. For example, with `curl`.

This page shows common `kubectl` and `curl` examples for these Custom Resources:

| Kind                          | Short name      | Purpose                                       |
| ----------------------------- | --------------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| `PerconaServerMongoDB`        | `psmdb`         | Database cluster definition and desired state |
| `PerconaServerMongoDBBackup`  | `psmdb-backup`  | On-demand backup request and backup status    |
| `PerconaServerMongoDBRestore` | `psmdb-restore` | Restore request and restore status            |

For every field and option, see:

- [Custom Resource options](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/operator.html)
- [Backup Resource options](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/backup-resource-options.html)
- [Restore options](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/restore-options.html)
- [Custom resource statuses](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/cr-statuses.html)

For general Kubernetes API access and authentication, see the [official Kubernetes API documentation](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/) .

## Prerequisites

1. Deploy the Operator and install the CRDs in your cluster. See [Install on Kubernetes](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/kubectl.html).

1. Create a namespace (or use an existing one) and export it:

   ```
   export NAMESPACE=my-namespace-name
   kubectl create namespace $NAMESPACE
   ```

1. Set the API server address:

   ```
   # set correct API address
   KUBE_CLUSTER=$(kubectl config view --minify -o jsonpath='{.clusters[0].name}')
   API_SERVER=$(kubectl config view -o jsonpath="{.clusters[?(@.name==\"$KUBE_CLUSTER\")].cluster.server}" | sed -e 's#https://##')
   ```

1. Get the token:

   ```
   export KUBE_TOKEN=$(kubectl create token percona-server-mongodb-operator -n $NAMESPACE)
   ```

   The `curl` examples below use `https://$API_SERVER` and `Authorization: Bearer $KUBE_TOKEN`. In production, use a dedicated ServiceAccount with the RBAC you need.

Warning

The `-k` flag in the `curl` examples skips TLS certificate verification. Prefer proper trust configuration for production use.

## Cluster lifecycle

### Create a cluster

Create a `PerconaServerMongoDB` object. The usual path is to maintain `deploy/cr.yaml` and apply it. The same object can be posted as JSON to the API.

**kubectl**

```
kubectl apply -f deploy/cr.yaml -n $NAMESPACE
```

**curl**

```
curl -k -XPOST \
  "https://$API_SERVER/apis/psmdb.percona.com/v1/namespaces/$NAMESPACE/perconaservermongodbs" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $KUBE_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Accept: application/json" \
  -d @cluster.json
```

Minimal `cluster.json` shape (expand with the options you need from [Custom Resource options](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/operator.html)). Update the `"namespace"` field with your value:

```
{
  "apiVersion": "psmdb.percona.com/v1",
  "kind": "PerconaServerMongoDB",
  "metadata": {
    "name": "my-cluster-name",
    "namespace": "my-namespace-name"
  },
  "spec": {
    "image": "percona/percona-server-mongodb:8.3.13-4",
    "replsets": [
      {
        "name": "rs0",
        "size": 3,
        "volumeSpec": {
          "persistentVolumeClaim": {
            "resources": {
              "requests": {
                "storage": "3Gi"
              }
            }
          }
        }
      }
    ],
    "sharding": {
      "enabled": true,
      "configsvrReplSet": {
        "size": 3,
        "volumeSpec": {
          "persistentVolumeClaim": {
            "resources": {
              "requests": {
                "storage": "3Gi"
              }
            }
          }
        }
      },
      "mongos": {
        "size": 3
      }
    },
    "backup": {
      "enabled": true,
      "image": "percona/percona-backup-mongodb:2.15.0"
    }
  }
}
```

### List clusters

**kubectl**

```
kubectl get psmdb -n $NAMESPACE
```

**curl**

```
curl -k -XGET \
  "https://$API_SERVER/apis/psmdb.percona.com/v1/namespaces/$NAMESPACE/perconaservermongodbs?limit=100" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $KUBE_TOKEN" \
  -H "Accept: application/json"
```

Kubernetes list responses can include a `metadata.continue` token when more results remain. Pass it on the next request:

```
curl -k -XGET \
  "https://$API_SERVER/apis/psmdb.percona.com/v1/namespaces/$NAMESPACE/perconaservermongodbs?limit=100&continue=$CONTINUE_TOKEN" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $KUBE_TOKEN" \
  -H "Accept: application/json"
```

See [Kubernetes paginated lists](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/using-api/api-concepts/#retrieving-large-results-sets-in-chunks) for details.

### Get cluster details and status

**kubectl**

```
kubectl get psmdb my-cluster-name -n $NAMESPACE -o json
kubectl get psmdb my-cluster-name -n $NAMESPACE -o jsonpath='{.status.state}{"\n"}{.status.host}{"\n"}'
```

**curl**

```
curl -k -XGET \
  "https://$API_SERVER/apis/psmdb.percona.com/v1/namespaces/$NAMESPACE/perconaservermongodbs/my-cluster-name" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $KUBE_TOKEN" \
  -H "Accept: application/json"
```

Useful fields in the response:

- `status.state` — overall state (`initializing`, `ready`, `error`, `paused`, and others)
- `status.host` — connection endpoint hostname
- `status.ready` / `status.size` — ready Pods versus desired size
- `status.replsets` — per replica set status

Full state values and conditions are documented in [Custom resource statuses](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/cr-statuses.html).

### Scale a replica set

Prefer a JSON Patch that changes only `size`, so you do not overwrite the rest of the replica set spec.

**kubectl**

```
kubectl patch psmdb my-cluster-name -n $NAMESPACE --type=json -p='[
  {"op": "replace", "path": "/spec/replsets/0/size", "value": 5}
]'
```

**curl**

```
curl -k -XPATCH \
  "https://$API_SERVER/apis/psmdb.percona.com/v1/namespaces/$NAMESPACE/perconaservermongodbs/my-cluster-name" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $KUBE_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json-patch+json" \
  -H "Accept: application/json" \
  -d '[
    {"op": "replace", "path": "/spec/replsets/0/size", "value": 5}
  ]'
```

Replace `/spec/replsets/0` with the index of the replica set you want to change.

#### Scale to zero

Setting `replsets[].size` to `0` scales that replica set down. It does **not** delete the `PerconaServerMongoDB` object, and data on Persistent Volume Claims remains unless you delete those volumes separately.

To use a size below the Operator’s safe defaults (including `0`), enable the corresponding unsafe flag, for example `spec.unsafeFlags.replsetSize: true`. See [unsafeFlags](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/operator.html#operator-unsafeflags-section).

To remove the cluster itself, [delete the Custom Resource](#delete-a-cluster).

### Add a replica set

The following command adds a new shard (deployed as the replica set) to the sharded cluster. This command is available only for sharded clusters. To expand the replica set deployment, see [Scale a replica set](#scale-a-replica-set).

**kubectl**

```
kubectl patch psmdb my-cluster-name -n $NAMESPACE --type=json -p='[
  {
    "op": "add",
    "path": "/spec/replsets/-",
    "value": {
      "name": "rs1",
      "size": 3,
      "volumeSpec": {
        "persistentVolumeClaim": {
          "resources": {
            "requests": {
              "storage": "3Gi"
            }
          }
        }
      }
    }
  }
]'
```

**curl**

```
curl -k -XPATCH \
  "https://$API_SERVER/apis/psmdb.percona.com/v1/namespaces/$NAMESPACE/perconaservermongodbs/my-cluster-name" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $KUBE_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json-patch+json" \
  -H "Accept: application/json" \
  -d '[
    {
      "op": "add",
      "path": "/spec/replsets/-",
      "value": {
        "name": "rs1",
        "size": 3,
        "volumeSpec": {
          "persistentVolumeClaim": {
            "resources": {
              "requests": {
                "storage": "3Gi"
              }
            }
          }
        }
      }
    }
  ]'
```

### Remove a replica set

To remove a shard (deployed as a replica set) from a sharded cluster, you must first drain the shard of all data. Follow this process:

1. **Drain the shard:** Use [MongoDB’s drain procedure](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/tutorial/remove-shards-from-cluster/) to remove all data and move chunks from the shard you want to remove. Wait until MongoDB reports that the shard is fully drained and safe for removal.
1. **Remove the shard from the cluster:** After the shard is fully drained, remove the replica set from the cluster specification.

Remove by array index (check the current order with `kubectl get psmdb my-cluster-name -o json` first):

**kubectl**

```
kubectl patch psmdb my-cluster-name -n $NAMESPACE --type=json -p='[
  {"op": "remove", "path": "/spec/replsets/1"}
]'
```

**curl**

```
curl -k -XPATCH \
  "https://$API_SERVER/apis/psmdb.percona.com/v1/namespaces/$NAMESPACE/perconaservermongodbs/my-cluster-name" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $KUBE_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json-patch+json" \
  -H "Accept: application/json" \
  -d '[
    {"op": "remove", "path": "/spec/replsets/1"}
  ]'
```

### Update the MongoDB image

**kubectl**

```
kubectl patch psmdb my-cluster-name -n $NAMESPACE --type=json -p='[
  {"op": "replace", "path": "/spec/image", "value": "percona/percona-server-mongodb:8.3.13-4"}
]'
```

**curl**

```
curl -k -XPATCH \
  "https://$API_SERVER/apis/psmdb.percona.com/v1/namespaces/$NAMESPACE/perconaservermongodbs/my-cluster-name" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $KUBE_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json-patch+json" \
  -H "Accept: application/json" \
  -d '[
    {"op": "replace", "path": "/spec/image", "value": "percona/percona-server-mongodb:8.3.13-4"}
  ]'
```

### Delete a cluster

Deleting the `PerconaServerMongoDB` Custom Resource deletes the cluster. Finalizers control whether PVCs and related objects are removed. By default, PVCs are kept so you can recreate the cluster without losing data. See [Delete the database cluster](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/delete.html#delete-the-database-cluster).

**kubectl**

```
kubectl delete psmdb my-cluster-name -n $NAMESPACE
```

**curl**

```
curl -k -XDELETE \
  "https://$API_SERVER/apis/psmdb.percona.com/v1/namespaces/$NAMESPACE/perconaservermongodbs/my-cluster-name" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $KUBE_TOKEN" \
  -H "Accept: application/json"
```

### Connection details

Starting with Operator version 1.23.0, the Operator creates a Kubernetes Secret with ready-to-use MongoDB connection strings. For the default `databaseAdmin` user, the Secret is named `<cluster-name>-databaseadmin-conn-str`.

Example for a sharded cluster:

**kubectl**

```
kubectl get secret my-cluster-name-databaseadmin-conn-str -n $NAMESPACE \
  -o jsonpath='{.data.databaseAdmin_mongos_connectionString}' | base64 --decode && echo
```

**curl**

```
curl -k -XGET \
  "https://$API_SERVER/api/v1/namespaces/$NAMESPACE/secrets/my-cluster-name-databaseadmin-conn-str" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $KUBE_TOKEN" \
  -H "Accept: application/json" \
  | grep '"databaseAdmin_mongos_connectionString"' \
  | awk -F '"' '{print $4}' \
  | base64 --decode && echo
```

For a non-sharded replica set, use the `databaseAdmin_rs0_connectionStringSrv` key instead. See [Connection secrets](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/connection-secrets.html) for all available keys.

## Backup lifecycle

Backup storage, schedules, and retention live on the cluster Custom Resource under `spec.backup`. On-demand backups are separate `PerconaServerMongoDBBackup` objects. See [Backup and restore](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/backups.html) and [Configure backups](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/backups-configure.html).

To manage backups, you must configure the backup storage. See [Configure storage for backups](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/backups-storage.html) for details.

### Configure backup settings and retention

Patch `spec.backup` on the cluster. Example: enable backups, set a schedule, and keep the last 3 successful backups:

```
kubectl patch psmdb my-cluster-name -n $NAMESPACE --type=merge -p '{
  "spec": {
    "backup": {
      "enabled": true,
      "storages": {
        "s3-us-west": {
          "type": "s3",
          "s3": {
            "bucket": "my-bucket",
            "region": "us-west-2",
            "credentialsSecret": "my-cluster-name-backup-s3"
          }
        }
      },
      "tasks": [
        {
          "name": "daily-s3",
          "enabled": true,
          "schedule": "0 0 * * *",
          "storageName": "s3-us-west",
          "retention": {
            "type": "count",
            "count": 3,
            "deleteFromStorage": true
          }
        }
      ]
    }
  }
}'
```

For every backup option, see [Custom Resource options](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/operator.html#operator-backup-section) and [Make scheduled backups](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/backups-scheduled.html).

Note

A merge patch that replaces `storages` or `tasks` overwrites those objects/arrays. Prefer editing your maintained `deploy/cr.yaml` and applying it when you manage complex backup configuration.

### Create a backup

**kubectl**

```
kubectl apply -f deploy/backup/backup.yaml -n $NAMESPACE
```

Example Backup object:

```
apiVersion: psmdb.percona.com/v1
kind: PerconaServerMongoDBBackup
metadata:
  name: backup1
  finalizers:
    - percona.com/delete-backup
spec:
  clusterName: my-cluster-name
  storageName: s3-us-west
  type: logical
```

**curl**

```
curl -k -XPOST \
  "https://$API_SERVER/apis/psmdb.percona.com/v1/namespaces/$NAMESPACE/perconaservermongodbbackups" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $KUBE_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Accept: application/json" \
  -d @backup.json
```

`backup.json`:

```
{
  "apiVersion": "psmdb.percona.com/v1",
  "kind": "PerconaServerMongoDBBackup",
  "metadata": {
    "name": "backup1",
    "finalizers": [
      "percona.com/delete-backup"
    ]
  },
  "spec": {
    "clusterName": "my-cluster-name",
    "storageName": "s3-us-west",
    "type": "logical"
  }
}
```

### List backups and check status

**kubectl**

```
kubectl get psmdb-backup -n $NAMESPACE
kubectl get psmdb-backup backup1 -n $NAMESPACE -o jsonpath='{.status.state}{"\n"}{.status.size}{"\n"}{.status.destination}{"\n"}'
```

**curl**

```
curl -k -XGET \
  "https://$API_SERVER/apis/psmdb.percona.com/v1/namespaces/$NAMESPACE/perconaservermongodbbackups/backup1" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $KUBE_TOKEN" \
  -H "Accept: application/json"
```

Useful status fields: `status.state` (`waiting`, `running`, `ready`, `error`, …), `status.size`, `status.destination`, `status.type`, `status.completed`. See [Backup status](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/cr-statuses.html#perconaservermongodbbackup-status).

## Restore lifecycle

Restores are `PerconaServerMongoDBRestore` objects. You can restore onto the same cluster, onto a new cluster, run point-in-time recovery, or restore selected namespaces (databases/collections). Details and limitations:

- [Restore on the same cluster](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/backups-restore.html#restore-on-the-same-cluster)
- [Restore to a new cluster](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/backups-restore.html#restore-on-a-new-cluster)
- [Selective restore](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/backups-restore.html#selective-restore)

### Restore to the same cluster

**kubectl**

```
kubectl apply -f deploy/backup/restore.yaml -n $NAMESPACE
```

Example Restore object:

```
apiVersion: psmdb.percona.com/v1
kind: PerconaServerMongoDBRestore
metadata:
  name: restore1
spec:
  clusterName: my-cluster-name
  backupName: backup1
```

**curl**

```
curl -k -XPOST \
  "https://$API_SERVER/apis/psmdb.percona.com/v1/namespaces/$NAMESPACE/perconaservermongodbrestores" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $KUBE_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Accept: application/json" \
  -d @restore.json
```

`restore.json`:

```
{
  "apiVersion": "psmdb.percona.com/v1",
  "kind": "PerconaServerMongoDBRestore",
  "metadata": {
    "name": "restore1"
  },
  "spec": {
    "clusterName": "my-cluster-name",
    "backupName": "backup1"
  }
}
```

### Restore to a new cluster

1. Create the target `PerconaServerMongoDB` cluster (create flow above).
1. Create a `PerconaServerMongoDBRestore` that points at that cluster and at the backup source (often via `spec.backupSource` when the backup object does not exist in the new environment).

See [Restore to a new cluster](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/backups-restore.html#restore-on-a-new-cluster) for storage, Secrets, and `backupSource` examples.

### Selective (partial) restore

For a logical backup, you can restore specific databases or collections with `spec.selective`:

```
apiVersion: psmdb.percona.com/v1
kind: PerconaServerMongoDBRestore
metadata:
  name: restore-selective
spec:
  clusterName: my-cluster-name
  backupName: backup1
  selective:
    withUsersAndRoles: true
    namespaces:
      - "db1.collection1"
      - "db2.*"
```

### Check restore status

**kubectl**

```
kubectl get psmdb-restore -n $NAMESPACE
kubectl get psmdb-restore restore1 -n $NAMESPACE -o jsonpath='{.status.state}{"\n"}'
```

**curl**

```
curl -k -XGET \
  "https://$API_SERVER/apis/psmdb.percona.com/v1/namespaces/$NAMESPACE/perconaservermongodbrestores/restore1" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $KUBE_TOKEN" \
  -H "Accept: application/json"
```

See [Restore status](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/cr-statuses.html#perconaservermongodbrestore-status).

## Image tag format

Image tags have the format:

`[component_name]-[component_version]`

where:

- `component_name` is the name of the component. For example, `percona-server-mongodb`
- `component_version` is the version of the component. For example, `8.0.4-1`.

Note, that PMM Client images have their own tags. They contain the version of PMM.

[Find images for previous versions](https://docs.percona.com/legacy-documentation/)

# Retrieve Percona certified images

When preparing for the upgrade, you must have the list of compatible images for a specific Operator version and the database version you wish to update to. You can either manually find the images in the [list of certified images](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/images.html) or you can get this list by querying the **Version Service** server.

Security builds use numbered tags that the Version Service does not list. See [Operator security builds](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/security-builds.html) to find and use those tags.

### What is the Version Service?

The **Version Service** is a centralized repository that the Percona Operator for MySQL connects to at scheduled times to get the latest information on compatible versions and valid image paths. This service is a crucial part of the automatic upgrade process, and it is enabled by default. Its landing page, `check.percona.com`, provides more details about the service itself.

### How to query the Version Service

You can manually query the Version Service using the `curl` command. The basic syntax is:

```
curl https://check.percona.com/versions/v1/psmdb-operator/<operator-version>/<psmdb-version> | jq -r '.versions[].matrix'
```

where:

- **`<operator-version>`** is the version of the Percona Operator for MongoDB you are using.
- **`<psmdb-version>`** is the version of Percona Server for MongoDB you want to get images for. This part is optional and helps filter the results. It can be a specific Percona Server for MongoDB version (e.g. 8.0.8-3), a recommended version (e.g. 7.0-recommended), or the latest available version (e.g. 8.0-latest).

For example, to retrieve the list of images for the Operator version `1.20.0` and the latest version of Percona Server for MongoDB 8.0, use the following command:

```
curl https://check.percona.com/versions/v1/psmdb-operator/1.20.0/8.0-latest |jq -r '.versions[].matrix'
```

Sample output

```

To narrow down the search and check the Percona Server for MySQL images available for a specific Operator version (`1.20.1` in the following example), use the following command:

```
curl -s https://check.percona.com/versions/v1/psmdb-operator/1.20.1 | jq -r '.versions[0].matrix.mongod | to_entries[] | "\(.key)\t\(.value.imagePath)\t\(.value.status)"'
```

# Frequently Asked Questions

## Why do we need to follow “the Kubernetes way” when Kubernetes was never intended to run databases?

As it is well known, the Kubernetes approach is targeted at stateless applications but provides ways to store state (in Persistent Volumes, etc.) if the application needs it. Generally, a stateless mode of operation is supposed to provide better safety, sustainability, and scalability, it makes the already-deployed components interchangeable. You can find more about substantial benefits brought by Kubernetes to databases in [this blog post](https://www.percona.com/blog/2020/10/08/the-criticality-of-a-kubernetes-operator-for-databases/) .

The architecture of state-centric applications (like databases) should be composed in a right way to avoid crashes, data loss, or data inconsistencies during hardware failure. Percona Operator for MongoDB provides out-of-the-box functionality to automate provisioning and management of highly available MongoDB database clusters on Kubernetes.

## How can I contact the developers?

The best place to discuss Percona Operator for MongoDB with developers and other community members is the [community forum](https://forums.percona.com/categories/kubernetes-operator-percona-server-mongodb) .

If you would like to report a bug, use the Percona Operator for MongoDB [project in JIRA](https://jira.percona.com/projects/K8SPSMDB) .

## What is the difference between the Operator quickstart and advanced installation ways?

As you have noticed, the installation section of docs contains both quickstart and advanced installation guides.

The quickstart guide is simpler. It has fewer installation steps in favor of predefined default choices. Particularly, in advanced installation guides, you separately apply the Custom Resource Definition and Role-based Access Control configuration files with possible edits in them. At the same time, quickstart guides rely on the all-inclusive bundle configuration.

At another point, quickstart guides are related to specific platforms you are going to use (Minikube, Google Kubernetes Engine, etc.) and therefore include some additional steps needed for these platforms.

Generally, rely on the quickstart guide if you are a beginner user of the specific platform and/or you are new to the Percona Operator for MongoDB as a whole.

## Which versions of MongoDB does the Operator support?

Percona Operator for MongoDB works with all active major versions of Percona Server for MongoDB. The exact version is determined by the Docker image in use.

The Operator uses Percona-certified Docker images, which you can find [here](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/images.html). For example, Percona Server for MongoDB 8.3 is supported with the following recommended version: 8.3.13-4.

Check the [Percona Server for MongoDB release notes](https://docs.percona.com/percona-server-for-mongodb/latest/release_notes/index.html) for more details on the exact version of the latest major version. Use the version switcher to check other major versions.

## How can I add custom sidecar containers to my cluster?

The Operator allows you to deploy additional containers to the Pod. Such containers are called *sidecar* containers.

You can use sidecar containers to run debugging tools, some specific monitoring solutions, etc. Add such sidecar container to the `deploy/cr.yaml` configuration file, specifying its name and image, and possibly a command to run:

```
spec:
  replsets:
  - name: rs0
    ....
    sidecars:
    - image: busybox
      command: ["/bin/sh"]
      args: ["-c", "while true; do echo echo $(date -u) 'test' >> /dev/null; sleep 5; done"]
      name: rs-sidecar-1
    ....
```

You can add `sidecars` subsection to `replsets`, `sharding.configsvrReplSet`, and `sharding.mongos` sections.

Note

Custom sidecar containers [can easily access other components of your cluster](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/#resource-sharing-and-communication) . Therefore they should be used carefully and by experienced users only.

Find more information on sidecar containers in the appropriate [documentation page](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/sidecar.html).

## How to provoke the initial sync of a Pod?

There are certain situations where it might be necessary to delete all MongoDB instance data to force the resync. For example, there may be the following reasons:

- rebuilding the node to defragment the database,
- recreating the member failing to sync due to some bug.

In the case of a “regular” MongoDB, wiping the dbpath would trigger such resync. In the case of a MongoDB cluster controlled by the Operator, you will need to do the following steps:

1. Find out the names of the Persistent Volume Claim and Pod you are going to delete (use `kubectl get pvc` command for PVC and `kubectl get pod` one for Pods).

1. Delete the appropriate PVC and Pod. For example, wiping out the `my-cluster-name-rs0-2` Pod should look as follows:

   ```
   kubectl delete pod/my-cluster-name-rs0-2 pvc/mongod-data-my-cluster-name-rs0-2
   ```

The Operator will automatically recreate the needed Pod and PVC after deletion.

# Glossary

This page explains the Kubernetes and MongoDB terms used in the Operator documentation. The examples use a cluster named `my-cluster-name` with a replica set named `rs0`.

## Arbiter

A replica set member that votes in [elections](#election) but holds no data and can’t become [primary](#primary). It gives a replica set with an even number of data-bearing members an odd number of votes.

See [Arbiter, non-voting and hidden nodes](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/arbiter.html).

## Cluster

The word *cluster* has two meanings in these docs. A *Kubernetes cluster* is the set of machines that Kubernetes manages. A *database cluster* is what one [Custom Resource](#custom-resource) describes: one replica set, or a sharded cluster with its shards, config server replica set and `mongos` routers. One Kubernetes cluster can run several database clusters. Pages that say “the cluster” mean the database cluster, unless they say “Kubernetes cluster”.

See [Design and architecture](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/architecture.html).

## Config server replica set

The replica set that stores the metadata of a sharded cluster: which data lives on which [shard](#shard). The Operator names its Pods `my-cluster-name-cfg-N`.

See [Sharding](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/sharding.html).

## Custom Resource (CR, cr.yaml)

The Kubernetes object that describes the cluster you want, for example `PerconaServerMongoDB`. The Operator reads it and makes the cluster match. A [CustomResourceDefinition](#crd) tells Kubernetes that this object type exists.

The `deploy/cr.yaml` file in the Operator repository is the example manifest of this object. See [Change the cluster through the Custom Resource](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/architecture-responsibilities.html#change-the-cluster-through-the-custom-resource).

For all options, see the [Custom Resource options reference](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/operator.html).

## CustomResourceDefinition (CRD)

A Kubernetes object that adds a new object type to the Kubernetes API and defines its fields. The Operator uses four CRDs in the `psmdb.percona.com` API group: `PerconaServerMongoDB`, `PerconaServerMongoDBBackup`, `PerconaServerMongoDBRestore` and `PerconaServerMongoDBClusterSync`. They are in the `deploy/crd.yaml` file of the Operator repository.

CRDs are cluster-wide objects, so installing them needs cluster-level permissions. You install and upgrade them yourself, before the Operator. The Operator never applies them.

See [Upgrade the Operator and CRD](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/update-operator.html).

## Election

The vote in which the members of a replica set choose a new [primary](#primary). A candidate needs the votes of a majority of the voting members. MongoDB holds an election when the primary becomes unreachable or steps down.

See [Primary failover](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/architecture-workflows.html#primary-failover).

## Feature compatibility version (FCV)

The MongoDB setting that turns on the features of a major version that change the data format. Until you raise it after an upgrade, you can still downgrade.

See [Major version upgrades](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/update-major.html).

## Finalizer

A key in `metadata.finalizers` that makes Kubernetes wait for a cleanup step before it deletes an object. The Operator uses finalizers such as `percona.com/delete-psmdb-pvc` to clean up volumes and Secrets.

See [Finalizers](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/objects-created.html#finalizers).

## Headless Service

A Kubernetes Service without a cluster IP. DNS returns the addresses of the Pods behind it, and a DNS name for each Pod. The Operator creates one for each replica set, such as `my-cluster-name-rs0`. Drivers that use `mongodb+srv` connection strings find the members through it.

See [Services and ports](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/services.html).

## Hidden member

A data-bearing replica set member that applications don’t see and that can’t become [primary](#primary). Use it for backups, analytics or reporting.

See [Arbiter, non-voting and hidden nodes](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/arbiter.html#hidden-nodes).

## Initial sync

A full copy of the data from another member to a member that starts with an empty data directory or fell too far behind. During an initial sync, the member is in the `STARTUP2` state.

See [Health checks and probes](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/architecture-probes.html).

## Lease

A small Kubernetes object that works as a lock. The Operator uses a Lease so that only one backup runs at a time.

See [Objects the Operator creates](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/objects-created.html).

## mongos

The query router of a sharded cluster. Applications connect to `mongos`, and `mongos` sends each query to the [shards](#shard) that hold the data. `mongos` stores no data.

See [Design and architecture](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/architecture.html#sharded-cluster).

## Node

The word *node* has two meanings in these docs. A *Kubernetes node* is a machine, physical or virtual, where Pods run. A *database node*, or *member*, is one `mongod` process of a replica set, running in a Pod such as `my-cluster-name-rs0-0`. By default, the Operator requires the members of a replica set to run on different Kubernetes nodes.

See [Control Pod scheduling](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/constraints.html).

## Non-voting member

A data-bearing replica set member without a vote, which can’t become [primary](#primary). Use it to add read capacity, or members beyond the limit of 7 voting members.

See [Arbiter, non-voting and hidden nodes](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/arbiter.html#non-voting-nodes).

## Oplog

The operations log: a special collection in which a member records every write. Secondaries copy the oplog of another member and apply it. For point-in-time recovery, PBM saves the oplog to backup storage.

See [Point-in-time recovery](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/architecture-workflows.html#point-in-time-recovery).

## Percona Backup for MongoDB (PBM)

The tool that makes backups and restores. Its agent, `pbm-agent`, runs in the `backup-agent` container of each database Pod. The Operator sends PBM the backup and restore commands.

See [Backup and restore](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/backups.html).

## PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC)

A request for storage. Each data-bearing member has a PVC that holds its data. The StorageClass and the Container Storage Interface (CSI) driver provide the actual volume.

See [Resize storage](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/scaling-storage-resize.html).

## PodDisruptionBudget (PDB)

A Kubernetes object that limits how many Pods of a StatefulSet can be unavailable during voluntary disruptions such as a node drain. The Operator creates one for each StatefulSet.

See [Pod Disruption Budgets](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/constraints.html#pod-disruption-budgets).

## Primary

The replica set member that accepts writes. A replica set has at most one primary. The other data-bearing members are secondaries.

See [Design and architecture](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/architecture.html#percona-server-for-mongodb-in-brief).

## Reconcile

One pass of the Operator loop: it compares the Custom Resource with what exists in Kubernetes and in the database, and corrects the difference. The Operator repeats it about every five seconds.

See [How the Operator reacts to changes](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/architecture-reconciliation.html#what-a-reconcile-is).

## Replica set

A group of `mongod` processes that hold the same data: one [primary](#primary) and one or more secondaries. The Operator runs each replica set as a StatefulSet.

See [About high availability and topology](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/ha-topology.html).

## Shard

A replica set that holds part of the data of a sharded cluster.

See [Sharding](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/sharding.html).

## Smart Update

The Operator update strategy that restarts the members one at a time, secondaries first and the primary last after a step-down. It doesn’t start while a backup or restore is running.

See [How Smart Update works](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/architecture-reconciliation.html#how-smart-update-works).

## StatefulSet

A Kubernetes workload that gives each Pod a stable name and its own volume, for example `my-cluster-name-rs0-0`. The Operator runs each replica set and `mongos` as StatefulSets.

See [Objects the Operator creates](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/objects-created.html).

## Write concern

The number of members that must confirm a write before MongoDB reports it as successful. With the `majority` write concern, a write survives the loss of the primary. Set the cluster-wide default with the `defaultRWConcern` section of the Custom Resource.

See [About high availability and topology](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/ha-topology.html#read-and-write-concerns).

# Telemetry

The Telemetry function enables the Operator to gather and send basic anonymous data to Percona, which helps us to determine where to focus the development and what is the uptake for each release of Operator.

Telemetry is enabled by default and is sent to the [Version Service server](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/update-db.html) when the Operator connects to it at scheduled times to obtain fresh information about version numbers and valid image paths needed for the upgrade.

The landing page for this service, [check.percona.com](https://check.percona.com/) , explains what this service is.

## Cluster and software versions

The Operator reports the following for every cluster:

- Custom Resource ID (`metadata.uid`)
- Kubernetes version
- Platform (Kubernetes or OpenShift. Starting with Operator version 1.24, the Operator also collects the Kubernetes provider and appends it to the platform name. For example, `kubernetes-gke` for a Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster. If the Operator does not detect the provider, the value ends in `-unknown`)
- Operator version
- Percona Server for MongoDB version
- Percona Backup for MongoDB (PBM) version
- Whether Percona Monitoring and Management (PMM) is enabled, and the PMM version
- Cluster size
- Whether the Operator is [deployed with Helm](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/helm.html)
- Whether [sidecar containers](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/sidecar.html) are used

The Operator does not gather anything that identifies a system. The Custom Resource ID is a unique ID that Kubernetes generates for each Custom Resource.

## Disable telemetry

You can disable telemetry with a special option when installing the Operator:

- if you [install the Operator with helm](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/helm.html), use the following installation command:

```
helm install my-db percona/psmdb-db --version 1.23.1 --namespace my-namespace --set disable_telemetry="true"
```

- if you don’t use helm for installation, you have to edit the `operator.yaml` before applying it with the `kubectl apply -f deploy/operator.yaml` command. Open the `operator.yaml` file with your text editor, find the value of the `DISABLE_TELEMETRY` environment variable and set it to `true`:

```
env:
  ...
  - name: DISABLE_TELEMETRY
    value: "true"
  ...
```

# Percona Operator for MongoDB 1.23.1 (2026-10-05)

[Get started with the Operator](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/quickstart.html) [Upgrade](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/update.html)

## What’s new at a glance

This release focuses on day-to-day operations. It adds persistent logging for mongos Pods, so you can troubleshoot the query router after a restart. You can also set how often the Operator contacts HashiCorp Vault for system user passwords.

## Release Highlights

### Persistent logging for `mongos`

`mongos` is the query router in a sharded cluster. Its logs record connection failures, slow queries, authentication errors, and which shard received a query.

Starting with this release, persistent logging also covers `mongos` Pods. This enables you to see what the router did after a rollout, an out-of-memory restart, a node drain or another incident.

The Operator adds the `logs` (Fluent Bit) and `logrotate` sidecars to each `mongos` Pod. Those logs survive a Pod restart only when you configure the storage for them via the `sharding.mongos.logs.persistentVolumeClaim` section in the Custom Resource. The Operator then creates one Persistent Volume Claim (PVC) per `mongos` Pod and stores the log file on that volume.

Resize that PVC the same way you resize storage for replica set and config server Pods. Automatic storage resizing for `mongos` is not supported yet.

If you turn persistent logging off, the Operator removes the sidecars but keeps existing `mongos` log PVCs. Files already on the volume stay readable.

`logrotate` uses one cluster-wide policy for `mongod` and `mongos`. It rotates logs daily, when they exceed 100 MB and keeps up to 7 rotated files. When you change that policy, include the configuration for both `mongod` and `mongos`.

Read more in the [persistent logging](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/persistent-logging.html#for-mongos-pods) and [log rotation](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/logrotate.html) documentation.

### Control how often the Operator contacts HashiCorp Vault

When you store system user passwords in HashiCorp Vault, you can now configure how often the Operator reaches Vault to read those passwords and to sign in. The Operator creates a Vault client to sign in, and uses it for password reads.

Use these options in the Custom Resource:

- `vault.requestInterval` sets how often the Operator reads passwords from Vault. A longer interval sends fewer requests when passwords change infrequently. Leave it unset to read Vault on every reconciliation.
- `vault.reinitInterval` sets how often the Operator creates a new Vault client and signs in again. Shorten it when your Vault tokens expire quickly. The default is 30 minutes.

If you update the Vault token in `vault.syncUsers.tokenSecret`, the Operator creates a new Vault client on the next reconciliation and uses that token.

```
spec:
  vault:
    reinitInterval: 30m
    requestInterval: 1m
```

Learn more in [Manage system users with Vault](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/system-users-vault.html).

## CRD Changes

- The `.status.oci.credentials.secretName` field has now the minimum length of `1` and maximum length of `253`. An empty name is rejected, and a name longer than 253 characters is rejected.
- The `status.oci.credentials` field requires the `secretName` to be present when `credentials.type` is `userPrincipal`.
- New fields added:
- `sharding.mongos.logs.persistentVolumeClaim` to configure persistent log storage for `mongos` Pods.
- `vault.requestInterval` and `vault.reinitInterval` to control Vault password-read and client reinitialization intervals.

## Changelog

### New Features

- [K8SPSMDB-1795](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPSMDB-1795) - Added persistent logging for `mongos` Pods so you can keep query router logs after a Pod restart or rollout. Those logs survive a restart only when you configure `sharding.mongos.logs.persistentVolumeClaim`.

### Improvements

- [K8SPSMDB-1778](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPSMDB-1778) - Added Custom Resource options so you can set how often the Operator reads system user passwords from HashiCorp Vault and how often it creates a new Vault client to sign in. A longer `vault.requestInterval` sends fewer Vault requests when passwords change infrequently, `vault.reinitInterval` can match short-lived tokens (default 30 minutes), and an update to `vault.syncUsers.tokenSecret` applies on the next reconciliation.

### Bug Fixes

- [K8SPSMDB-1794](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPSMDB-1794) - Fixed Percona ClusterSync target connection failures caused by a missing slash in the generated MongoDB URI. The Operator now writes a valid `target-uri` so Percona ClusterSync for MongoDB can connect to the target cluster.
- [K8SPSMDB-1817](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPSMDB-1817) - Fixed a deadlock where Smart Update stayed blocked while Percona ClusterSync for MongoDB (PCSM) held the cluster lease and scheduled backups sat in Waiting. Smart Update no longer waits forever on backups that are parked because PCSM is replicating.
- [K8SPSMDB-1834](https://perconadev.atlassian.net/browse/K8SPSMDB-1834) - Fixed endless Smart Update Pod restarts after you upgrade from Operator 1.22 to 1.23 when `spec.tls.issuerConf.kind` is `ClusterIssuer`. The Operator now keeps leaf certificate `issuerRef.kind` set to `ClusterIssuer`, so cert-manager no longer reissues those certificates in a loop.

## Supported software

The Operator was developed and tested with the following software:

- Percona Server for MongoDB 6.0.29-23, 7.0.43-23, and 8.0.32-14
- Percona Backup for MongoDB 2.15.0
- PMM3 Client: 3.9.1
- cert-manager: 1.21.0
- LogCollector based on fluent-bit: 5.1.2-1

Other options may also work but have not been tested.

## Supported platforms

Percona Operators are designed for compatibility with all [CNCF-certified](https://www.cncf.io/training/certification/software-conformance/) Kubernetes distributions. Our release process includes targeted testing and validation on major cloud provider platforms and OpenShift, as detailed below:

- [Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE)](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine) 1.34 - 1.35
- [Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS)](https://aws.amazon.com) 1.34 - 1.36
- [Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS)](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/services/kubernetes-service/) 1.34 - 1.36
- [OpenShift Container Platform](https://www.redhat.com/en/technologies/cloud-computing/openshift) 4.19 - 4.22
- [Rancher](https://www.rancher.com/) with Rancher Kubernetes Engine (RKE2) 1.34 - 1.36
- [Minikube](https://github.com/kubernetes/minikube) 1.39.0 with Kubernetes v1.37.0

This list only includes the platforms that the Percona Operators are specifically tested on as part of the release process. Other Kubernetes flavors and versions depend on the backward compatibility offered by Kubernetes itself.

# Percona Operator for MongoDB 1.23.0 (2026-07-23)

[Get started with the Operator](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/quickstart.html) [Upgrade](https://docs.percona.com/percona-operator-for-mongodb/1.23.1/update.html)
